News.title: Face coverings ban and police given special powers ahead of Southampton anti-migrant protest
News.content:
Face coverings ban and police given special powers ahead of Southampton anti-migrant protest

Anti-migrants protests are set to take place on the south coast with police warning demonstrators not to wear face coverings with a dispersal order in place

View Image Masked men previously blocked vehicles attempting to enter or leave the Port of Dover (Image: Toby Mackenzie)

Demonstrators have been warned that face coverings are banned and police have been given special powers ahead of expected anti-migrant protests on the south coast.

‌



‌



Anti-migration protesters South Coast Patriots and anti-racism demonstrators from Southampton Stand Up To Racism are expected to gather today in Southampton where a dispersal order and a ban on face coverings will be in place.

‌



Similar scenes are expected to unfold in Dover, in Kent. South Coast Patriots is not among the regional groups listed on its website as affiliates of Patriot Platform, the network founded by anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas – known to his supporters as Danny Tommo.

‌



Meanwhile, online posts advertising the protest in Dover carry the name English Defence League and the Patriot Platform affiliate Kent Patriots posted on Instagram stating their members would not attend.

It comes after major disruption was caused last month when hundreds of masked activists dressed in black and wearing face coverings blocked roads in an anti-migrant demonstration, stopping traffic going in and out of the port.

Video circulated online showed dozens of men gathered at the port on September 5 and the Port of Dover confirmed that the disruption is affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town. And since then there have been similar protests on the south coast notably in Portsmouth.

‌



Hampshire Police said officers have been given additional policing powers and several restrictions have been placed on the protesting groups.

Those taking part in the Patriots procession must follow a specific route and cannot make any stops, while the counter-protest has been allocated a specific location and is not permitted to travel south of the Bargate.

An area known as a "neutral zone" will ensure the two groups will not come into contact with each other during the demonstrations, police have said. The Stand Up To Racism group's procession will start after the South Coast Patriots group has passed.

‌



A message from Superintendent Alex Charge, district commander for Southampton, posted on the force's website, said officers have implemented a dispersal order under Section 34 of the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 to cover a specific area from 7pm on Friday until 7am on Sunday.

He said: "The order gives officers the power to order a person to leave the area, with no return within a specified time period. Those who refuse to comply with the order are committing a criminal offence and are liable for arrest.

"Powers under Section 158 of the Crime and Policing Act 2025 will be in place across the same area as the Section 34, but between 11am and 5pm on Saturday October 3. This prohibits the wearing of face coverings used to conceal identity during any protest activity.

‌



"This will assist in preventing offences, increasing public confidence, protecting communities, and supporting the lawful exercise of democratic rights by all participants.

"Failing to comply with the conditions is an offence and can lead to arrest. Police have spoken with the protests’ organisers. They are aware of the conditions and will share these with those attending."

Southampton Itchen MP Darren Paffey said anyone out to cause disorder should stay away, and people in Southampton "will not welcome so-called patriots flocking to our city to whip up fear and division".

‌



He added: "Whatever their intentions, these protests make local residents feel unsafe in their own communities, and that’s unacceptable. While people have a right to protest, that doesn’t extend to causing disruption and intimidation. Anyone who just wants to stir up disorder should stay away and should be dealt with firmly if they do not."

Kent Police said "robust" preparations are in place to keep disruption to a minimum ahead of the demonstration in Dover. The force said a "substantial" number of highly-trained officers will be stationed in the town centre on Saturday.

A counter-protest will be held at Pencester Gardens although officers "anticipate the two groups may attempt to come together". Police announced a face covering ban will be in force on Saturday from 8am to 9pm and will apply to those taking part in the protest.

Article continues below

It covers parts of Dover, including Buckland, Whitfield, Guston, St Margaret's-at-Cliffe and surrounding areas. People covering their faces for religious, health or work-related reasons are not affected.

Detective Chief Superintendent Elly Maggs, east division commander, said: "Everyone has a right to peaceful protest but that right is not unlimited, and we will not tolerate anyone who acts in a violent or criminal manner. If you are coming to Dover intent on causing trouble, then you will be arrested and brought before the courts."

News.title: Widdecombe suspect charged with planning terror act against Farage
News.content:
The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Counter terror police said Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts.

The charge relates to activity which is alleged to have taken place between May 2024 and July 2026.

Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she knew the fresh charge would be "extremely concerning" and her "profound sympathies" were with Farage and his family.

"Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.

"This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve."

The BBC contacted Reform UK for comment and a party source said: "This is exactly why Nigel needed Â£5m to protect his security for life."

Farage is currently facing a parliamentary standards watchdog probe into a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor before he returned as an MP in 2024. The Reform leader has previously said the money was for his personal security.

Deputy leader of Reform UK, Richard Tice, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the murder of Ann Widdecombe had made everyone take security more seriously.

"What's particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him [Farage] is sometimes he's not been believed, not been listened to."

Tice added that he personally had security arrangements in place and his habits had changed which was a "consequence of the world we live in" arguing the "online world has clearly hindered this whole process".

Asked if Reform had done enough to dial the temperature down and whether comments from politicians added to public anger, Tice said "the passions that flow through democratic debate should be completely separate to the way that people respond

"It's the nature of democracy... it's part of the joy of it is that there will be robust debate but at the end of it one should be able to shake hands."

Counter Terrorism Policing Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said the charge on Friday was the result of a "hugely intensive and complex investigation".

"This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge," she added.

Kerry, from Rotherham, is due to appear in court over the terror charge on Wednesday, police said.

Frank Ferguson of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division said prosecutors "worked closely" with police to bring the charge and would continue to work alongside them as the investigation continued.

Widdecombe was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing and would later become a Reform UK spokeswoman.

News.title: Woman deceived ex-partner that she had given birth to his babies, judge rules
News.content:
A woman convinced her former partner she had given birth to two children who most likely did not exist in what a High Court judge described as an "extraordinary" and "elaborate campaign of deceit".

The man, who has not been named but was referred to as John in the judgement, applied to the Family Court after he was told the woman had sold their two children for a combined Â£500.

The case heard that the man received messages and photos of the children and paid the woman around Â£30,000 over the course of two years.

But in a hearing in February, the woman, who was referred to as Jane, told the judge she had lied about the pregnancies for revenge, claiming the man had abused her.

The court heard the man believed he was the children's' father because in late 2022 his partner told him she was pregnant, sent pictures of an ultrasound image and had become "visibly pregnant" as time went on.

In May 2023, shortly before the first baby was due, the woman called the police alleging she had been assaulted by the man.

He was arrested and subsequently held on remand for several months, Mrs Justice Judd said in her ruling which was published on Friday.

Following this, the woman sent a message to his stepfather saying the baby had been born as well as sharing baby photos.

At one stage she is said to have sent voice notes to her former partner's mother in the middle of the night with the sound of a baby crying in the background.

Later, she told the man she was pregnant again and the baby was due in August 2024.

However, before the due date, the couple split up and did not reconcile.

The woman would go on to tell the man's mother the baby had been born.

The woman admitted to the court she had told him she was pregnant when they were together, and afterwards, but conceded she had told a series of elaborate lies and that there were, in fact, no children.

She argued she was menopausal at the time and could not have been pregnant and bank statements show she attended a tanning shop on the day she said she had given birth, Mrs Justice Judd said.

In her judgement, the judge concluded that the "factors that weigh against the children genuinely existing were very strong, stronger than the factors pointing the other way".

She said the man was the victim of a "sustained and elaborate campaign of deceit" which also impacted his mother and closest friend.

"Added to this, the behaviour was cruel, leading a man and his mother to believe they had children and grandchildren respectively.", the Judge said.

The judge added she was unable to conclude the woman's motive for her behaviour but said financial fraud was a "possibility" and that the "complex mental health problems" she suffered from may have also played a part.

News.title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
News.content:
The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.

Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis.

Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off.

Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October.

That is the equivalent of about Â£60 per year - or Â£5 per month - taking an annual bill to Â£1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to Â£1,999.

News.title: Traitors claim their first victim as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the second episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

A comedian, a journalist, an actor and a TV presenter walk into a church. But sadly, the punchline for one of them was becoming the first victim of this year's Celebrity Traitors.

As Friday's episode got under way, a delicious new twist saw traitors Richard E Grant and Maya Jama invite James Acaster to join them in the turret, and simultaneously murder a fellow player.

Unfortunately, it fell to Amol Rajan to become the Paloma Faith of this series - being taken away in a coffin in episode two before even having the chance to take part in a banishment.

"It's gutting to be the first out," Rajan said afterwards, noting that perhaps it was because he had been "a bit bullish with Richard" earlier in the day.

"But you know what, games are games, and just as there are winners, so there have to be losers."

The next morning, presenter Claudia Winkleman confirmed the University Challenge host's murder to the other players, joking: "That's what I call a starter for 10."

Acaster, meanwhile, reflected: "I'm gutted to not be a faithful anymore, I don't like lying. But if I don't join them, they'll kill me." You can't fault his logic.

The decision meant that Grant, an Oscar-nominated actor with a Razzie-worthy traitor strategy, did at least manage to commit one successful murder despite his shambolic first day.

News.title: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
News.content:
Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.

Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.

It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.

Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.

So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?

Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.

It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.

"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.

News.title: Spoiler alert! How music fans and artists are staying ahead of gig reveals
News.content:
Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.

You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view.

When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings.

But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.

Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online.

Tours by Harry Styles, Charli XCX and Ariana Grande have also been filmed from every angle and shared over the past few months.

While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise.

News.title: Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'
News.content:
Hayden and Savannah had never set foot in Scotland before they decided it was the perfect place to get married last May.

The couple, from Pennsylvania in the US, wanted a destination wedding that would take their family and friends on an adventure with them.

They considered locations across Europe, before deciding on Scotland after Savannah saw photographs of a castle wedding online.

"I think it was on Pinterest," she said. "Somebody got married in a castle and I was like 'Oh, I have to do that'."

The pair are far from alone in seeing Scotland as the ultimate romantic destination.

News.title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
News.content:
For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity.

With just two months left of the defined hurricane season, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all.

This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane.

The biggest reason for this is El NiÃ±o, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific.

The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this.

With a very strong El NiÃ±o forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes.

September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity.

But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic.

News.title: Men charged over alleged plot to target Manchester Jewish community
News.content:
Two Iranian nationals who arrived in the UK by small boat have been charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester.

Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool, are accused of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on or before 20 September.

The men were arrested in Manchester's Northern Quarter on the eve of Yom Kippur, considered the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said news that two Iranian men had been charged over the alleged plot would be "deeply distressing" to Manchester's Jewish community, as the city marks one year since the Heaton Park Synagogue attack.

Counter Terrorism Police (CTP) allege the two men were in contact with a third-party overseas, who may be in Iran, in relation to the plot.

According to CTP, the men are accused of obtaining instructions to make a chlorine bomb, acquiring liquids, components and equipment for such a device, researching potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the suspects had arrived via small boat in 2020 and 2023. One was granted asylum, and the other has a live asylum claim.

She added: "These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors.

"Two suspects have been charged with planning a terrorist attack against Jewish communities in Manchester.

"This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

"I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue.

"The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further on this case. But I can say that we will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security."

News.title: Tories pledge to build 50,000 new prison places
News.content:
The Conservatives have promised to build 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales to stop criminals being released early, if they return to government.

The party said it would cost Â£2bn per year to build and run the new prisons, funded by spending cuts including to the foreign aid budget.

On Thursday hundreds of prisoners were released early, under new rules introduced to prevent jails reaching capacity, with around 4,500 due to be freed by next summer.

Labour blamed the previous Tory government for leaving "our criminal justice system at breaking point" and said the party's proposals were not "credible".

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday.

Prisons in England and Wales have been running close to capacity for years, with the latest government figures showing they are 98% full.

Under the latest early release scheme, eligible prisoners can now be released on a community licence after serving one-third of their jail sentence.

Those excluded include prisoners convicted of murder, manslaughter, a sexual or grooming-related offence, or a driving offence that led to a death.

The government has also effectively scrapped one-year jail terms.

The Tories said they would use extra prison capacity to reverse these measures.

An early release programme introduced by the previous Conservative government saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024.

News.title: King's Caribbean tour will not shy away from 'darkest days of our past'
News.content:
King Charles's upcoming Caribbean tour will not shy away from "the darkest days of our past", Buckingham Palace has said.

During the visits, the King is expected to face renewed calls to apologise for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade and be questioned on potential reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade.

The King and Queen Camilla are set to travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, with visits also to Bahamas and Guyana as part of the eight-day trip starting on October 27.

According to PA news agency, it is understood the government has not advised the King to apologise or offer reparations.

News.title: Met Police urge students to move 7 October protest
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police is calling on the organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march planned to take place on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks on Israel to move the event.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman said the force had been unable to identify the organisers behind the group, which calls itself the University of London Coalition.

He said that while the march did not meet the strict legal threshold at which police could request the home secretary to ban a protest, many Londoners would be marking "a day of mourning" with vigils to remember those who died.

The BBC has contacted the group for comment via social media accounts they appear to be associated with.

Harman said around 300 students were expected to march through central London, from King's College London in the Strand on Wednesday, finishing at University College London in Holborn.

He said they had demanded an end to what they described as a "genocide in Gaza".

"Serious concerns have been expressed about the impact of this march on students and staff, particularly those who are Jewish, the route, and the day it is being held," Harman said.

He urged anyone intending to join the protest to "reflect on the impact and distress it will cause on this very significant day, and exercise your right to protest on a different date".

Harman said the force had written to four London universities to ask them to engage with their students and staff and to take "all reasonable steps" to ensure students did not feel "excluded, targeted or unsafe" due to activity on their premises.

He said the letter acknowledged "the importance of freedom of expression, peaceful protest and academic debate" but also pointed to findings from the Community Security Trust over a rise in antisemitic incidents at UK universities since the attacks in 2023.

News.title: Man jailed for piloting small boat carrying 26 others
News.content:
A man has been jailed for 18 months for piloting a small boat carrying 26 other people, including six children, towards the Kent coast.

Jemal Abdela, 32, was sentenced after pleading guilty to the offence of endangering others during a sea crossing to the UK without valid entry clearance on July 25.

Winchester Crown Court heard Abdela, who is Eritrean, had also attempted to disguise the fact he had been driving the black inflatable across the Channel when it was approached by immigration officers.

A Home Office spokesman said Abdela was the 20th small boat pilot to be imprisoned in four months for endangering lives at sea.

Matthew Parris, prosecuting, told the court that the defendant was seen piloting the boat, which was being followed by French authorities.

He said Abdela had "dived into the centre of the boat and moved to another location wearing a hat" before being identified, adding that the vessel did not have flares, GPS or maps onboard.

The court heard that Abdela told police he had paid â¬800 (Â£680) for the crossing, which had begun at 17:00 BST the previous day.

He also claimed to have been sat by the captain of the boat, but was then made to take over control of the vessel by the other passengers.

News.title: Daniel Thomas in court accused of entering migrant site
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has appeared in court charged with entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, is accused of committing the offence on 31 March, according to court documents.

Thomas is further accused of using threatening words or behaviour in the Kent town on 1 April and obstructing a person engaged in a lawful activity on 6 April.

He is also charged with entering or remaining in Dover Docks without having lawful business or permission, the documents say.

Thomas faces another charge of racially aggravated harassment by allegedly using threatening or abusive words.

He appeared at Margate Magistrates' Court on Friday via videolink wearing a grey T-shirt and rosary beads.

District Judge William Nelson sent his case for a further case management hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 4 November.

Earlier this week, Thomas was refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel.

News.title: 'No jobs on a dead planet' - ex-commissioner defends helping scrap M4 relief road
News.content:
Howe said the debate over the M4 road had not played out as a simple "economy versus environment argument", and instead included questions over how it would fit in with things like making a healthier Wales, how it would boost social interactions, and how it would be in line with a more equal country.

"Because 25% of the lowest income families in this region don't own a car," she said. "So are you saying you're spending the entire of the government's borrowing capacity building something that benefits only the already better off?"

She said she "probably" would have taken the government to court had it gone ahead with the relief road and a Section 20 Review, external to make sure it fit in with wellbeing goals - but that in the end she "didn't actually have to".

"The public arguments that we had, I suppose, were enough," she said, and agreed with the interviewer that she had an ally in Drakeford.

Drakeford said in 2019 he would not have gone ahead with the road even if it had been affordable, saying he "took a different view" to a planning inspector who had concluded the project would not have a disproportionately harmful impact.

The inspector's report criticised Howe, saying that a suggestion by her that the inquiry had not properly considered future generations legislation "were and are wholly unwarranted".

It said the M4 scheme had been "anything but short term", stating it had been a "long-term solution to long-term needs".

News.title: UK diesel prices top £2 a litre for first time, RAC says
News.content:
The average price of diesel has risen above Â£2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group.

Diesel has now hit an average of 200.01p a litre, the RAC said, and petrol prices are also still rising, reaching 174.71p a litre on average.

The motoring group said price rises were "showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery onto motorists".

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide.

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refiners have further constrained supplies of diesel on the world market. China has also restricted exports of refined fuels.

Separately on Friday, G7 nations agreed at an urgent meeting to release 100 million barrels of oil to head off further price increases.

The G7 also agreed member countries would not impose export restrictions on each other, after US President Donald Trump threatened to ban shipments of American diesel overseas.

The move would have pushed up global prices of the fuel, but helped ease pressure on US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections.

RAC policy head Simon Williams said Â£2 was a "price threshold no one wanted to cross".

"This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders," he added.

UK businesses and consumers already feel like they are bearing the brunt of higher prices, with many saying it has made their lives increasingly difficult.

Even people who do not drive a diesel vehicle themselves face a knock-on effect from rising delivery costs or the higher cost of producing food.

Nigel Farage has “not been listened to” over his safety concerns, Richard Tice has said after the man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe was also charged with a terror plot against the Reform leader.

Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts relating to alleged activity between May 31 2024 and July 8 2026, Counter Terrorism Policing said on Friday.

Mr Tice, Reform UK’s deputy leader, said the allegations were “particularly upsetting for those of us in and around (Mr Farage)”, and would make politicians take potential threats against them more seriously.

Reform spokeswoman and former Tory minister Ms Widdecombe, 78, died on July 8 after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard.

open image in gallery Reform UK’s Richard Tice (left) has spoken of alleged safety concerns for his party leader Nigel Farage (PA) ( PA Archive )

Kerry, of Byrley Road, Rotherham, South Yorkshire, is also accused of her murder, and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Mr Tice said: “When actually things occur that are very close to home, so to speak it’s pretty shocking and makes one take a a big intake of breath.”

He continued: “(Mr Farage’s) security and the risks to it, he’s talked about over over many times, many occasions, over many years.

“And I think what’s particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him is sometimes he’s not being believed, not being listened to, and you know we have just got in a sense deep regret over everything that’s happened over a long period of time.”

Asked if Mr Farage had met with the Home Office to discuss his security, Mr Tice said: “A number of meetings have taken place with a number of people at the higher level of Reform.

“The information and intel I now get about the threats in and around myself and others is a very significant shift in the approach taken by the authorities, and we appreciate that.”

In August, CTP reopened a year-long probe into an alleged firebomb attack at Mr Farage’s home in south London.

The Metropolitan Police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary”, but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

open image in gallery Court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Joshua Kerry, 28 ( PA Wire )

Following its reopening, CTP London identified a line of inquiry which it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), previously said they were investigating the “conduct” of a CTP London staff member after an allegation that the employee “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry”.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said her “profound sympathies” are with Mr Farage and his family, and said the development “raises serious questions about the security of those in public life”.

She said she will update MPs on work to strengthen protections for them when Parliament returns later this month.

India completed a golden double in ​the Asian Games cricket after the men's team beat arch rivals Pakistan by 19 runs in the final in Nisshin.

The Twenty20 world champions piled up 211-6, the highest total of the Aichi-Nagoya Games, thanks to blistering half-centuries from opener Abhishek Sharma (61) and Tilak Varma, who smashed 51 not out off 22 balls. Hasan Nawaz's defiant 96 kept Pakistan in the hunt, but they finished on 192-6.

Abhishek took charge after India captain Shreyas Iyer chose to bat at the Korogi Sports Park. Pakistan opened with spin from both ends, but Saad Masood was pulled from the attack after his first over went ⁠for 24.

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, who had hit Masood for two sixes, botched a reverse `sweep against Saim Ayub and was caught behind. Ayub sent the 15-year-old off with a rocking-baby celebration. Sanju Samson soon followed, but Abhishek, ranked second in the world among T20 ‌batters, raced to a 20-ball fifty with ‌a burst of big hitting.

open image in gallery Abhishek Sharma blasted India to an imposing total ( Reuters )

It was far from a chanceless innings though. Abhishek survived a run-out chance, and in one over he twice hit shots that landed agonisingly short of Ayub. He struck seven sixes and three fours in his 28-ball knock before Arafat Minhas had him stumped in the eighth over, ending the onslaught.

The sixes dried up after that, but India were well placed at 114-3 at the halfway mark. Minhas then bowled Ishan Kishan, but Varma, who reached his fifty in 21 balls, took India past 200 with a late ‌surge.

Chasing 212, Pakistan needed a fast start but limped to 76-3 at the halfway stage instead. Jasprit Bumrah kept things tight, ‌and spinner Axar Patel removed Usman ⁠Khan and Maaz Sadaqat (23) to leave Pakistan struggling.

Nawaz kept their `hopes alive but got little support and fell to the last ball of the match. Earlier, Sri ‌Lanka beat Bangladesh ​by 63 runs to take bronze.

India's women won gold after beating Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final on September 22.

Formula 1 returns to a fan-favourite circuit this weekend as the Sepang circuit in Malaysia hosts the Bahrain Grand Prix in a one-off event.

George Russell got his season back on track with a first victory in three months at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix last time out, pipping Max Verstappen to the line to narrow the deficit on championship leader and Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli to 66 points.

Antonelli, who crashed out of qualifying, recovered from the back of the grid to finish fifth while Isack Hadjar joined Verstappen on the podium on a positive day for Red Bull. However, it was a tricky day for McLaren and Ferrari, who both struggled for form and pace.

As for this weekend, Bahrain’s original grand prix date in April was cancelled due to the war in the Middle East. The Gulf country have, however, opted to pay the hosting fees to have their name attached to Sepang’s return to the calendar for the first time in nine years this weekend.

Latvians are electing a new parliament on Saturday as pro-Ukraine Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs seeks a full term. The vote comes as the small republic on NATO's eastern flank contends with growing concern about potential Russian aggression.

A political crisis in May over the handling of stray drones suspected to be from Ukraine brought down the governing coalition that had been under strain due to multiple other issues. The parliament, or Saeima, then approved a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs of the centrist United List party, previously in opposition.

Latvia, like its Baltic neighbors Lithuania and Estonia, strongly supports Ukraine in its fight against Moscow’s invasion. It borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus.

Kulbergs, 47, is now seeking his own mandate from voters.

A multiparty coalition will almost certainly be needed to govern in a splintered political landscape. Parties must take at least 5% of the vote to win parliamentary seats.

Nearly 1.56 million people in the nation of more than 1.8 million are entitled to choose the 100 members of the single-chamber Saeima for a four-year term.

Concern about potential Russian hybrid attacks — a term used for non-conventional hostile acts such as sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and an array of other methods — has been mounting across parts of Europe in recent months; Latvia, among other nations on NATO’s eastern edge, is particularly exposed.

NATO has reinforced its protection of Latvian airspace for the election period, with Germany sending four Eurofighter jets to Latvia for about a week.

The Latvian State Security Service said last week that it hadn't yet detected any significant or systematic efforts by Russia or others to influence the election in favor of any party or candidate, the LETA news agency reported.

Polls are expected to close at 1700 GMT.

Broadcaster Amol Rajan has reflected on his short-lived stint on the new series of The Celebrity Traitors, conceding that he played "the wrong game" after becoming the debut participant to be murdered on the show.

The 43-year-old was targeted during Friday's episode of the BBC reality show by secret traitors, actor Richard E Grant and TV presenter Maya Jama. Meanwhile, comedian James Acaster was brought in as the third traitor for the series.

During Thursday's broadcast, Rajan and Acaster had met Grant and Jama to argue why they should be recruited rather than eliminated.

Appearing on spin-off show The Celebrity Traitors: Uncloaked on Friday, Rajan said: "It’s hard not to watch it and think I, obviously, with 20/20 hindsight, I played the wrong game.

"That was a crazy, crazy once-in-a-lifetime (opportunity)."

The former Today Show presenter explained that he felt he would have performed well as a traitor if given the chance to switch sides.

open image in gallery The Traitors chose to recruit James Acaster over Amol Rajan ( BBC )

He said: "Obviously, I wish I’d been chosen, and I wish I’d been a traitor.

"I can say, hand on heart, that if I’d been chosen as a traitor in the first, when Maya and Richard were, if I got the nod or the tap at the roundtable, I think it would have thrown me a bit.

"I’d be like, ‘what am I doing? what’s going on?’, having genuinely spent a day as a faithful, if I’d then been recruited, I think I would have been quite a good traitor because I’d actually known what it was like to be a faithful."

Following his exit, the journalist suggested Acaster would prove to be "brilliant" in his new role.

Rajan acknowledged that entering the game as "the journalist who asks all the awkward questions" meant he had warned himself to "shut up" in an effort to avoid being murdered or banished early on.

Friday’s instalment ended on a suspenseful note after Grant drew significant suspicion at the roundtable.

open image in gallery Scrutiny of Richard E Grant intensified in Friday’s episode at the first round table ( PA )

The actor had accidentally revealed his traitor identity to several participants shortly after discovering his role in Thursday’s episode.

Discussing Grant's slip-up, Rajan said: "What was that about? I mean no one’s ever done that. I mean who knows?

"I think the one tactic that you should try to abide by is to keep a little bit, you know, fly under the radar a little bit for the first few days. Just shut up for the first few shows."

The Celebrity Traitors returns on Thursday at 8pm on BBC One and iPlayer.

Wall Street has a busy week ahead with a mix of economic updates and details about the Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates at its most recent meeting.

The updates include fresh data on the health of the services sector, unemployment and consumer sentiment. Those reports can help give investors and economists more insight into how businesses and households are adapting to persistently high inflation. The minutes from the Fed's last meeting will also give Wall Street more details about the central bank's decision-making process for interest rate policy.

On Monday, the Institute for Supply Management will releases its monthly service sector index for September. The sector makes up the bulk of U.S. economic activity, and the report focuses on whether it is expanding.

On Wednesday, Wall Street will get more details on the decision-making process behind the Fed's interest rate increase at its previous meeting. The minutes from that meeting could provide insight into what the central bank thinks about inflation and the job market and how they factor into interest rate policy.

On Thursday, Wall Street will get its weekly update on unemployment claims, which remain historically low. They are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed.

On Friday, the University of Michigan releases its consumer sentiment survey for October. It measures how consumers feel about the economy. The September survey showed that households are worried about higher fuel prices and stubbornly high inflation.

When the first reports about a diverted flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv came through on Wednesday, it appeared to have been caused by a tussle between two pilots.

Early claims even suggested one was Russian and the other Ukrainian.

But, in the age of social media, the true chaos aboard the FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 quickly came to light. Footage and images sent from the plane by blood-covered passengers showed them overpowering the co-pilot, who it later emerged was an Omani national.

The plane, a Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, was carrying over 170 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it plunged more than 17,000ft in two minutes as the fight broke out. An emergency alert was sent out and the plane changed course towards Jordan, eventually landing in Saudi Arabia.

open image in gallery Passengers onboard the Flydubai flight revealed what was happening in bloody social media posts ( Social media )

Aviation experts told the BBC that the rapid descent led to damage pictured on the plane’s rudder adding that the incident could easily have led to the plane breaking up in mid-air.

Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was identified as the victim of the attack, while his arrested co-pilot was identified as Hamam al-Hammami on Saturday by sources cited in CNN.

The motive for the incident is still being determined but Netanyahu’s administration suggested early on that it was a suspected terror attack.

open image in gallery Cpt Smit Machchhar was attacked by his co-pilot as passengers overwhelmed the attacker. Both were pictured covered in blood ( Social media )

‘Blood everywhere’

A six-year-old on her way to the toilet accompanied by her mother, was the first to raise the alarm when the pair heard shouting coming from the cockpit, prompting cabin crew to rush to the scene. What they saw was a blood-spattered scene.

“There was blood all over the cockpit and very, very sharp fighting moves,” Nina Manes’ mother, Tali Manes told Israel’s Channel 12.

“I screamed, ‘He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!’ People looked at me and didn’t understand.”

Her husband Tzvika Manes said: “The shrieks of my daughters when the plane nose-dived [are still with me]. They said, ‘Dad we don’t want to die.’ [Their cries] were the triggers that caused me to run inside the cockpit.”

open image in gallery The flight had been headed from Dubai to Tel Aviv but was diverted to Saudi Arabia ( Flightradar24.com )

One passenger recorded the ordeal on his phone and later shared the footage to social media. With blood dripping down his face, he declared that the passengers had “subdued the terrorists”. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” he added.

On Saturday, UAE prosecutors said Cpt Machchhar had been attacked by a “crash axe”, a tool kept in the cockpit in case of emergencies, bypassing stringent security protocols.

Yaniv Hayun, a 50-year-old owner of a sewage plumbing company, was travelling with his wife and two daughters when the incident took place.

In his blood-spattered t-shirt, he was hailed as a hero by Netanyahu who personally thanked him for helping to subdue the attacker and to prevent the plane from crashing.

Along with Tzvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan, he broke into the cockpit to stop the attacker. By mimicking gestures he says he’d see on television, Hayun “grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles”. He said he’d learned the techniques from watching Air Crash Investigation.

open image in gallery A six-year-old girl played a crucial role in preventing disaster when she asked to go to the toilet at the same time as the attack took place ( Channel 12 )

He said it took 20 to 25 minutes to fully subdue and bind the pilot and they used cords from headphones linked to the plane’s entertainment system.

Hayun was helped by a dentist, Dr Shota Musayev, who administered “life-saving medical treatment” to Cpt Machchhar, including treating him for severe wounds to his head and cuts to his fingers. He helped to successfully stop the bleeding and to stabilise his blood pressure before emergency surgery.

All five are expected to receive Israel’s Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, president Isaac Herzog said on Thursday.

Both pilots have been transferred to the UAE for further investigations and for medical treatment.

‘Suicidal and indoctrinated’

Netanyahu told Fox News that the attacker was “suicidal” and called out to the crew: “kill me, kill me!” after he was subdued.

“It’s clear he was suicidal, that’s not a question,” he added. The Israeli leader said that he had undergone a “Islamist radical indoctrination” and promised to reveal whether he had connections to Iran in the coming days.

The prime minister said those onboard managed to “prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening”, claiming that the intent may have been to crash the plane.

A regional official familiar with the FlyDubai investigation told the Associated Press that investigators in Saudi Arabia were working with authorities from the UAE, US, Oman and Israel, and that “all possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into”.

“Nothing is ruled out for now”, the official said.

open image in gallery Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national and flydubai pilot who was stabbed by a colleague aboard a plane, told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi about the ordeal on a video call ( Reuters )

Al-Hammami was banned from flying last year over concerns that he had radical ideological views, according to Saudi state media.

Two Israeli security officials said that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, according to their initial assessments.

He was arrested by Saudi security forces after the plane landed in Tabuk, northwest Saudi Arabia, and was being questioned by investigators.

On Saturday, the UAE prosecutor general said that al-Hammami had attempted to carry out a “terrorist” attack, according to the country’s state news agency WAM.

Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.

Netanyahu said: “It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue.”

open image in gallery Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meets with Yaniv Hayoun, Or Fradilov, Dr. Shota Musayev and his wife, Sigalit, who he described as heroes for helping prevent disaster ( Reuters )

Warnings and questions over security

Opposition leader Yair Lapid said on Wednesday that politicians had been warned in a national security briefing the night before that Israel’s enemies could attack in the run up to the country’s elections due to take place on 27 October.

A ban on pilots from states without formal relations to Israel was not enforced appropriately, according to a report cited by the Times of Israel.

Under the law, pilots from nations including Oman, which does not have formal ties with Israel, were banned from flying but airlines and security agencies did not enforce the rule.

open image in gallery Assaf Regavim, who filmed the first widely circulated video from inside the cabin and helped overpower the pilot ( Getty )

Furthermore, Israel’s security agency, Shin Bet, had raised concerns about flights from the UAE for months before the incident.

Shin Bet director David Zini had reportedly clashed with Israeli airlines over restrictions on flights to the UAE, reasoning that security measures at Emirati airports were insufficient, according to Israel’s N12 News.

Israeli authorities were concerned with possible missile attacks or attacks at an airport, the outlet reported on Thursday. A scenario like Wednesday’s hijacking attempt was “not raised in any discussion”, they said.

News.title: Bath complete revenge mission on Exeter despite imperious Feyi-Waboso
News.content:
Bath held off a furious Exeter comeback led by the irrepressible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso to avenge their Gallagher Prem semi-final defeat here in June.

It felt as if lightning might strike Bath twice. Once again Exeter overturned a 26-10 half-time deficit, to manufacture a second-half lead thanks to a pair of blistering finishes by Feyi-Waboso. Four months ago, Bath failed to take a drop goal in the closing stages, but this time with the reassuring presence of Finn Russell at fly-half, they kept their cool.

The Scotland playmaker twice sent penalties deep into the Exeter 22 from where Stephen Varney conceded a yellow card and penalty try before Bath replacement Ted Hill powered through a thicket of Exeter tacklers.

“Finn is one of the world’s best 10s in the world and I thought he had a very good game,” Bath head of rugby Johann van Graan said. “His decision making is above most players in the world and I thought that came through tonight.”

Despite the appearance of yet another high-scoring shootout, both teams defended with real bite, although Bath struggled to lay a finger on Feyi-Waboso who ended up in a scrap with a fan in the stands here when he was a spectator in May. He exacted a measure of revenge beating eight defenders and carried for 132 metres.

“Manny still needs game time,” Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter said. “When he’s on the ball, you see something incredible, but it is ability to get on the ball again is just getting his game minutes and match fitness up.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco, which is placed between the cheek and lower gum, is particularly popular in south Asia. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Eight tips for improving your laptop’s performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

News.title: Lethal Trent Alexander-Arnold sends Tuchel a statement in England victory
News.content:
Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

I knew exactly where I wanted to go, where I needed to go but I needed some guidance. I think the same way as him [Jude]. We don’t think there’s any limit on what we can achieve, wanting to win, wanting to win in a good way by going for the throat. Fearlessness.

It ate me up for a good couple of weeks after [losing the semi-final]. I’d scored… on the same pitch as Messi, the man I idolised as a kid. It was the highest possible moment of my entire life. And within 20 minutes it had come completely crashing down. There’s been a lot of controversy, a lot of talk about that. Going forward, if we are going to lose a game, it’s going to be like how we lost to Spain. We went for their throats, we missed a penalty and lost the game. But the way we went for them, no regrets. I want to stay as far away from that [regret] as possible.

[Did you ever think you would sign for Barcelona?] Yes. No one ever achieves anything in life by playing it safe. My personality is based on being bold, taking risks and going for whatever you want.

At this level we’re all as talented as each other but only the most mentally competitive and driven people can maintain success for a long time.

I always thought in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never respected my quality and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick. In Barcelona if you’re not technical, if you’re not smart, you’d stand out like a sore thumb.

[Where do you see this squad in two years?] European champions.

THE UAE has threatened Andy Burnham with pulling billions of pounds out of a UK major tech project following Man City’s guilty verdict.

Labour ministers had courted investors for the “UK’s Silicon Valley” in the Oxford-Cambridge corridor, it is understood.



It comes after it was revealed the club’s chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, visited No10 to meet the business secretary just days before the Premier League’s ruling.

Abu Dhabi-owned City were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules after a four-year investigation.



The club artificially inflated its financial results by more than £900million and used “sham contracts”, according to the findings of an independent commission published on September 29.

MPs and tax experts say City may owe more than £20million and could face a criminal probe but the Premier League club deny any wrongdoing.



The UAE has reportedly warned the government that sanctions facing City risk impacting the Gulf state’s interest in future major investments.

It is now threatening to scrap billions of pounds of private investment for a hi-tech Silicon Valley-style hub between Oxford and Cambridge, reports The Telegraph.



This follows reports the bombshell dispute and subsequent fallout is appearing to sour broader diplomatic ties between the UK and the UAE.

The PM is facing mounting questions after it emerged his senior team met with City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak days before the club’s guilty verdicts.

Al Mubarak visited Downing Street on September 14 to meet Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds to discuss the UAE’s investments in Britain.

It’s understood the City supremo asked for the private meeting in his capacity as CEO of Mubadala Investment Company, the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund.

Insiders say he was given the red carpet treatment, met by one of Burnham’s special advisers, and whisked past security but insist there was no mentions of the on-going case.

Ministers are said to be convinced that senior individuals in the region must have known about the scale of the club’s financial misconduct despite earlier firm assurances that no rules were broken.



On Thursday, Downing Street insisted the guilty verdict against City is “serious”, after Andy Burnham was accused of making a “frankly extraordinary” intervention in support of the football club’s owners.

A No 10 spokesperson issued the statement after the Prime Minister said he would be “really concerned” to see the current owners sell up.

Over the past five years, the UAE has poured more than £30 billion into major UK sectors, including defence, life sciences and technology.

But the two nations are eager to maintain their financial partnership, and an investment summit is pencilled in for October.

City, who deny any wrongdoing and claim to have “irrefutable evidence” of their innocence, lodged an appeal yesterday on the day of the deadline.

The Prime Minister was previously blasted for saying he would be “really concerned” if they quit after the Premier League revealed a damning £900million of financial breaches.

But his comments — described as “extraordinary” by Tory critics — sparked fears of undue pressure placed on the government-backed football regulator, who may have to rule if City’s ownership model is “fit and proper”.

Mr Burnham rowed back amid mounting criticism. A No10 spokesperson said: “The Prime Minister has stressed it’s an ongoing independent process.

“It’s essential that it’s allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.



“Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.”

City’s owners spent hundreds of millions on housing and infrastructure projects in Manchester while Mr Burnham was mayor.

They include the £450million Co-Op live venue, a £200million football facility and £300million for the Etihad Stadium’s north stand.

There was also a £1billion, ten-year deal with the council to build up to 6,000 properties in Ancoats and New Islington, north-east of Manchester city centre.

Asked by the BBC earlier this week if he was worried about the current owners selling the club, Mr Burnham said: “I would be really concerned to lose them.

Sports.title: ‘Piece of c***’ – Man Utd flop Fred launches savage attack on former Red Devils boss who ‘fought with Cristiano Ronaldo’
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED flop Fred lambasted former manager Erik ten Hag by dubbing him a “piece of c***.”

The 33-year-old joined United in 2018 from Shakhtar Donetsk and spent five years at Old Trafford playing under the likes of Jose Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Ralf Rangnick and Ten Hag.



The midfielder, who now plays for Atletico Mineiro in his native Brazil, worked with the Dutch tactician for a year until his departure for Fenerbahce in 2023.

Fred was full of praise regarding the ex-Ajax boss’ tactical nous but didn’t hold back when it came to squad management.



He claimed Ten Hag “argued with everyone” and named the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Casemiro and Marcus Rashford among the players the manager fell out with.

The Brazilian also suggested the ex-Bayer Leverkusen boss was “clique-ridden” because he favoured Dutch players.



Fred told the Charla Podcast: “Ten Hag was tactically very good, but with the group he was a piece of c***.

“He argued with everyone. He argued with me, with Cristiano, with Casemiro, with Rashford… he wouldn’t put me in to play, sometimes it got stressful.

“[With Ten Hag] Only his Dutch players played. A clique-ridden coach. But, tactically, one of the best I’ve ever worked with.

“He wanted the team to run, but Cristiano [was already] older. He took Cristiano out [of the starting lineup], and then there was a falling out.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Fred also reminisced on his time with Solskjaer, with whom he worked for three years until the United legend’s dismissal in 2021.

He presented the Norwegian tactician as the exact opposite to Ten Hag.

The central midfielder claimed Solskjaer had great people skills but needed help from his then assistants Kieran McKenna and current Man Utd manager Michael Carrick in the tactical side.

Fred added: “Solskjaer was good with the group, but he was helped [in training] by the assistants. He united the group.”

Sports.title: ‘We tamed a beast’ – Arsenal fans baffled as Viktor Gyokeres breaks Nations League record by scoring again

ARSENAL fans ruthlessly hit out at boss Mikel Arteta – after Viktor Gyokeres shattered a goalscoring record on international duty.

The striker, 28, has fallen down the Gunners’ pecking order in the early stages of their title defence.



But Gyokeres, who saw the funny side when Manchester City were found guilty of financial breaches, made history after finding the net in Sweden’s 1-1 draw with Bosnia and Herzegovina.

And that meant the Arsenal No14 became the first star to score in SIX consecutive Nations League showdowns.



His clinical finish came after also being on target against Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Estonia, while he hit four when he faced hapless Azerbaijan.

Gyokeres was put through on goal when Alexander Bernhardsson regained possession and he sent a vicious strike beyond Bosnian keeper Salko Hamzic.



Baffled Arsenal fans raced onto social media to question Arteta’s decision to regularly snub the marksman despite playing a key role in ending a 22-year wait for Premier League glory last season.

One said: “We tamed a beast.”
