'It just seems that he's gone through a difficult period. I'm not sure how much is his fault, sometimes you just enter a strange spiral in your life, a downward spiral. My thoughts of with him of course, the belief is always that he can turn it around and I wish him the best.'

Sports.title: Inside Jamie and Rebekah Vardy's new life... at Burnley! Why family made abrupt return from Italy, why striker chose unfashionable new club and how he's taking on Gary Neville and Gary Lineker
Sports.content:
Inside Jamie and Rebekah Vardy's new life... at Burnley! Why family made abrupt return from Italy, why striker chose unfashionable new club and how he's taking on Gary Neville and Gary Lineker

It's now been a month since Jamie Vardy opted to return to English football with Burnley, following his year-long rollercoaster of an adventure with Italian minnows Cremonese.

The 39-year-old did have the option to continue his stay in the quaint city of Cremona, but after the club’s relegation back to Serie B, he made the decision at the end of last season to move on.

Vardy, his wife Rebekah and their children moved back home almost immediately after his contract came to an end, with the striker’s future in football still uncertain.

The former England international took his time to decide his next step before, at the beginning of September, agreeing to move to a struggling Burnley side who were - and still are - bottom of the Championship.

The Lancashire club are winless following relegation from the Premier League last season, picking up just the one point from the two games Vardy has featured in. The veteran has only made cameos off the bench so far.

The big question posed by many since the move was confirmed is: why did Vardy choose Burnley?

Jamie Vardy switched Cremonese in Italy for Championship side Burnley this summer

Why trade the beautiful Lake Garda, where his family’s £2million mansion was surrounded by the scenery of the stunning Gardesane Prealps and deep blue water, for the industrial town of Burnley?

It may seem like a confusing choice to your average Joe who dreams of a life of luxury such as the one the Vardys were living on the Italian lakes - but for Jamie and Rebekah, the decision to return to England was more straightforward.

Daily Mail Sport understands that from a family perspective, they felt they rushed their decision to uproot their life and make the move to Cremonese in 2025.

While they enjoyed the experience in many ways, they had issues living away from home, as showcased in their three-part reality documentary series on ITV, The Vardys.

The move, which they originally thought might last two seasons, was far from plain sailing not just for the parents, but for their four children as well.

Homesickness swept the Vardys' lavish Italian apartment, and things were made worse when it was raided by burglars, leaving Rebekah 'on edge 24/7'.

‘The biggest challenge was trying to balance the excitement of a completely new adventure with the emotional reality of leaving behind a life we'd built over more than a decade,’ Rebekah said in the documentary.

‘Leicester was home for us in every sense - our friends, routines, schools, memories, so uprooting wasn't just about packing boxes and moving country, it was about starting again emotionally.

The 39-year-old had been living by beautiful Lake Garda while playing in Serie A last season

Vardy, his wife Rebekah, and their four children struggled during their year in Italy

‘Moving is one of those major changes in life, but moving abroad? Honestly, nobody had prepared me for that. I do think that home is where you make it though. For me it's not bricks and mortar, it's simply where my favourite people are.’

The entire family are now understood to be back in their Grantham home in Lincolnshire, which housed them for much of Vardy’s legendary 13-year stint at Leicester City, where he scored 200 goals in 500 appearances - with 24 of those leading the club to a historic and miraculous Premier League title in 2016.

Once Vardy had returned to the UK, his next step was to decide which club he wanted to move to. There was interest from MLS clubs in the United States, a potential move back to Serie A and even São Paulo in Brazil were interested.

But sources made it clear to Daily Mail Sport that an English club was always Vardy’s preference.

He had a whole host of options on the table, including Championship leaders West Ham, who ended up signing Joel Piroe from Leeds, a number of Premier League teams, a potential fairy tale move to boyhood club Sheffield Wednesday – that was blocked by the EFL – and Hollywood-owned Wrexham attempted to lure him to Wales.

However, Burnley quickly became Vardy’s number one option. They had wanted him after promotion to the Premier League under Scott Parker, and maintained their interest when aware of the striker’s free agency.

The Clarets made it clear to Vardy that he was going to be their main man up top after the departure of Zian Flemming to Ipswich Town, and still hungry to play regularly and compete at the highest level, the former Foxes man was sold on the project.

He has an option of a second year if they get promoted, which may seem unlikely at the time of writing, but is still more than possible if under pressure boss Nicky Hayen can get a tune out of Vardy.

Jamie and Rebekah wanted to relocate back to England after feeling they rushed their decision to move to Italy in 2025

Vardy has now also ventured into podcasting with the Jamie Vardy's Havin' A Party show

Upon signing for the club, he told the club website: ‘I'm really happy to now be here at Burnley. This club has a proper footballing history and passionate fans who deserve a team that represents them and their town.’

Vardy may be keen to continue as a professional at the top level well into his 40s, but this summer has shown he is already setting up for life away from the pitch.

The Clarets forward wants a piece of the podcasting pie, after seeing the success of Gary Neville and Gary Lineker as media moguls in the ever-evolving landscape of the industry.

With Neville building The Overlap empire and Lineker his Goalhanger platform, which includes the hugely successful The Rest Is Football, Vardy signed with Banijay Entertainment at the start of the summer and has started the Jamie Vardy’s Havin’ A Party podcast.

It has made a flying start, securing a win over Neville’s Overlap by winning the rights to show Bundesliga games. The rights focus on live games. Vardy has also secured a TV deal with Samsung TV, with the mega electronics company creating a dedicated channel, which is also available on Amazon Prime.

The podcast has already gone viral due to former referee Mike Dean’s bombshell admission that he used to play ‘minigames’ while taking charge of Premier League matches.

And while his quotes received backlash, Vardy may have been privately pleased they were made on his show, as he looks to challenge the likes of Neville and Lineker within the footballing podcast industry.

Sports.title: It's a disgrace that a case as seismic as City's is STILL shrouded in secrecy - we don't even know who was on the panel that found them guilty: OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
It's a disgrace that a case as seismic as City's is STILL shrouded in secrecy - we don't even know who was on the panel that found them guilty: OLIVER HOLT

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

This is the top flight of English football now, this faceless parade, this feast of redaction, this lawyers’ jamboree, this case without end, this land of double-speak and deflection and filibuster and prevarication and delay and uncertainty, this wrangle still cloaked in such absurd levels of secrecy, threat and paranoia that it makes the trial in The Trial look transparent.

The interminable, impenetrable battle between the Premier League and Manchester City, one of its member clubs, has been a ludicrous, ruinous shambles of a process that has brought only ridicule and shame on the English game. Amid its agonising and its navel-gazing, its threats and its suspicion, it has forced a league that was once supposed to be the envy of the world to its knees.

There is no prospect of it rising to its feet any time soon, either. Football still does not even know the identities of the three members of the commission that handed down the initial judgments. Those ruled that Manchester City were guilty of all the charges of financial misconduct that had been levelled at them by the Premier League back in the mists of time.

The top flight is a cast filled with bad actors and a medium laden with foul tribal abuse and so some degree of anonymity while the case was ongoing is understandable but to preserve the mystery now has allowed City and their acolytes to attempt to provoke disquiet about their possible allegiances.

City have referred to the independent commission as a ‘Premier League commission’ and its judgment as an ‘opinion’. Speculation has been allowed to form that perhaps one of the panel members was a supporter of a rival team. It is standard disinformation but the conspiracy theories could be easily dispelled if the process were more transparent.

There is precedent, after all. After City and the Premier League went to arbitration in October 2024 over the league’s Associated Party Transaction rules, the hearing took place behind closed doors at the International Dispute Resolution Centre in front of a three-member tribunal made up of former High Court judge Sir Nigel Teare, former Supreme Court Justice Lord Dyson and Monckton Chambers’ Christopher Vajda KC.

Pep Guardiola smiles at the Premier League trophy but his successes are now tainted

The interminable battle between the Premier League and his former club Manchester City has been a ludicrous, ruinous shambles of a process which some have taken to poking fun at

Yet the transparency of that example has not been followed here. It is hard not to feel that much of the bitterness of the case, the inflamed tensions it has created throughout the game and the grave damage it has done to football in this country would have been diminished if the proceedings had taken place in open court and been held up to the light.

The scale of the secrecy surrounding the case has felt unnecessary and self-defeating from the start. No one knew when the hearings were taking place or if they were taking place or if evidence was still being given or which witnesses were being called or when verdicts might be close. Other cases are held in camera, of course, but this is a row about football, for goodness’ sake.

The lack of transparency that has dogged it all the way through has spawned all manner of other conspiracy theories and continues to undermine it even now. Much of the judgment that has been released publicly is redacted. The judgment speaks of witnesses accused of lying to the commission but sheds no light on who they are.

Kyle Phillips, a partner at one of the United Kingdom's leading law firms, Howard Kennedy, told ESPN earlier this week: ‘It's very difficult to read because a lot of it is redacted and there's no evidence or appendices that they keep referring to… Although the panel's names are redacted, you'd expect them to be experienced lawyers.

‘There will be a fuller balanced judgment that we don't have sight of: that's the problem, so we can't assess the language that's used from that perspective. But you would think everything they said is supported somewhere by their evidential findings, and that they have got good grounds for making the points that they have.’

When it was put to Phillips that the commission referred to witnesses in support of City’s evidence about the source of their sponsorship funding and that they had been found to have given false and dishonest evidence, he pointed out: ‘Yes, but we don't know which witnesses are accused of that, do we?’

The first trial of Manchester City is over and their owners have been found guilty of all of the most serious charges. Now it is about to begin all over again because they have appealed - and it may be that their punishment is announced within 30 days, and then rescinded if an appeal is successful, and no one knows when football might be able to breathe anew.

‘The Club’s firm position,’ City’s statement said on Friday as they revealed they had lodged their appeal at 7pm on Thursday, ‘is that on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.’ It is time, they declared, for Round Two.

Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, gives Pep Guardiola a league winner's medal during his time at Manchester City

Lord David Pannick KC (right) has represented Manchester City before in their fight against the Premier League over accusations of financial wrongdoing

The Premier League’s interminable pursuit of City, which became our game’s closest approximation to Jarndyce v Jarndyce since its inception in February 2023, appeared to reach a conclusion a little over a week ago when it was announced that the club had been found guilty of the vast majority of charges levelled against it. Now, it has got a second wind.

The case is still couched in so many uncertainties and concealments that it has continued to sow confusion and distrust. This was supposed to be the case that restored faith in the Premier League as a competition but instead it feels as though the game is running out of control and lurching towards chaos. It feels as if football is lost in the murk somewhere and we are no closer to getting it back.

That level of concealment creates a vacuum which City try to fill. City and their chief executive, Ferran Soriano, continue to bleat about the ‘irrefutable evidence’ they possess that proves their innocence in all of this and yet it appears from what we know of the judgment of the Independent Commission, which ruled on the charges, that the irrefutable evidence has already been refuted.

Germane to that is evidence that City believe proves their principal sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club’s stated owner, the Abu Dhabi United Group. City are thought to be ready to argue in their appeal that the money received by Etihad, the state airline, came directly from the Abu Dhabi government and that state-owned entities are allowed to sponsor clubs under Premier League rules.

Others are deeply sceptical about that argument. City claim not to be state owned but the problem with state ownership is that lines become blurred very quickly and grow so opaque that, just like so much with this case, it is almost impossible to tell where one entity begins and another ends.

If City are really not owned by Abu Dhabi, then why is Abu Dhabi so enraged and threatened by the verdicts handed down by the independent commission? Bloomberg reported on Friday morning that United Arab Emirates officials had warned the UK government that the severity of any punishment of City could harm the relationship between the two.

The report said the City affair may undermine ‘their appetite for future grand-scale commitments in Britain, and that the UAE consider the Premier League’s actions to have an influence on the bilateral state relationship’. If feels like quite an over-reaction if City are not state-owned.

The layers are not being peeled away. They are multiplying. What now? That is still a question with no easy answer. A new anonymous three-person independent panel will be appointed to hear City’s appeal but that will run separately to the process of punishing City for the guilty verdicts in the initial judgment.

Manchester City's Enzo Fernandez and Rayan Cherki may lead the team to victory over Liverpool at Anfield on October 11 but how much importance should we attach to that result?

It is impossible to run a sport with that kind of uncertainty hanging over it. City could be hit with a penalty that relegates them. But then they might win the appeal which would invalidate the initial verdicts

Once the sanction is decided, there are then 30 days to announce it. But there is no timetable for how long it will take to arrive at the chosen punishment. Some experts have said they think it is possible there could be an announcement of punishment before the end of the season. Others have said it could be up to five years.

It is impossible to run a sport with that kind of uncertainty hanging over it. City could be hit with a penalty that relegates them. But then they might win the appeal which would invalidate the initial verdicts. Which would then invalidate a sanction already visited upon them. It’s chaos, which is exactly what City’s chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak always promised it would be.

And somewhere in the middle of all this wreckage, fans will still turn up to watch men playing football. But they will not know what to believe. If City beat Liverpool at Anfield on October 11, for instance, and go further clear at the top of the Premier League, how much importance should we attach to that result?

Fans will not know whether the result of the game they are watching will mean anything by the end of the season. Nor will the players. Nor will the managers.

Nor will the television companies who pay billions of pounds to broadcast something that may be a sham. They will not know whether what they are watching is real. Or whether these matches are ghost games soon to be declared invalid.

And in that miasma of gloom and uncertainty, sport starts to die.

Sports.title: 'If you play for your country, there's no way you can behave like that': ECB chief RICHARD THOMPSON on England's booze culture, why he was desperate to keep Brendon McCullum and why the 18 counties are stronger than ever before
Sports.content:
It would be wrong to say there’s a spring in Richard Thompson’s step as he ticks off another lap of Lord’s to raise money for the Alzheimer’s Society. After all, it’s been only two weeks since he had knee surgery, and medics have told him to divide the 100 laps between clockwise and anti-clockwise, to ease pressure on the joint.

But the ECB chairman is feeling more chipper than he did during a summer in which English cricket was at times going in one direction only – round and round in circles, and getting absolutely nowhere.

We are speaking the day after the season ended with England’s one-day series win against Sri Lanka at the Oval and the last gasps of the County Championship, decided 24 hours earlier in Warwickshire’s favour. When Thompson says ‘it’s been a rollercoaster’, he isn’t joking.

The overall headline, he believes, is positive: the English game is better placed at the end of the season than it was at the start. After losing the Test series to New Zealand, triggering the retirement of Ben Stokes and the sacking of Brendon McCullum, England won their remaining five series across the three formats, and appear to have placed the right men in the right jobs: McCullum in charge of an increasingly impressive white-ball set-up, and Stephen Fleming set for the Test role.

Thompson speaks admiringly of the ‘alchemy’ between McCullum and Harry Brook, the limited-overs captain – under them, the T20 side have won 23 games out of 26 – and says Fleming is ‘very committed to doing a role that he’s always wanted to do’.

But it’s fair to say the path to clarity has been strewn with chaos and confusion – even carnage – as drinking escapades elbowed runs and wickets off the back pages. The charge sheet is now part of history: Brook in Wellington, Ben Duckett in Noosa, Stokes and Gus Atkinson in the Rex Rooms, Brydon Carse in Derby. And while Thompson has forgiven, he can’t entirely forget.

‘We’re through the worst of it,’ the ECB chairman Richard Thompson says of the England cricket team's rollercoaster summer. ‘But there was behaviour that was totally unacceptable'

Thompson, with radio presenter Jamie Theakston, completes 100 laps of Lord's to raise money for the Alzheimer’s Society

‘We’re definitely through the worst of it now,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘But I think the point is that there was behaviour that was just totally unacceptable. If you play for your country, there’s no way you can behave like that.

'You’re measured by a far higher standard. We certainly want to learn, and I think the changes we’ve made demonstrate that.’

Has the penny finally dropped? ‘As much as I hope it can. Something that happened three years ago that we don’t know about could suddenly blow up.

'But, culturally, when you’ve got a new captain and a new coach, it provides an automatic reset, and that’s now happened. The way Joe (Root) spoke in particular about the more recent issues could not have articulated it any better.’

Thompson says suggestions that McCullum should have been removed from the Test job immediately after the Ashes were impractical, since England were heading straight to Sri Lanka for a white-ball tour, followed by the T20 World Cup.

And he dismisses the argument that the ECB erred in making him all-format coach as ‘hindsight’. More important, he says, is where England have ended up: ‘We’ve retained Baz. If we had lost him completely, that would have been a real loss, because we still knew he had so much to offer.’

All the while, the Hundred embarked on its first season under part-private ownership, and with concerns mounting among the 11 non-host counties that they will eventually be left behind – despite the £25million windfall guaranteed each club by the sale of the eight franchises.

Thompson insists that a gap has always existed between the ‘haves and the have-nots’ of the county game. But he points to Northamptonshire’s victory in the T20 Blast as a reminder that the smaller clubs continue to pack a punch on the field. Indeed, in the last 20 years, only Derbyshire among the 18 first-class counties have failed to win one of three main trophies.

‘We’ve retained Baz (McCullum, right). If we had lost him completely, that would have been a real loss, because we still knew he had so much to offer'

'Nothing’s ever perfect, but I don’t think the 18-county structure has ever been more financially secure,’ Thompson says of the domestic game

‘Prior to the Hundred, you could say, well, are the 18 counties safe?’ he says. ‘And, arguably, I would say I’m not sure. Since we’ve done the Hundred deal, they absolutely are, and I always have been an 18-county advocate.’

At a time when football is threatening to be torn apart by the Manchester City scandal, Thompson is proud of cricket’s relative stability.

‘All the counties are completely underwritten, all toxic debt has been taken out. We’re the only sport in the country that isn’t held back by debt and spurious owners or other issues that are causing tension.

‘Our game is driven principally by its members. It’s far more transparent in its leadership and its ownership structures. Nothing’s ever perfect, but I don’t think the 18-county structure has ever been more financially secure.’

Thompson says speculation about a separate TV deal for the Hundred, driven by private investors keen to recoup their expenditure, is ‘not happening any time soon’, and says the investors are ‘very happy’ about the way the first year went, despite concerns about ticket pricing.

And he stresses that it is the ECB who are still in control of the competition – pre-empting the argument that the board have given up the prime month of August to foreign businessmen.

‘There was a suggestion that Pakistani players would not be picked up,’ he says. ‘It was a scurrilous rumour that should never have circulated in the first place, and we soon made sure that was never going to be the case.

'But it showed that the ECB still provide that influence around the tournament. The team owners recognise their role, and where the boundary exists between owning a team and running a competition.’

Thompson says private investors are ‘very happy’ about the way the first year of the revamped Hundred, won by Manchester Super Giants (above), unfolded

Thompson speaks admiringly of the ‘alchemy’ between McCullum and Harry Brook

Thompson, who is excited about the future of the English game, talks tactics with pace bowler Jofra Archer

Thompson, who turns 60 this month, will be in the chair until the end of the 2028 season, by which time he will have served six years in the role.

They have not been dull, encompassing the rise and fall of Bazball, the partial privatisation of the home summer, off-field headaches, even the return of Kevin Pietersen.

With about 75 laps to go, Thompson still has the energy to exude optimism: ‘Both on and off the field, despite the challenges we’ve had, I think we’ve managed them as best we can, and we’ve come out of it stronger.’

He may be right. But few would care to predict where the rollercoaster goes next.

Sports.title: Controversial NBA star JR Smith accused of 'hitting, grabbing or pushing' a woman in shocking court filing
Sports.content:
Controversial NBA star JR Smith accused of 'hitting, grabbing or pushing' a woman in shocking court filing

JR Smith 'intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly' caused 'bodily injury' to a member of his family or household or someone with whom he was dating, according to excerpts of the criminal complaint filed against the retired NBA star on Friday.

As previously reported by The Daily Mail, Smith was arrested Monday in Hunt County, Texas on a warrant out of Southlake and subsequently booked on a misdemeanor count of 'assault caused bodily injury family violence.' The 41-year-old has denied the allegations through his attorney in a statement provided to The Daily Mail earlier this week.

Now, The California Post has obtained a copy of the criminal complaint out of Tarrant County that accuses Smith of 'hitting, grabbing or pushing' a woman 'with [his] hand.'

The Daily Mail has sought the criminal complaint from authorities in Tarrant County, Texas.

Smith was released from jail Tuesday on a $5,000 bond.

The arrest took place Monday afternoon when Royse City Police received an alert about a suspect traveling eastbound on Interstate 30. An officer observed the vehicle and checked the license plate before pulling over the suspect. Smith was with his brother at the time of his arrest and the younger sibling took possession of his car, according to the Royse City police press release.

JR Smith 'intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly' caused 'bodily injury' to a member of his family or household or someone with whom he was dating, according to a criminal complaint

As previously reported by The Daily Mail, Smith was arrested Monday in Hunt County, Texas on a warrant out of Southlake and subsequently booked on a misdemeanor assault charge

'The wanted person was Earl Joseph [JR] Smith III and the charge was for Family Violence Assault Causing Bodily Injury,' read Tuesday's press release out of Royse City. 'A traffic stop was conducted and the driver of the vehicle was identified as Earl Joseph Smith III. The warrant was confirmed and Mr. Smith was taken into custody.'

His attorney has since issued a denial on Smith's behalf.

'JR is eager to see this matter resolved and has full confidence in the legal process,' attorney Justin A. Moore told The Daily Mail in an email. 'He is presumed innocent, and we will address this matter in Court. We ask that everyone respect the privacy of all involved throughout the process.'

The 16-year NBA veteran won two titles alongside LeBron James – one with the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2016 and another with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020 – before retiring and briefly becoming a college golfer at North Carolina A&T State University. He graduated last spring with a bachelor's degree in Liberal Studies.

Smith does have a non-violent criminal history that includes a conviction for reckless driving over a car accident that killed his friend. Smith would later serve 24 days in prison.

Smith (right) won two titles alongside LeBron James (left) – one with the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2016 and another with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020 – before retiring and focusing on golf

Smith of the North Carolina A&T Aggies greets playing partner Pedro Rabadan of the Elon Phoenix before the start of the Phoenix Invitational at Alamance Country Club in 2021

And in 2018, he ultimately paid $600 after throwing a fan's cell phone into a Manhattan construction site.

Smith's basketball career is largely remembered for his frequent run-ins with coaches and the league.

Not only was he fined twice for untying opponents' shoes during a game, but he seemingly referenced gangs in a 2009 Twitter post and in 2012 he was arrested for failing to appear in court after being cited for operating a motor-scooter without a valid license.

He also once threw a bowl of hot chicken tortilla soup on Cavs assistant coach Damon Jones in 2018.

Smith also raised eyebrows by going shirtless for several consecutive days while celebrating the Cavs' 2016 title, prompting then-president Barack Obama to ask head coach Tyronn Lue to intervene.

'Tell JR Smith to put on a shirt, though,' Obama told Lue. 'He can't just be walking around without a shirt for the [inaudible].'

A former Sixth Man of the Year, Smith averaged 12.4 points a game for his career with the Charlotte Hornets, Denver Nuggets, New York Knicks, Cavs and Lakers.

Sports.title: Watching Lee Carsley's England's U21s is a breath of fresh air and they will embrace the target on their backs in pursuit of a historic Euros three-peat next summer
Sports.content:
England men's U21s qualified for next summer's European Championships with a game to spare after their goalless draw against Slovakia.

The reigning champions are seeking their third consecutive European crown under manager Lee Carsley and sealed qualification undefeated, winning seven and drawing two of their nine fixtures.

They now head to Ireland next week, with Carsley saying emphatically at full time that he 'definitely' does not plan to mix things up in a bid to secure a perfect record.

Daily Mail Sport football reporter Tara Anson-Walsh was at Stoke City's Bet365 Stadium to bring you the things we learned…

1. Most importantly, get the job done

Carsley can sleep easy tonight knowing the first obstacle has been cleared on the road to a historic Euros three-peat with England's U21s.

Qualification? Check. Goals? Plenty of them. Fun? Well, based on England's journey through this qualifying campaign, it certainly looks like it.

Lee Carsley can sleep easy tonight after England U21s secured qualification for next year's Euros

England found the back of the net 22 times in their previous eight qualifying matches, and the beauty of this side is that goals can come from virtually anywhere.

Against Kazakhstan last week, centre backs Josh Acheampong and Max Alleyne got on the scoresheet before Middlesbrough striker Will Lankshear sealed the victory.

With four goals scored in three of their previous four matches, confidence was sky high. 'Every time I step on the pitch I believe I'm going to score,' Lankshear said after that game.

There was something slightly ironic, then, that England's first match without a goal was the one that simultaneously secured their place at next summer's tournament.

In front of 8,313 fans at Stoke City's Bet365 Stadium, England knocked on the door all evening but simply could not find a breakthrough.

Lankshear came closest. Fresh from scoring on his debut, the Middlesbrough striker twice escaped his marker at the back post but could not keep his headers on target.

There was frustration at full time after 16 shots at goal failed to find the back of the net, but Carsley was quick to remind his squad that qualification was the priority.

'They were very frustrated at the end of the game, but I made the point to them that to play in a major competition it's the story of a season, not just one game,' he said.

'They've put themselves in a great position now to do something no other country has done before in terms of potentially winning the tournament for a third time, so it's exciting times.'

2. Carsley leads the charge

It is worth a quick reminder that England went 39 years without winning this tournament before retaining it at the first time of asking last year.

The quality and depth of young talent available to Carsley is jaw-dropping, but the England boss has also played a significant role in creating the environment that allows those players to flourish.

Carsley's importance to this team's success cannot be overstated, though he would probably be the last person to say so.

Asked last week how he maintained continuity despite the constant turnover that comes with Under21 football, he instead praised the mentality of his players, particularly their ability to stay ready even when they might 'think it's not going to be their day'.

Will Lankshear had been freescoring before drawing a blank against Slovakia in Stoke on Friday

Manchester City's Rico Lewis and his team-mates knocked on the door all night but could not find the back of the net

Watching Carsley's England is a breath of fresh air. The shackles are off, and this is a team that wants to dominate possession, move the ball quickly and attack.

England had 69 per cent possession against Slovakia and registered 16 shots to their opponents' four. Against Kazakhstan, they enjoyed 81 per cent of the ball. Before that, they recorded 74 per cent possession against Moldova.

They have dominated this qualifying group from start to finish, with a 1-1 draw against Andorra and this one against Slovakia the only mild blemishes on an otherwise outstanding campaign.

No wonder they are embracing the target on their backs heading into next summer.

3. England tie up loose ends with Alleyne the man of the hour

Slovakia, sitting second in the group, should have posed a sterner test than bottom-placed Kazakhstan.

But unlike against Kazakhstan, where England conceded twice through lapses in concentration and Carsley admitted they would need to 'play better if we're going to be a serious team', they were far more assured against a stronger Slovakian side.

At the heart of that defensive display was Max Alleyne.

The Burnley centre-back, on loan from Manchester City, delivered another assured performance and the numbers backed it up.

Four tackles made and four tackles won. Four interceptions. Six of eight duels won. Eleven recoveries.

'He was outstanding,' Carsley said. 'There was once or twice in the first half where they counterattacked, one-v-one and Max cleaned it up. We shouldn't be in that position, but it was only because of Max's outstanding attributes that we got away with that.

'I thought Max, Ash (Phillips), Josh (Acheampong) and Rico (Lewis) were outstanding tonight. The concentration is something that we have to be better at in terms of Under 21s.

'Generally, when they perform with their senior teams, they've got older, more experienced players around them that are constantly talking them through the game. But they really stood up for themselves tonight. As forward-thinking as we were, I thought we were solid at the back.'

Sports.title: Revealed: Man City's claim that 'sham' sponsorship deals were funded by Abu Dhabi government was DENIED by Etihad to a US investigation in 2015
Sports.content:
One of Manchester City's key defences in their case against breaching the Premier League's financial rules could be in tatters after previous statements made by their main sponsor came to light.

City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 charges, many of which allege City cooked the books to the tune of nearly £900million through money artificially pumped into the club by their Abu Dhabi owners over a nine-year period.

An appeal was confirmed by the club on Friday, with much of their defence suggesting commercial contracts were paid for by the Abu Dhabi government rather than their owner.

Now, though, it has emerged that sponsors Etihad, the state-owned national airline of the United Arab Emirates, told the United States' department of commerce, transportation and state in 2015 that suggestions the government have paid for sponsorships are 'false'.

The statement was made as part of an investigation into state-owned airlines. It read: 'We are government-owned and have been since our founding. We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government, and that we are financed through a combination of equity, shareholder and commercial loans.

'Our shareholder's equity and loans are not subsidies under any applicable definition; they are the means by which the Abu Dhabi government has sensibly invested in a successful business model.'

A key defence around Manchester City's appeal against the Premier League could be in tatters after a previous statement emerged

New Premier League rules state that a hearing must be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing, which can only last five days, concluding. Any punishment could, therefore, be imposed this season.

City claim they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that they have worked within rules in the form of bank statements and witness accounts.

They said in a statement on Friday: 'The club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

'The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.'

The club's 'disguised funding' process – where the ownership group was topping up commercial partnerships to the tune of £830.69million – it found, allowed them to illegally sign the players that ushered in an era of success at the Etihad Stadium.

However, those with knowledge of the situation claim that City's argument is that the monies were actually paid by the government, which owns the sponsors, rather than the club's owners Abu Dhabi United Group – a private company owned by Sheikh Mansour – and as such, no rules were broken.

Sponsorship deals with government-funded companies are commonplace throughout the Premier League, particularly in the case of airlines, and are not banned.

Thomas Tuchel has admitted England's Man City players are anxious following the revelation

Thomas Tuchel, meanwhile, has revealed that England's Manchester City stars Marc Guehi, Elliot Anderson and Nico O'Reilly are worried for their immediate futures after this week's bombshell guilty verdict for breaching financial rules.

The trio have been inundated with calls and messages over the past week, with O'Reilly now having flown back to Manchester for treatment on an injury.

'Are they worried or are they concerned? I think that would be a very human reaction if you don't know what's going on for the club that you signed,' Tuchel said.

'They're still young. They're ambitious. They're told they are totally innocent and don't know what's going on.

'We speak about it at dinner and at a table of eight or 12 people. Of course, we speak about it at breakfast.'

Tuchel – whose side face Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday afternoon - claimed that the news around City being found guilty of the vast majority of charges had represented a 'distraction' before then clarifying that the City trio had been focused in meetings and training sessions.

'It's a big topic in camp,' he added. 'We had some time off between the matches and it is a big subject. How can it not be a topic? We talk with them but only briefly.'

The Football Association are also 'carefully considering' the implications of the findings into City's breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

A statement from the FA read: 'The independent commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game. We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

'As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely.'

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
