World.title: From anger to money and infighting: The comical attack on Standard Group
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

What was billed as an attack on the Standard Group offices in defence of President William Ruto ended as a shouting match among the protesters.

When the Bunge la Mwananchi crowd stopped shouting and heckling human rights activists and leaders who were standing in solidarity with The Standard Media Group, the protesters turned on their leaders over how much they were to get for their services.

As things got heated, one of the leaders sought the safety of police who had offered the media company security. The angry protesters left one by one, some walking kilometres back home after failing to get paid. They promised a dramatic storming of the media house, but their much-hyped bang ended in a whimper.

The confrontation outside Standard Group headquarters on Mombasa Road on Friday was the culmination of weeks of escalating tension. What began as online criticism had hardened into a physical siege, with rival camps clashing over the media house's coverage of President William Ruto's administration.

Days before the protest, a group identifying itself as Bunge la Mwananchi announced plans to mobilise thousands of people to demonstrate at Standard Group over what it called "negative and critical headlines targeting the government".

The group accused The Standard and KTN News of persistently publishing content critical of President Ruto, with some members alleging that former Baringo senator Gideon Moi had influenced the media house's editorial coverage.

In a video circulating online, a group member issued a direct warning: "Many people have warned you for a very long time that you ought to change, but every day, you write inflammatory statements and useless things. We as youths, we are going to surprise you".

The Standard Group reported the matter at South B Police Station and notified the DCI officer in charge of Makadara. The media house heightened security at its premises, stating it would not be intimidated into abandoning its journalistic responsibilities.

A key face in the attack was Sally Raghet, identified as a member of YURO —Youth for Ruto 2027, a youth movement formed in June 2025 to support President William Ruto's re-election bid.

The movement, also known as YR27, declared "unwavering support" for Ruto while denouncing "rising acts of violence and anarchy". Sally Raghet, one of the leaders of hired protestors who stormed Standard Group headquarters on Mombasa Road on October 2, 2026. [Maxwell Agwanda, Standard]

Its official launch was announced for June 25, 2025, at Nyayo Stadium. YURO positioned itself as a counterweight to opposition mobilisation, with activists like Kasamuel McOure leading efforts to rally young people behind Ruto's broad-based government ahead of the 2027 general election.

Raghet's role within this movement placed her at the centre of the pro-government mobilisation that would eventually converge on Standard Group's gates. Bunge la Mwananchi is led by Francis Awino, who was declared president of Bunge la Mwananchi on December 8, 2023, taking over from Calvince Okoth, popularly known as Gaucho.

The election, held at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi, was briefly disrupted when police intervened, demanding authorisation letters from the Regional Commander. Despite the interruption, the election committee proceeded to count the votes already cast. Awino garnered 37 votes, defeating Mishael Kira (5 votes), Isaac Otieno (3), Patrick G Kamotho (4), and two others who received zero votes. Maurice Masinga was declared his deputy.

Bunge la Mwananchi was founded in the early 1990s as a social movement during Kenya's one-party state, with the aim of keeping the ruling government in check. It has active members in 26 counties and holds elections for president, vice president, speaker and women's representative at its headquarters in Jeevanjee. Awino's leadership has been marked by aggressive confrontations with institutions and figures he perceives as hostile to the government.

On April 7, 2026, he was brutally attacked while holding a press conference at Nation Centre in Milimani, Nairobi. He had been questioning why Energy Cabinet Secretary Opiyo Wandayi had not resigned despite being implicated in an ongoing substandard fuel scandal.

Awino claimed that soldiers at Nation Centre pushed him back into the crowd of attackers, who struck him on the head after he fell. He was rushed to Savanna Hospital by fellow activists, including one identified as Komrade Bush, who accused Wandayi of sending goons to silence whistleblowers.

Just two weeks later, on April 22, 2026, Awino was arrested without a warrant and charged with attempted extortion. The prosecution alleged that on January 14, 2026, at the Kenya Wildlife Service headquarters in Lang'ata, he threatened KWS Director General Erastus Kanga with the filing of a petition for his removal from office over alleged violations of Chapter Six of the Constitution on leadership and integrity, in a bid to obtain Sh1.7 million.

Awino had indeed filed such a petition in January 2026, and prosecutors alleged he weaponised it as leverage to extract money rather than pursue it in genuine public interest. He denied the charge before Milimani Chief Magistrate Teresia Nyangena and was released on bail. Moses Gazemba, one of the leaders of hired protestors who stormed Standard Group headquarters on Mombasa Road on October 2, 2026. [Maxwell Agwanda, Standard]

Yesterday, Bunge la Mwananchi members converged at Standard Group gates to deliver a letter protesting the media house's coverage. They were met by human-rights activists who had gathered in defence of the media house, arguing that criticism of journalistic content should not be used to intimidate journalists or undermine press freedom. The confrontation brought into focus the growing tensions surrounding media coverage of the government.

The group defending Standard argued that journalists have a constitutional right to publish stories without intimidation, provided they operate within the law and professional standards. Bunge la Mwananchi maintained that media houses should be held accountable for coverage it considered unfair or hostile to the government.

The threats come against the backdrop of increasingly public attacks on the Standard Group, with criticism by broad-based government-allied lawmakers this week during the opening of the Fifth Session of 13th Parliament being the latest instance.

Endebess MP Robert Pukose initiated the fire on The Standard and KTN when he made a personal statement on the floor of the house on Tuesday. The MPs castigated the two SG editorial platforms, accusing them of what they described as “irresponsible and misleading” reporting. This follows an exposé by The Standard and KTN on alleged irregular registration of Ugandan nationals as Kenyan voters at the Suam border in Trans Nzoia County.

Some legislators called for tougher action against the media, including possible restrictions on media freedom and even closure of the Standard Group.

“For Standard, we should even ban it completely. We don't need that. We don't need such a media in the country,” said Homabay Town MP Opondo Kaluma. Human Rights Defenders confront pro-government goons who had planned to paralyse operations at Standard Group headquarters on Mombasa Road on October 2, 2026. [Benard Orwongo, Standard]

The latest confrontation also comes barely a month after the Group's Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich was abducted by armed men believed to be police officers. Authorities are yet to arrest anybody involved in the abduction or provide answers even as they claim investigations into the matter remain alive.

Kiprotich was abducted at Gilgil bridge along Nairobi-Nakuru Highway on the evening of September 1 and was, the following day, discovered dumped in Ekalakala village near Masinga Dam, Machakos county.

In a statement released yesterday, The Standard Group condemned the attack as an affront to media freedom and democracy and reiterated that it position on publishing news and disseminating information will not change.

"The Standard Group PLC condemns, in the strongest terms, the unwarranted protest and name-calling outside our premises along Mombasa Road today. A group of youths, purporting to speak for the president and the Kenya Kwanza administration, picketed our offices and hurled profanities at our company... We will not be cowed by a few individuals helbent on instilling fear and nurturing dictatorial tendencies. We will keep exposing what the powerful would rather hide. No threat will stop us from calling out injustice and defending democracy," the statement read.

In June, President Ruto himself also took to his X account for two days straight to attack SG for its critical journalism against the State, terming the news outlet an "extortionist propaganda" through its newspaper headlines, alleging its coverage is motivated by greed and blackmail.

"GMoi, your STANDARD media’s 5 days a week EXTORTIONIST propaganda HEADLINES on me & my administration’s transformative track record will get you NOTHING & NOWHERE!" A clearly displeased Ruto wrote. He added: "BLACKMAIL to yield to your GREED? NEVER. Kenya belongs to all Kenyans, not you alone. Jaribu 8 days a week. Do your WORST!"

The Group, through its Chief Executive Officer, responded: “He is the country’s leader and when he fails, Kenya fails. But The Standard will not cheer on failure; we will instead point it out."

Similarly, the media giant has encountered several online attacks with sponsored hashtags as well as numerous calls by government officials, either condemning its style of coverage or calling for its closure altogether. The episode therefore raises questions over whether warnings directed at the Standard Group have moved beyond political rhetoric into a sustained campaign aimed at putting pressure on the country’s oldest media house.

According to Tony Gachoka, a veteran journalist, the harassment and intimidation of Standard Group offends Article 34 of the Constitution which protects the freedom of press.

"This is regressive and barbaric. We condemn a government that cannot be held to account," he said outside SG offices along Mombasa Road when he came to stand in solidarity with the media house. He urged Ruto's regime not to drive the country back to the era when journalists were being attacked, blackmailed and injured, noting that it took hard-fought reforms to achieve the freedoms Kenyans enjoy today.

Lawyer Abel Nabutola observed, "Today the target may be The Standard. Tomorrow it could be Nation, Citizen, an independent digital platform or an individual journalist. Kenya must therefore draw a clear democratic line, protest peacefully if you disagree with journalism, challenge falsehoods with evidence and use lawful accountability mechanisms but keep political intimidation away from newsrooms".

World.title: Pregnant woman found dead by roadside in Kirinyaga with head, hip injuries
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The National Police Service (NPS) has launched investigations after the body of a pregnant woman was found by the roadside in the Itangi area of Mwea East Sub-County, Kirinyaga County.

The woman, identified as Catherine Njeru, was found early Friday morning along the Piai-Itangi Murram Road with visible injuries to her head and hip.

In a statement, NPS said the incident is being investigated as a suspected murder.

"The NPS condoles with the family, relatives, and friends of the deceased and commits to expeditious and conclusive investigations to ensure that any person or persons responsible for this barbaric crime are brought to justice," read the statement.

Police have urged residents of Itangi to remain calm and refrain from speculation as the investigation continues.

Anyone with information that could assist the investigation has been asked to report to the nearest police station or a law enforcement officer.

The matter is being investigated by Kirinyaga County Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) officers, local Sub-County police and Central Regional Police Command, led by the Regional Criminal Investigations Officer.

According to NPS, the Inspector General of the National Police Service has also been briefed on the incident and directed the Director of Criminal Investigations to expedite the probe and establish the facts surrounding the woman's death.

World.title: Ruto downplays rivalry over oil refinery in East Africa
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Former Nigeria President Olesugun Obasanjo, Ali Dangote, President William Ruto and Uganda President Yoweri Museveni during launch of the Lamu Refinery on September 30, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has played down suggestions of rivalry between Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania over competing refinery projects, saying East Africa’s growing demand for petroleum products can support several facilities across the region.

Speaking during a media interview at State House Mombasa, Ruto said Kenya had no objection to Uganda and Tanzania pursuing their own refinery projects, arguing that the different facilities could complement rather than compete with one another.

“There is no bad blood at all. There is no problem,” Ruto said.

His remarks came a day after he presided over the groundbreaking of the Lamu refinery project, which the government is positioning as a major component of a wider industrial complex on the Kenyan coast.

Ruto said he had discussed Uganda’s plans with President Yoweri Museveni and agreed that Kampala could proceed with a smaller refinery without threatening Kenya’s investment in Lamu.

He said Kenya would even be prepared to buy petroleum products from Uganda if they could reach the Kenyan market at competitive prices.

“If it is manufactured there in Uganda and the oil from that place is near Busia, and it can reach Busia at a lower price, we will buy oil from anywhere and bring it to Busia,” Ruto said.

The President argued that the size of the regional petroleum market meant there was room for more than one refinery.

“This one in Lamu cannot serve all of us; it will be necessary to expand,” he said, adding that East Africa had “enough opportunity” for multiple facilities.

Ruto also extended the same approach to Tanzania, saying Kenya could participate in a refinery project in Tanga if it is eventually developed.

“Even if the one in Tanga is built, we as Kenya will go and buy some shares there. There is no problem,” he said.

The comments point to a regional energy market in which petroleum products could move across borders depending on availability, transport costs and prices. Rather than treating refinery projects as competing national investments, Ruto said the facilities could strengthen economic cooperation within the East African Community.

The President said the Lamu refinery would also address some of the challenges Kenya faces from dependence on imported refined petroleum products.

“Lamu will give us an opportunity to have fuel without the fluctuations that we have now,” he said.

He linked the proposed refinery to the need to reduce Kenya’s exposure to international oil price shocks, disruptions caused by instability in oil-producing regions and costs associated with transporting petroleum products over long distances.

Ruto said local refining could reduce expenses related to insurance and transportation while providing Kenya with greater access to locally processed fuel.

However, he said the larger economic opportunity would extend beyond the refinery itself. The government plans to develop industries around the facility, including petrochemical, chemical and plastics manufacturing.

The refinery could also provide raw materials for industries producing fertiliser and bitumen, potentially reducing reliance on imports of some petroleum-based products.

The broader development is expected to create opportunities for employment, investment and trade while strengthening Lamu’s position as an industrial and logistics centre.

Ruto said Kenya’s policy would be guided by competitiveness, allowing businesses and consumers to obtain petroleum products from whichever regional facility can supply them efficiently and at favourable prices.

The President maintained that Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania therefore did not need to view their refinery plans through the lens of rivalry.

Instead, he said, multiple facilities could create a larger and more integrated petroleum market capable of serving the needs of East Africa.

World.title: Outrage as KDF officers detain human rights team along Malindi-Lamu highway
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Activists clashed with police at a Gamba roadblock after being stopped en route to Lamu. [Vocal Africa]

Six members of Muslims for Human Rights (MUHURI), including five staff and a board member, were detained by Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) officers along the Malindi-Lamu highway, prompting condemnation from human rights organisations.

The incident occurred on Monday as the team travelled from Lamu to Mombasa after a field mission. The officers reportedly intercepted them between Gamba and Minjila, detained them for about two hours, then released them.

The Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC) and MUHURI said the officers covered their faces and refused to identify themselves when the human rights team challenged them.

The five staff members were identified as Francis Auma, Abdulrahman Mwanga, Fredrick Okado, Lathan Yusuf and Mohamed Abdla, while the board member was identified as Khelef Khalifa.

In a joint statement, the two organisations said the officers' actions violated a High Court ruling by Justice Bahati Mwamuye requiring security personnel to wear clearly visible name tags or identifiable service numbers on their uniforms.

The ruling also prohibits security officers from wearing hoods, balaclavas or face masks to conceal their identities.

"We call on the KDF and other security agencies to comply with the court order. Officers who violate the directive should be held accountable and face legal consequences," the joint statement read in part.

The organisations also demanded immediate compliance with a recent court order lifting the dusk-to-dawn curfew that had been imposed for more than a decade along the Minjila-Lamu highway.

They argued that the curfew had created conditions for arbitrary stops, harassment and detention of travellers using the route, citing the detention of the MUHURI team as an example.

The organisations urged security agencies to respect court orders and protect the rights of travellers using the highway.

However, a senior Anti-Terror Police officer aware of the incident told The Standard that the officers from the Border Police Unit (BPU) manning such roadblocks and tactical borders conceal their faces to protect their identities.

"In high-risk areas prone to insurgent or terrorist retaliation, including Kanyoyo in Kitui heading to Garissa, Moyale and Lamu, anonymity is framed as a matter of personal and operational survival," she stated.

World.title: Kalonzo signals at working with Ruto if 2027 poll is free and fair
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County on September 27, 2026. [Clinton Ambujo, Standard]

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka has signalled that the Opposition could accept the outcome of the 2027 General Election and consider working with President William Ruto if he wins through a free and fair contest.

Speaking at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County, Kalonzo said the political class must commit itself to democratic competition and be prepared to accept the verdict of voters.

“If you beat us, we will have to consider if you have behaved yourself, and if we beat you, we have to look at all these things,” he said.

The Wiper leader also called for stronger democratic institutions, warning against political confrontation that could deepen divisions in the country.

“We have a nation here. We have to make this country truly democratic. I do not think we have a shortcut,” he said.

Kalonzo used the church service to make a broader appeal for a united and effective Opposition, saying political leaders had a responsibility to work together in the national interest.

“Kenya needs a functional official opposition; one that is united and does not thrive on disunity. As leaders, we have a responsibility to work together and play our part in fixing this nation,” he said.

He said he had remained in the Opposition even when some political allies moved into government.

“I have stood in the opposition all these years. Even when others joined government, my brother Eugene Wamalwa and I remained steadfast, and we will continue to stand firm,” he said.

Kalonzo also turned his attention to Parliament, claiming that the National Assembly had been “captured” and challenging lawmakers in both Houses to exercise their constitutional responsibilities.

“The National Assembly has been captured. Let this message reach every leader in the National Assembly and the Senate: you have the power to change things, not just to complain later,” he said.

He urged legislators to defend the interests of the people who elected them and to put the country ahead of political considerations.

The former Vice President also defended retired President Uhuru Kenyatta against claims that he is financing the Opposition ahead of the 2027 contest.

Kalonzo argued that presidential campaigns have historically relied on networks of political allies and supporters rather than family resources alone.

“But here we are saying, please let Uhuru rest; he is a retired President. Stop saying he is our financier,” he said.

Kalonzo cited previous presidential campaigns involving Uhuru, former President Mwai Kibaki and Raila Odinga, arguing that major political campaigns require support from friends and associates.

“Even when Uhuru was running for President, or Kibaki and even Raila, no family has enough resources to support a presidential campaign. It is friends who support you,” he said.

He warned that Kenya was at a delicate political moment and urged leaders to avoid actions that could deepen instability.

“We should not allow the country to get to a worse situation than where it is. We are on the edge of a cliff; the country is at a crossroads,” he said.

World.title: ODM delegates reject Sakaja using the party for gubernatorial bid
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi ODM chairman George Aladwa addressing the media over the upcoming ODM nominations in Nairobi. [Collins Oduor, Standard]

Nairobi ODM delegates have resolved to reject and lobby against attempts by some people in President William Ruto's broad-based government to give Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja the ODM ticket in the 2027 gubernatorial race.

Party members, delegates and branch chairpersons met in Makadara, where they agreed that ODM be allowed to field their own candidates instead of the party allowing UDA leaders to vie on the party ticket.

They also resolved to back Makadara MP George Aladwa. With Tutam songs renting the air during the meeting, they also agreed to back President Ruto's re-election.

"Aladwa should be the party's candidate for Nairobi governor, and every candidate should seek the seat through their own political party," said an agitated delegate from Kasarani.

They insisted ODM should not allow an outsider to join the party and use its ticket to contest for the gubernatorial seat, arguing that the ODM ticket should be reserved for a candidate who enjoys the support of its members.

"We will not allow someone from another party to come and vie using ODM while we have our own members. As a party our only candidate is Aladwa," said delegate chairs.

They added that their position follows a series of meetings held across all 17 constituencies in Nairobi, with Makadara being the final constituency to hold its meeting.

They further argued that the Nairobi gubernatorial seat requires a leader with experience and leadership skills, warning ODM members against supporting candidates they believe lack the necessary political and leadership experience.

They also sustained their criticism towards former president Uhuru, alleging that he is undermining the party and dividing it, and they will not allow it.

George Aladwa backed the ODM members' position, saying every politician seeking elective office should do so through their own political party.

The delegates maintained that ODM should protect its identity and ticket, insisting that candidates from outside the party should not be allowed to use the ODM ticket to pursue elective positions when active and loyal members are sidelined.

The delegates are calling on ODM to ensure that the nomination process is free, fair and transparent, giving party members an opportunity to choose the candidate they want to represent them.

World.title: Oil rig arrives in Mombasa ahead of Kenya's first commercial drilling
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Oil rig arrives in Mombasa ahead of Kenya’s first commercial drilling. [Courtes]

Kenya has moved closer to commercial oil production after a 1,500 horsepower drilling rig arrived at the Port of Mombasa ahead of its deployment to the South Lokichar Basin in Turkana County.

The GW70 rig, leased by Gulf Energy E&P BV from Great Wall Drilling Company, docked at Kilindini Port on Friday aboard MV Transit Sedanka after sailing from Duqm Port in Oman.

It is expected to be transported to Turkana, where drilling is scheduled to begin on November 1.

“All workstreams at Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ are running to a tight project management schedule, and the project remains on course for First Oil production in December 2026,” Gulf Energy Chief Executive Officer Paul Limoh said.

The arrival marks a step in the commercial development of the South Lokichar Basin, more than a decade after oil was first discovered in Turkana in 2012.

The first phase of the project is expected to produce about 20,000 barrels of crude oil per day, with output projected to rise to 50,000 barrels per day in the second phase.

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) says Kenya is targeting first oil in December 2026, while the first crude exports through the Port of Mombasa are expected in the first quarter of 2027.

The GW70 will undergo commissioning and acceptance checks before drilling begins. Gulf Energy has contracted Baker Hughes for integrated well services and SLB to provide an early production facility for the first phase.

World.title: Two more suspects arrested over lawyer Kyalo Mbobu murder
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The two suspects are currently in custody undergoing processing as detectives pursue additional leads.

Detectives have arrested two more suspects in connection with the fatal shooting of lawyer Kyalo Mbobu, as an intelligence-led operation targeting people linked to the September 9, 2025 murder intensifies.

The two boda boda riders Nicholas Lemiso Naula and Noah Kipkirui Langat were arrested in Nairobi’s Central Business District, following sustained efforts by detectives to trace individuals suspected to have been involved in the killing.

According to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), Lemiso is a boda boda rider who allegedly ferried the main suspect, Police Constable Julius Cheruiyot, to and from the scene of the murder, while Langat was arrested over alleged surveillance on Mbobu before his killing.

"With three suspects now in custody, detectives are intensifying the hunt for other persons suspected to have played a role in the meticulously planned killing," DCI stated.

His arrest comes shortly after detectives arrested Cheruiyot in connection with the killing.

“The dragnet over the fatal shooting of lawyer Kyalo Mbobu has widened, with detectives arresting a second suspect as an intelligence-led operation targeting persons linked to the murder intensifies,” DCI said.

The two suspects are currently in custody undergoing processing as detectives pursue additional leads and seek to identify and arrest other people who may have been involved. The DCI said the operation remains active as investigators work to establish the circumstances surrounding Mbobu’s murder.

“The DCI is leaving no stone unturned in its efforts to unravel the full circumstances surrounding Lawyer Mbobu’s murder and bring all those responsible to justice,” the agency said.

World.title: Police and high school students clash across France in protests over underfunded education
World.content:
Paris —

Students fought running battles with police and several schools were ablaze Friday as violence gripped France with no end in sight to protests that have rocked the country.

More than 400 schools remained closed on Friday as authorities scrambled to calm tensions after days of demonstrations that have seen hundreds of teenagers taken into custody.

Young people in Strasbourg, eastern France, were building barricades in tear gas-clouded streets, while more peaceful protests were underway in Lyon and other cities Friday.

The protestors say France’s education sector is under-resourced and overstretched. Students complain of overcrowding in classrooms and say that absent teachers aren’t being replaced and schools are in a state of serious disrepair.

Demonstrating in the Paris suburb of Pantin, 15-year-old Kesia told Reuters: “We are 35 per class, we don’t have enough chairs in classrooms, the one hour lunch break (is too short) for everyone to get food.”

Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin expressed fears that the unrest would carry on through the weekend, saying on Friday: “We’ve moved from student protests to a question of public order.”

Nationwide union-led protests in support of the high schoolers are planned for Tuesday.

With no obvious off-ramp for the protests and tensions rising as the violence continues, the government is scrambling to contain the situation outside high schools.

After meeting with French Education Minister Édouard Geffray, parents and staff on Friday, student representatives called for non-violent protests to continue.

“We disassociate ourselves from the urban violence,” said Nathanaël Combary, of the student union Renouveau Lyceen. “These are people who are not there to champion our demands.”

Authorities in several parts of the country banned gatherings around the schools that were closed Friday, but the measure appears to have had little effect.

Speaking to radio station RTL, Darmanin proposed making parents pay for the damage incurred by students, an idea shot down as “absurd” by the far-left France Unbowed party, whose politicians have drawn criticism by center-right and far-right lawmakers for rallying with students.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday criticized elected officials for appearing to condone the violence.

“In no case can those politically responsible (elected officials) – it’s a term that’s perhaps poorly chosen – legitimize violence,” he said.

Officials from the hard-right National Rally party have blamed their hard-left political opponents, who are currently positioned to reach the presidential run-off next year.

On Thursday, government officials called on parents to prevent their children from taking part in violent protests.

A student holds a flag of the France Unbowed party as French high school students gather outside the Lycée Voltaire high school in Paris on Friday. Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

Many of the protests at high schools are peaceful, but the images of arson and strong-arm police tactics are dominating the public debate in France. High schools in poorer suburbs of cities across the country have been at the center of the ongoing tensions with police.

In the Ile-de-France region, which includes Paris, damage from the unrest is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.9 million), according to regional authorities, with 3 million euros’ worth of damage estimated in the southern region of Occitanie.

Police said some 2,000 people had been taken into custody over the student protests on Thursday alone. Two students suffered serious injuries after allegedly being struck by crowd-control rounds fired by police.

Amnesty International accused the police of using disproportionate force against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. “Authorities must prioritize dialogue and de-escalation, not resort to weapons,” Amnesty said on X. The interior ministry said it had opened three investigations into police violence, Reuters reported.

In a post on X on Thursday, the Paris police prefecture said that its officers had been “challenged by individuals determined to clash” during Thursday’s protests. Agathe Foucault, a spokesperson for French police, told CNN affiliate BFMTV on Friday that officers “are required to use force in a necessary and proportionate manner.”

CNN’s Kara Fox contributed reporting.

World.title: Trump touted big economic projects in two key Senate states this week. Both announcements soon crumbled
World.content:
President Donald Trump has made it abundantly clear that he’s happy to use official government resources in ethically dubious ways to try to win the 2026 midterm elections.

He promised to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 if Republicans win. He’s sending $500 to some Obamacare recipients with a very political letter enclosed. And now he’s running government-funded ads that promote himself and are obviously geared towards the election.

But wait. There’s more.

Twice this week, Trump has held White House events announcing a major economic project that happens to benefit a state holding a key, competitive Senate race — first in Iowa, then in Alaska.

And both times, his promises have proven to be overzealous, at best.

The Iowa steel plant

Trump announced the Iowa project on Monday at an Oval Office event featuring Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson and many others. It was for a new $15 billion Mesabi Metallics steel plant in Lee County in eastern Iowa — one that could create thousands of jobs and make Iowa the second-largest steel-producing state in the United States.

US Rep. Ashley Hinson, second from right, watches as Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds speaks during an announcement of a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, in the White House in Washington, DC, with Donald Trump on September 28. Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

And when a reporter inquired about how definite the plans were, Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick assured they were effectively written in stone.

“I think this deal is done. This deal is done,” Lutnick said. “They’ve already worked it out. That’s why we’re all together with the president. The president doesn’t bring people together unless it’s a done deal. You guys know that already.”

Trump then jumped in, claiming: “They’ve already started building.”

That’s not true.

Indeed, just a day later, Republican Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds called an emergency special session of the state legislature focused on tax incentives for the project — exactly the issue that Lutnick was asked about when he declared the deal done .

The same day, local TV station KWQC reported that the project still hadn’t acquired land or applied for permits, and Lee County officials said they didn’t have details about the project.

There are also real doubts about whether any of this will ultimately prove to be real, as CNN’s Eric Bradner and Jeff Zeleny report. Big projects like these can prove quite difficult to get across the finish line. Some locally are comparing the project to Foxconn, a Taiwanese electronics company that never delivered a $10 billion Wisconsin plant — one that, like the Iowa steel plant, Trump announced at a White House event in 2017.

“It sounds too good to be true, and it just might be,” a top Iowa GOP official told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to avoid inflaming the Trump administration.

Hinson dismissed the Foxconn comparisons.

“I don’t think so,” she told CNN. “I trust our governor, who has been working on this deal for months to make sure that we secure that investment here in Iowa.”

But even those comments implicitly acknowledge the deal isn’t nearly as done as Trump and Lutnick claimed it was.

And it’s downright bizarre that Trump said construction had begun. He was either lying or had no idea about the subject of the entire event he was hosting.

The Alaska natural gas pipeline

The story is quite similar with another Trump announcement on Wednesday: that South Korea would spend more than $50 billion on a struggling natural gas pipeline in Alaska.

As with the Iowa announcement, Trump made this one at the White House next to the vulnerable GOP senator, Dan Sullivan.

US President Donald Trump speaks to US Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska as he makes an announcement with US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 30. Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

And as with the Iowa announcement, Trump and Lutnick treated this as a done deal. Trump said South Korea had agreed to invest large sums in the US to lower its tariffs, and “part of that money is going into this project” — the pipeline.

“It’s the combination of your deal-making and your trade deal that allowed this to happen, and this is extraordinary,” Lutnick told Trump. “This will change Alaska, and it will change geopolitics.”

Trump said politicians had been talking about the project for five decades but failed to deliver. He said it would be “one of the largest energy projects in American history.” He said it would save Alaskans thousands in energy bills.

Sullivan’s office called it a “historic $54 billion investment by South Korea.”

But by Thursday, South Korea disputed Trump’s claims.

“Putting figures or using definitive language goes far beyond what was agreed,” Minister of Trade Industry and Resources Kim Jung-kwan said, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap.

Kim said South Korea was still reviewing whether to proceed with the pipeline.

When asked about the discrepancy, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers didn’t explain it.

“Wednesday’s joint announcement was historic for the great state of Alaska, the United States, and the Republic of Korea,” Rogers said instead.

And then later Friday, Trump insisted his announcement hadn’t been premature – even while seeming to allow South Korea hadn’t signed anything.

“Well, I didn’t jump the gun. I mean, they were there and they were represented,” Trump told reporters at the White House just before departing for a rally in Alabama. “And let’s see. If they don’t want to do it, that’s OK with me. I’ll just charge you more.”

Why voters should be cautious

It would seem rather coincidental that two major projects in two states majorly important to the Senate battle would suddenly come together around the exact same time with about a month to go in the 2026 midterms.

And it would also seem rather curious that, in both cases, Trump’s and his team’s claims about how ironclad these projects are were quickly knocked down.

Of course, as Foxconn and plenty of other examples show, Trump often jumps the gun when it comes to touting such projects and his successes in facilitating them. He loves a big announcement; he rarely worries about how it might look later when the things he says fall apart.

That doesn’t mean these projects won’t ultimately happen. It’s just that, if they don’t, we’ll likely learn that long after Hinson’s and Sullivan’s electoral fates will be decided.

Kind of like how, if those $5,000 checks never materialize — as plenty doubt they will, given the more than $1 trillion price tag and the legal issues — it’d be too late for voters to get a mulligan on the 2026 election.

And voters in Iowa and Alaska would do well to view these announcements in the context of things like that. Because right now, Trump seems to have an anything-goes attitude towards trying to win the 2026 election.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Breaking down Trump’s new ‘drug factories’ claim about Iranian nuclear sites
World.content:
President Donald Trump has said a lot of things about the three Iranian nuclear facilities the US attacked last year. Until Thursday night, he had never publicly claimed these facilities were also “drug factories.”

Trump’s comments at a rally in Oklahoma bewildered not only average Americans but also experts on Iran’s nuclear program.

“Wow…That one is new to me,” James Acton, co-director of the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said in a Friday email after CNN sent him a video of Trump’s remarks. “To my knowledge, the Fordow facility, whose destruction Trump is describing, was not being used for drug production and neither had I previously heard any allegation (credible or otherwise) that it was.”

The White House refused to offer any explanation for Trump’s comments when CNN inquired on Friday. But if you watch the full video of Trump’s speech, an obvious theory quickly emerges.

It appears likely that he made a simple mistake, and then – as he has for years – doubled down instead of correcting himself. For a president who has declared himself “right about everything,” even an admission of minor verbal error is usually a bridge too far.

Trump’s claim came after remarks about drugs in the Caribbean

Trump made the claim about “drug factories” near the end of a long day. He had traveled from the White House to an event in Texas, then arrived about two hours late for the rally in Oklahoma after bad weather forced him to drive rather than fly.

While discussing his efforts to combat Iran, Trump spoke of the stealth bombers that attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in the June 2025 operation codenamed “Operation Midnight Hammer.” Some of the planes dropped bombs aimed at Fordow’s ventilation shafts.

Trump said, “And then at 1 o’clock in the morning with no moon, dark as can be, these unbelievable machines led by the most incredible pilots in the world, they unloaded; every single bomb went right down air chutes into this, uh, drug factories, really. That’s what they were doing – they were nuclear and drug. They were doing drugs, but they were doing the nuclear. But these drug factories-slash-nuclear factories were hit so hard.”

Why did Trump say this? We might never know for sure. But just before he started talking about Iran, he had been talking about his attempts to thwart illegal drug trafficking in the Caribbean and about the US military operation that captured then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Trump’s initial remark about bombs hitting Iranian “uh, drug factories, really” seemed likely to be a slip triggered by the preceding remarks about illegal drugs and Venezuela.

Trump has long refused to acknowledge even insignificant speaking stumbles, instead preferring to act as if he had really meant to say the mistaken thing he said – even something as insignificant as whether a federal agent he praised in a 2018 address is nicknamed “CJ” or “DJ.” Here, instead of just amending the “drug factories” assertion, he ad-libbed three additional lines reiterating the assertion.

The White House wouldn’t try to explain

The White House, which tends to declare that “President Trump is right” even in response to questions about some of Trump’s most inaccurate remarks, wouldn’t offer a defense of this one. “Refer to POTUS’ comments,” an aide said in an unsigned Friday email.

Acton, trying to think of a “possible explanation,” said it’s possible Trump remembered how Iran has sometimes pointed out that legal drugs known as “radiopharmaceuticals,” which are used to diagnose and treat certain medical conditions, “are produced in nuclear reactors.”

But Acton then noted that the Fordow facility Trump very much seemed to be talking about Thursday is an enrichment center with no reactor, “so, even under this (generous) interpretation, Trump’s statement would be inaccurate.” He said it’s more plausible Trump simply made a mistake.

And, of course, it would be highly misleading for Trump to go from talking about the trafficking of illegal drugs in the Caribbean to talking about Iran operating “drug factories” in its nuclear facilities without ever explaining he was now referring to the production of lawful drugs.

So Trump having merely slipped up is actually the kindest possible defense of his “drug factories” remarks. Not that Trump or his team are willing to use it.

World.title: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
World.content:
Smit Machchhar, the hero Flydubai captain who fought off a savage attack by his copilot, kept fighting because he could not “let everybody else die,” he said in his first public remarks since Wednesday’s suspected hijacking attempt.

“In that moment, I was fighting for my life,” Machchhar told India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was so severely wounded that I had fallen down… at that time, I was thinking what if I don’t get up?”

A horrific mid-air catastrophe on flight FZ 1073 heading to Tel Aviv was averted in a stunning turn of events on Wednesday when passengers bravely rushed into the cockpit and stand-in pilots regained control of the aircraft.

Machchhar was badly injured while trying to fend off the attacker. Images showed a gruesome scene onboard, with blood splashed across the cockpit and the seriously wounded pilot lying on the floor, his pained face partially covered with a mask.

Machchhar told Modi he was on the ground in the cockpit when he realized the plane was going down.

“And I knew in that moment – one last push, Smit! Just do it. The door is right there,” he said. “And even at that time, he was beating me up.”

“And then I just opened it… and then everybody came,” he said, referring to several other passengers who then rushed into the cockpit and restrained his attacker.

“I was doing this for my life, but at the same time, I knew that I couldn’t let everybody else die.”

Modi praised Machchhar’s heroics, telling the veteran pilot that his “courage, patience and quick thinking… saved the lives of so many people.”

“You yourself were fighting the battle of life and death,” Modi said.

Machchhar is recovering at a hospital in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). He was initially treated for his injuries in Saudi Arabia, where the diverted plane was forced to make an emergency landing.

The father of two had suffered “massive blood loss” and was “severely wounded,” dentist Shota Musaev, a passenger on the flight who helped treat him, previously told CNN.

His bravery “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN on Wednesday.

Machchhar appeared emotional in the call with Modi while recalling the ordeal, and apologized to the prime minister for crying on the phone.

The two later spoke in Gujarati, the language predominantly spoken by people from India’s western state of Gujarat, which is where Modi is from.

Machchhar said his daughter had come to visit him in hospital but got scared seeing him in his condition. His youngest son, who is two, has not been able to meet him yet, he said.

Born into a family in the textile business, becoming a pilot wasn’t Machchhar’s “childhood dream,” he told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast in 2025. Initially, he’d enrolled in a textile engineering course after school.

Speaking to Modi, Machchhar said he felt a sense of pride.

“Now that you have called me, I am really really proud of myself,” Machchhar said. “I wasn’t proud before this, but now I am.”

His wife, Sonal Machchhar, told CNN affiliate CNN News18 that the family had not asked him yet about what happened because “we don’t want him to get flashbacks of the incident.”

Flight captain Smit Machchhar with wife, Sonal Machchhar. Sonal Machchhar/Facebook

“We want him to fully recover, and I’m sure once he is in the right space to talk, he will share it with everyone of how the incident went on with him,” Sonal Machchhar said.

What we know about the suspect

The plane’s co-pilot and Machchhar’s alleged attacker has now been transferred from Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed, to the UAE, where he faces a terrorism investigation.

A top UAE official on Friday described the mid-flight crisis as a “dangerous terrorist act.” Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic adviser to the UAE’s president, also cautioned against conspiracy theories as investigators look to establish the facts surrounding what happened.

The suspect is an Omani national, Netanyahu told CNN Thursday. Oman and Israel do not have formal diplomatic relations, and it is not yet clear how the Omani pilot would have obtained clearance to fly to Israel.

Authorities are yet to divulge the co-pilot’s identity. And there hasn’t been any confirmation of his motive or of the weapon he used in the violent altercation, though Netanyahu suggested to Fox News this might have been a knife or an axe.

In a video posted on his social media platforms Friday, Netanyahu said the alleged attacker had “undergone Islamist radicalization.” “He intended to crash the plane with its passengers on board,” he said.

“We are investigating whether he was sent by someone, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price,” Netanyahu continued. In comments to Fox News on Thursday, the Israeli leader said that it was too soon to say whether the attacker had connections to Iran or anyone else, although this would be established one way or another in the coming days. So far, he has stopped short of describing the incident as a terrorist act.

Netanyahu said the attacker was suicidal, adding that he had called out “kill me” after being restrained by other passengers.

US President Donald Trump suggested later Thursday the pilot may be linked to Iran, though he provided no details.

This story had been updated with additional details.

World.title: Egypt secures record hard-currency reserves as overseas transfers spike
World.content:
Egypt’s financial sector achieved its strongest foreign reserve position in six years, boosted by a massive influx of capital from citizens living abroad.

Latest data released by the Central Bank of Egypt reveals that net foreign assets held across the banking system scaled $31.2 billion as of August 2026—a peak figure not seen since 2020.

Driving this capital accumulation is a persistent upward trajectory in overseas worker remittances.

In July 2026 alone, Egyptians abroad sent home nearly $4.5 billion, representing a robust 20.0% surge compared to the $3.8 billion recorded in July 2025.

The steady growth in transfers underscores renewed confidence in official banking channels and provides crucial hard-currency liquidity for Cairo’s broader economic stabilization efforts.

World.title: African Union urges restraint as Egypt, Ethiopia, and Eritrea plunge Horn of Africa into crisis
World.content:
The African Union Commission expressed deep concern regarding the escalating tensions among Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt, emphasizing that it is closely monitoring developments among the three nations.

In an official statement, the AU Commission called on the three member states to exercise maximum restraint and refrain from any actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine peace and stability in the region.

The Commission stressed the paramount importance of dialogue, peaceful negotiations, and diplomatic channels to resolve all outstanding issues, affirming its readiness to support efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions and fostering peaceful resolution among the involved parties.

Emphasis on dialogue and diplomatic channels

The African Union statement underscored that constructive engagement and adherence to regional stability are essential for safeguarding security in the Horn of Africa and the wider continent.

This first official comment from the African Union comes following the mutual expulsion of diplomats between Cairo and Addis Ababa under a 48-hour deadline, alongside Ethiopia’s decision to close its embassy in Asmara, expel Eritrean diplomats, and Eritrea’s subsequent severance of diplomatic ties with Addis Ababa.

World.title: Egypt condemns attack on power station in Medina, Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Egypt expressed its strong condemnation of the attack targeting a power station in Medina, in the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

In an official statement, Egypt reiterated its full denunciation of this flagrant violation and the continued attacks and attempts to destabilize the security and stability of the Kingdom, emphasizing that such an approach represents a dangerous escalation that increases tensions across the region as a whole.

Egypt stressed its categorical rejection of any attempts to compromise the security and sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, reaffirming its full solidarity with any measures taken by the Kingdom to maintain its stability and safety.

Cairo renewed its position that the security of Saudi Arabia is an integral part of Arab national security and is inextricably linked to Egyptian national security.

World.title: Saudi Arabia denies rumors of bombing attempt at Al-Masjid al-Haram in Mecca
World.content:
Saudi security authorities in the Holy City of Mecca denied the accuracy of rumors circulating across certain social media platforms alleging that an individual attempted to blow himself up inside the Grand Mosque (Al-Masjid al-Haram).

Saudi security authorities clarified that the incident actually involved the apprehension of an individual for harassing pedestrians and inciting panic and terror among them.

They confirmed that the situation was handled immediately by the competent authorities, and necessary legal actions were taken against him.

Security authorities in the Holy City emphasized the falsehood of the circulating allegations regarding the incident, calling on the public to refrain from spreading rumors or unverified information and highlighting the importance of obtaining news solely from official, accredited sources.

World.title: SN Brussels Travelers from Liberia, Sierra Leone Face Tougher Scrutiny as Europe Hunts ‘Bolle Jos’
World.content:
MONROVIA – For many Liberian and Sierra Leonean families, the SN Brussels flight is more than a ticket. Brussels Airlines, still called “SN” by most travelers here after the carrier it succeeded in 2007, is the plane that brings a mother home for Christmas, carries a student to a European campus and returns a trader with goods for a Waterside shop.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

It is also, investigators in Monrovia and Brussels now say, a route drug networks have tried to exploit.



Caught at the carousel

On July 31, Belgian customs officers were checking passengers off a Brussels Airlines flight from Freetown when they stopped a 22-year-old woman from Anderlecht, according to the Halle-Vilvoorde prosecutor’s office and Belgian media. Her two suitcases held 51 kilograms of cocaine.

She had not been on the plane. Investigators believe she was sent only to collect the bags and are still trying to establish how she got into the baggage reclaim hall. A judge later moved her from detention to electronic monitoring.

Weeks earlier at Roberts International Airport (RIA), Liberian security officers flagged six cargo boxes labeled as Maggi cubes and lappa. Inside were 198 compressed plates of cocaine. The Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) said at the time the shipment, valued at US$19.2 million, was bound for Brussels Airlines’ Europe-bound operations. A Justice Ministry charge sheet later listed London as the final destination.

This week, those two scenes met in a single policy fight in Europe. And the people likely to feel it first are not the kingpins, but honest passengers queuing at RIA and Lungi.

‘Chubby Jos’ next door

The man at the center of Europe’s anger lives one border away. Jos Leijdekkers, known in the Netherlands as “Bolle Jos” (Chubby Jos), is that country’s most wanted criminal. Dutch media placed him in Sierra Leone in early 2025.

In the Netherlands he was sentenced to 24 years in prison for cocaine trafficking and an attempted assassination. In Belgium, his sentences across several cases total more than 100 years, Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported. In May, a court in Dendermonde, Belgium, sentenced him in absentia to eight years for his role in moving 11 tonnes of cocaine from Sierra Leone to the Port of Antwerp in October 2023, hidden in palm kernel meal. Twenty accomplices were also convicted.

The Economist’s 1843 magazine reported on September 18 that he lived in Sierra Leone under the name “Omar Sheriff,” posed as a wealthy investor and kept bodyguards from Ghana and South Africa.

Dutch media have reported that he has a relationship, and a child, with a daughter of President Julius Maada Bio. FrontPageAfrica has not independently confirmed this.

No treaty, no handover

The Netherlands and Sierra Leone have no extradition treaty. The Dutch formally delivered an extradition request anyway, and Freetown has yet to sign off on it. Van Weel said in June that Sierra Leone keeps telling him the procedures are under way.

That patience has run out. On X on Thursday morning, Van Weel announced that “the EU will no longer provide budget support to the authorities of Sierra Leone this year.” He told the Dutch daily De Telegraaf a day earlier that the suspension, about €18 million for 2026, was because Sierra Leone is not cooperating on the extradition. The Netherlands also wants a planned €22.5 million for next year held back.

The freeze hits money paid straight into the state budget. Development and humanitarian aid are excluded, so Europe is aiming at the government, not at Sierra Leoneans in need. Van Weel has called it bizarre that Europe should support a country sheltering one of the world’s biggest drug criminals.

Speaking to NOS in Luxembourg on Thursday, Van Weel welcomed the Commission’s decision. “It sends a very clear signal from the European Commission that Sierra Leone must stop harboring this criminal,” he said.

Asked whether the measure was too harsh on an impoverished country, Van Weel turned the question back on its government. Leijdekkers, he said, causes “immense destruction, including for the people of Sierra Leone.”

“They could resolve this within 24 hours by arresting and extraditing this man,” he said.

If the aid freeze does not work, Van Weel warned, “we will continue to increase the pressure through other channels.” He added: “We are fully committed to bringing this criminal to the Netherlands.”

The Dutch have also worked through Sierra Leone’s neighbors. Van Weel told De Telegraaf in July that Liberia and Ghana are aware of the risks and frustrated by Freetown’s refusal to act.

Ghana has already moved. In September, its Narcotics Control Commission arrested three men accused of representing Leijdekkers’ network there, after French customs seized nearly 3.9 tonnes of cocaine in Dunkirk. The drugs, valued at about €225 million, were hidden in a container of plastic waste shipped from Ghana.

The Economist estimates about a third of the cocaine reaching Europe now passes through West Africa. Liberia is on its route map.

Liberia’s own test

Liberia’s record this year shows how close the trade has come to home.

Police charged five men and the cargo firm Global Logistics Services (GLS) on July 4 over the June RIA seizure of about 237.6 kilograms. Among them was Michael U.S. Browne, whose release from prison after a 2024 drug charge the Senate has ordered investigated.

Prosecutors allege GLS operations manager Paul Jamaal King organized the shipment and then tried to recover it after it was flagged, including by offering money to airport security. King has pleaded not guilty and is presumed innocent. In July, the Monrovia City Court found probable cause and sent him and six co-defendants to Criminal Court “C” for trial. Days later, the case appeared stalled because certified records had not reached the court.

Investigators followed the airport leads to the VOA community on the RIA Highway. On July 22, joint security forces arrested two foreign nationals and uncovered a suspected cocaine cache officials valued at up to US$50 million.

When the guards are the thieves

On Tuesday, a jury in Kakata convicted two LDEA agents posted at RIA, Special Agent Joe Logan and Agent Lovette Flowers, along with Nigerian national Tony Obi. Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie of the 13th Judicial Circuit sentenced each to 20 years, the maximum.

Prosecutors said the agents took four of 14 seized plates of cocaine and sold them, and that the network paid about US$10,000 in bribes to LDEA officers. The case began in July 2025 with Quita Dolo Kosso, who landed at RIA from Thailand on a Kenya Airways flight with about 3.4 kilograms of cocaine. She pleaded guilty and is serving five years.

The lesson for travelers is uncomfortable. Drugs can be caught at the gate and still leak out the back door. Europe has noticed both.

Brussels takes aim

Van Weel is in Luxembourg, where EU justice and home affairs ministers meet Thursday and Friday. The agenda covers migration, the EU drugs strategic framework and how the geopolitical climate is affecting Europe’s security. He wrote on X that talks would include “the safety of Europe and the EU-sanctions regime for organized crime.”

He is urging ministers to adopt the regime swiftly, Politico Europe’s Playbook reported. He told Playbook the Bolle Jos case calls for measures against all organized criminals Europe cannot immediately detain, “not only against him,” and said he hopes the regime is concluded by year’s end.

An EU diplomat with the Dutch delegation told OCCRP that cross-border networks can be “very effective” when based in a third country whose authorities will not cooperate or extradite. “The standard criminal law approach isn’t achieving the results we want,” the diplomat said. “That is why there is a push to expand that toolkit.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the package in her 2025 State of the Union address, and the EU Council mandated work on it. On July 9, the Commission and the EU’s foreign policy chief proposed a regime covering drug trafficking, migrant smuggling, human and firearms trafficking and money laundering. It would freeze assets, impose trade restrictions and bar listed people from entering or transiting EU states.

It still has to be agreed, and adoption needs the backing of all 27 member states. Earlier efforts stalled because national police feared sanctions could tip off suspects and spoil investigations. Van Weel said support is stronger now.

What it means for SN Brussels passengers

Sanctions target kingpins, their financiers and fixers, not ordinary travelers. But passengers on the Monrovia–Freetown–Brussels line already live with the side effects, and those are likely to grow.

Tighter checks on arrival. The 51-kilogram arrest came during a targeted customs check of passengers off the Freetown flight. Expect more of those, and more bags opened.

Networks recruiting the young. This week, Belgian and French authorities announced 21 arrests in a ring that used Brussels Airport. It recruited “extractors” through social media, bought tickets just to reach baggage halls and paid airport workers to pull drugs from suitcases before they reached the carousel.

Your bag, someone else’s crime.

The RIA cases show cargo and luggage can be tampered with by insiders. Lock and label bags, and refuse parcels from anyone, even relatives, without seeing what is inside.

Travel bans for facilitators. Once adopted, the EU regime could bar listed people from entering or passing through Europe. Anyone working for a front company, freight forwarder or fixer tied to a listed network risks being swept up.

A reputation tax. Every bust adds to the suspicion attached to a Liberian or Sierra Leonean passport at a European counter. Honest travelers pay that bill in delays and questions.

For now, the man Europe most wants sits a short flight from Monrovia, beyond reach. Van Weel insists Freetown could change that in a day. The question for Liberia is whether it is seen as part of the problem or part of the fix. The 20-year sentences handed down in Kakata this week were a start. The next test is the US$19.2 million trial.

World.title: Hungry and Out of Options, More Poor Liberians Turn to Begging as Prices Outrun Income
World.content:
Members of Vamoma group seeking assistance in Monrovia. Photo: Fatu A. Kamara

Summary

As Liberia’s economy shows signs of recovery on paper, soaring food and fuel prices, worsened by a government fuel surcharge and new health care fees imposed after US aid cuts, have outpaced wage growth.

Ten Liberians interviewed in Monrovia say growing unemployment, lost livelihoods and financial hardship in the last two years have pushed them to depend on strangers and charitable support to survive.

Humanitarian organizations and government say they are seeing growing demand for assistance as families struggle with food, school fees, healthcare and other basic needs.

By Fatu Kamara with New Narratives

BROAD STREET, Monrovia – It has been a long day for Joseph. The sun is beginning to set, and the 48-year-old father of three has been trawling the streets of Monrovia since morning, asking for money.



On most days, he begs for money to feed his family. Today, he can’t even raise enough to get home to Brewerville, on the outskirts of the city.

“Since this morning, nobody has given me a dime,” he says.

Joseph lost his job in waste management in 2025 after the death of his boss. A high school graduate who earned L$10,000 (US$55) monthly, he spent about a year looking for another job without success.

He says he now has two options: begging or stealing. “It is not fair for me to be begging people in the streets, but I will not go to steal.”

Joseph is one of 10 people interviewed for this story who said they began begging within the past two years. Most said they had no jobs, had lost sources of income or lacked money to start a business. (FrontPage Africa/New Narratives is withholding the names of people in this story to protect them from stigma.) Liberia’s economy grew 5.1 percent in 2025, according to the African Development Bank, a jump from years before, but most families haven’t felt it. Growth came mostly from mining royalties to government, not job creation, and extreme poverty still rose to 35.8 percent.

The crisis deepened when the Trump administration canceled 27 of 29 USAID programs in Liberia in May 2025, cutting nearly US$360 million from health and education. Large cuts by other donors followed too. The government responded by adding a $0.25 per gallon petroleum surcharge and implementing new patient fees for healthcare. For families already struggling to afford food, the surcharge pushed up transport and food costs, and the hospital fees have deterred many from going for treatment or crippled them financially when they face emergencies. Baba Conteh, an economist, says economic recovery has not translated into meaningful jobs and stable incomes for ordinary households. Aid cuts have trickled down throughout the economy. “Job loss is one of the most common pathways into poverty,” Conteh says, particularly when the loss continues long enough for families to exhaust their savings and sell productive assets. In extreme cases, he says, people may become homeless, engage in high-risk survival activities, depend heavily on public charity or even resort to committing crimes.

That is exactly what is happening. At Vamoma house on Tubman Boulevard, in Sinkor, Esther Kamara leads a group of widows, elderly people and people with disabilities who gather to seek assistance. She says the group had about 280 members in 2024 and has since grown by 50.

People living in poverty gather at Vamoma house, on Tubman Boulevard, in Sinkor

“I have even started refusing people because the number just getting plenty and no help is coming,” Kamara says.

After more than a decade of leading the group, Kamara says the past two years have been the toughest. “Many days the women come to me when they or their children are sick and no money to take them to hospital, so we just buy drugs and they take it,” she says. The drugs are usually antibiotics, bought without a prescription and taken with no medical guidance, making the child likely to build antibiotic resistance.

Support groups under pressure from growing demand

The pressure is being felt by organizations that provide assistance. Siakeh Foundation and Kimbo Foundation, two organizations working with vulnerable Liberians, say requests for help have doubled over the last two years.

Four Hunger, a U.S.-registered nonprofit in Liberia, reports an increase in requests from families who previously managed to meet at least some of their basic needs but now struggle with food, school fees, healthcare and other essentials.

“The growing demand has put considerable pressure on our resources. One of the most difficult parts is that we often receive requests we genuinely want to respond to but cannot fully meet,” says co-founder Windell S. King.

At Rescue for Abandoned and Children in Hardship, or REACH, Ne-Suah Livingstone, founder and executive director, says she has also seen families pushed into situations they previously managed to avoid.

“One case that remains with me involved a family whose daughter’s annual school fees were about US$1,000. Her father had previously worked on a USAID-funded project but lost his job after the projects ended.”

She says the fees were far beyond the reach of the small organization.

REACH receives about twice as many requests for assistance as it did two years ago.

“This is one of the hardest tasks I face every day,” says Livingstone. “To say to a person in dire need that neither I nor my organization is able to help you; saying this can be like you have asked me to hurt someone.”

“I won’t steal” but begging comes with humiliation

At Vamoma, Hawa, a 43-year-old widow with two children, says asking for help became a last resort after she lost her husband in 2024. She says her youngest child, 14, is still in school through support from her church. Her older child is at home because she has not found the money to keep him in school.

“People were mocking me in my community because I am poor,” Hawa says. “I felt embarrassed and I could not bear the shame anymore.”

She says Vamoma offers more than the possibility of receiving money or food.

“At least when I am among my friends and we are laughing, the stress goes down,” Hawa says. “I don’t know what I was going to do if I had not joined the group.”

For some members, the hardship goes beyond asking strangers for help. Kamara says some elderly and vulnerable people face stigma in their communities.

“You know when people are like this, you will not find any family member coming around them,” she says. “They can abandon them. Sometimes they call them witches and wizards.”

Larwuo, a member of Vamoma, stands in front of her home. She says she was abandoned by her son.

Last month one elderly member of the group died here. Kamara had to ask government to collect the body.

Government response constrained by limited resources

Officials at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection have observed the growing need but have little money to help.

“The key gap in addressing the issues affecting these vulnerable groups is limited resources, preventing the ministry from reaching them,” says Alex Divine, the ministry’s assistant director of Programs, Partnership and Resource Mobilization.

The government tried to reduce the rapidly growing number of street children, which hit 366,000 according to a survey in 2023, before the cost-of-living crisis escalated. Through its “Support a Child, Save the Future” initiative, launched in 2024 to remove children from the streets through school enrollment, family reunification and support for caregivers. The government has conceded that it did not raise any of the $15 million cost of the project from donors and only budgeted a total of $1.3m itself. The ministry came under public fire this month when an official posted the names of children who were allegedly helped on Facebook. Since then, the ministry has refused to share details. There has been no independent audit of the project.

Women share cooked food donated by the Jetty company.

“While existing programs provide critical support, the support is insufficient because it reaches a limited number of the overall vulnerable population across the country,” Divine says.

At Vamoma, the group has no permanent shelter. Kamara says members once put together sticks and zinc to create a small shelter, but police later dismantled it.

“When the rain is falling, some people cover themselves with plastic,” she says. “Sometimes you see people trembling with the cold. We are disappointed in our leaders because they are sitting down and the people dying.”

The only help comes in food donations from groups like the Indian company Jeety Rubber or Yamah Brown, a dry goods seller in Red Light, who recently donated two bags of rice.

“They are our mothers. They don’t deserve it, but condition made them like this,” Brown says. “We will continue to help as long as we can afford.”

While assistance is important, Kamara says they want something reliable.

“What we really want is jobs for members, especially the widows, people who are able to work,” she says. “Many of them are strong and able to work, but we all come here and sit from morning to night because there’s nothing to do. If we had jobs, we won’t be here.”

Joseph agrees that breaking the cycle of dependency requires opportunities beyond daily charity.

“Even if I can get money to start a business, I would be grateful,” he says. “And a man is only respected when he provides for his family.”

For now, as the sun sets, Joseph gives up finding enough money to get transport home. He sets out on foot for a walk that may take hours and will end with the faces of disappointed and hungry children. He will wake up tomorrow and try again.

This report is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency which had no say in the story’s content.
