This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who runs the territory until then

Jean-Paul Fereira, the first vice-president, holds the interim by right. He already stood in during earlier periods when Serville was away from office, Guyaweb noted.

Fereira was mayor of Awala-Yalimapo from 2001 to March 2026, according to Guyane la 1ère. Since 2021 he has handled sustainable development and the energy transition at the CTG.

Continuity is the stabiliser here. An order dated 30 September renewed the signing powers of the CTG’s senior civil servant, France-Guyane said, a required formality.

A divided majority

Serville won the CTG in 2021 in alliance with Fereira and Jessi Américain, taking 54.83% of the vote. The assembly then elected him in the first round with 35 of 55 votes, Guyane la 1ère recalled.

That coalition has since frayed. France-Guyane said Américain and Muriel Briquet lost their portfolios, and three councillors formed a breakaway group called Guyane sans limites.

The paper added that recent plenary sessions reached a quorum only thanks to the opposition. It described the opposition as the largest and most united group in the chamber.

A third-round plurality could therefore produce a surprise. France-Guyane stressed this was speculation, and that no member had yet officially addressed the succession.

Whoever wins serves until the end of the term, which the paper put at March 2028. The new leader inherits the push for more autonomy and the ties of French Guiana Joins the Caribbean Bloc, Pulling France Closer.

Farewell first

Before any vote, the territory will bury its leader. A cultural vigil is planned at the Progt in Matoury on Friday 9 October, Guyaweb reported.

A religious service follows on the morning of Saturday 10 October, before burial in Matoury. Fereira will represent the CTG.

Serville’s seat in the assembly passes to the next name on his list, Andgreen Hutchinson, a former nurse, France-Guyane reported. If she declines, it goes to Fabien Canavy.

What Is Not Yet Known

The CTG has not published a formal convocation, so 30 October rests on Guyane la 1ère’s report. No candidate has declared, and it is unclear whether Fereira will stand.

It is also unknown how the dissident councillors and the opposition will vote. The number of vice-presidents will only be fixed at that session.

More: France Raises French Guiana Overseas Funds in Budget, from The Rio Times.

Who is running French Guiana’s local government now?

First vice-president Jean-Paul Fereira leads the CTG in the interim until the assembly elects a new president.

When will the new CTG president be elected?

Within one month of Serville’s death on 30 September. Guyane la 1ère reported that the vote is planned for 30 October 2026.

How does the vote work?

The 55 assembly members vote by secret ballot. An absolute majority is needed in the first two rounds, and a simple plurality decides a third.

Sources: Guyaweb, 2 October 2026; Guyane la 1ère, 2 October 2026; France-Guyane, 1 October 2026.

BUSINESS · HONDURAS

Key Facts — The country Honduras, which switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2023. Shops run by Chinese owners are now more visible in Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula.

— What happened On Friday 2 October, small-business leader Victorino Carranza said Chinese firms pay no import, sales, income or services taxes, El Mundo reported.

— Who is involved Gremipe, the guild of micro and small businesses, and Congress, which on 26 May voted 81 of 117 deputies present to supervise Chinese-owned shops.

— What it means for you Retailers and importers may see tighter tax and customs checks. Investors should treat the claim as unproven until the tax authority reports.

— Still open No documents were shown, and no official count of Chinese-owned shops exists. Results of the May congressional review have not been published.

A Honduran small-business leader has accused Chinese firms of operating without paying the main national taxes. Victorino Carranza, president of the micro and small business guild Gremipe, made the claim on a television forum on Friday 2 October.

The Tegucigalpa daily El Mundo reported his remarks the same day, noting that no tax documents were presented. Once Noticias, whose Canal 11 forum hosted the debate, said Carranza raised doubts about tax compliance by some Chinese shops.

What the small-business guild alleges

“We are fully certain that our Chinese brothers are not paying taxes on imports, sales tax, income tax or taxes on services,” Carranza said. He spoke of businesspeople from China who have set up in Honduras, not of a named company.

He did not say which law or decree would grant such exemptions. He also did not say whether the gap comes from formal tax breaks or from weak enforcement.

Carranza framed the issue as one of fair competition rather than of nationality. Honduran micro and small firms pay their taxes, he argued, and still struggle to obtain cheap credit.

“We are not being treated as we deserve,” he said. His demand is for equal conditions inside the Honduran market.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Honduras markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Congress already ordered a review in May

The question is not new in Tegucigalpa. On 26 May, the National Congress approved a motion to supervise shops of Chinese origin, with 81 votes from 117 deputies present.

The motion, tabled by deputy Mario Pérez, covers tax payments, the legality and origin of imports and the migration status of staff. It also asks about possible movements of foreign currency.

That review gives the state a channel to test the claim. The tax collector, the Revenue Administration Service (SAR), holds the records that could confirm or rule out any exemptions.

El Mundo said there is still no official figure for how many Chinese-owned businesses operate in Honduras. Their presence has grown most visibly in the two largest cities.

Why the dispute matters beyond shopkeepers

Honduras broke with Taiwan and opened relations with Beijing in 2023. See: In a historic move, Honduras inaugurates its Embassy in China after severing ties with Taiwan.

The retail complaint now tests that relationship at street level. It also reaches beyond the shop counter to customs and tax policy.

The complaint lands on two fronts for President Nasry Asfura (Who Is Nasry Asfura, the President of Honduras in 2026). It touches tax collection and the relationship with Beijing.

On the same forum, Alejandro Young of the Chinese chamber of commerce and industry defended free competition. “Why be afraid of competition?” he asked, according to Once Noticias.

There is a stabilising side as well. The guild asks for equal rules, not closures, and an audit can settle the facts without new legislation.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not known whether any Chinese firms in Honduras hold a formal tax exemption, or whether Carranza’s claim rests on observation. The allegation has not been independently confirmed.

Neither report of 2 October carried a response from the SAR or from the Chinese embassy. Findings from the review approved on 26 May have also not been made public.

Sources: El Mundo (Honduras), “Gremipe denuncia supuestas exoneraciones a empresas chinas y reclama competencia en igualdad de condiciones”, 2 October 2026; Once Noticias, “¿Negocios chinos vrs. hondureños? Comercio del gigante asiático gana terreno en Honduras”, 2 October 2026; remarks by Gremipe president Victorino Carranza on a television forum, 2 October 2026, as reported by El Mundo and Once Noticias.

SECURITY · HAITI

Key Facts — The country Haiti shares the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic. It plans its first elections in a decade on 13 December 2026, under pressure from armed gangs.

— What happened On Friday 2 October the US embassy in Port-au-Prince said it continues firm support for Haiti’s police and armed forces, Le Nouvelliste reported.

— The numbers The embassy says a US-backed programme will graduate 4,000 new police by early 2027. The prime minister said on 24 September that more than 2,000 had been trained this year.

— What it means for you Security sets the pace for travel, trade and the December vote. Duty-free US access for Haitian apparel now runs to the end of 2028.

— Still open What new money, if any, comes with the pledge, and whether the UN-backed anti-gang force reaches its 5,500 ceiling before its mandate ends on 31 March 2027.

US support for Haiti’s police and army will continue, the US embassy in Port-au-Prince told reporters on Friday 2 October. The Port-au-Prince daily Le Nouvelliste reported the briefing, held at the Karibe hotel to introduce new diplomats.

The message came days after the UN Security Council renewed the multinational Gang Suppression Force. Haiti has also just taken a one-year chair at CARICOM, the 15-member Caribbean Community.

What the US embassy said

Julien Kreuze, the embassy’s press attaché, said security is “the foundation on which everything else rests”, according to Le Nouvelliste’s French account. He said Washington led the push to reauthorise the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) this week.

He added that the United States wants the force’s operations to intensify as new contingents arrive this autumn and winter. He said Washington continues to give firm support to the Haitian National Police (PNH) and the Armed Forces of Haiti (FAd’H).

On the police, Kreuze said US backing for the P4000 programme will help recruit, train and graduate 4,000 officers by early 2027. Le Nouvelliste noted that he gave no detail of any support for the armed forces.

The briefing presented six US diplomats, three of them in acting roles. They include acting deputy chief of mission Holly Mackey and John Heinbeck, who heads the anti-narcotics and law enforcement office.

Haiti security build-up: P4000 police target against officers trained (24 September) and the Gang Suppression Force's authorised strength against troops deployed (29 September 2026). Source: PM Alix Didier Fils-Aimé at the UN and US statement, via The Haitian Times, 27 and 29 September 2026.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Haiti Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Where the security build-up stands

Haiti’s government gives a similar target, The Haitian Times reported. Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé told a UN meeting on 24 September that over 2,000 officers were trained this year.

He said another class should graduate in November. The paper noted that the figure counts officers trained, not a net rise in active police strength.

On 29 September the Security Council extended the GSF to 31 March 2027, with 12 votes in favour and three abstentions. The vote’s background is in Haiti Gang Suppression Force Faces UN Renewal Vote After Reprisal Kills at Least 11.

The force is authorised for 5,500 military and police personnel. The United States says more than 1,500 troops are already deployed, with over 4,000 more expected in the coming months.

Trade and aid alongside security

Kreuze said security and democratic government cannot deliver lasting stability without economic prospects. He tied this to the extension of HOPE/HELP, the US trade preference laws for Haiti, to the end of 2028.

The laws give Haitian apparel duty-free access to the US market. The Haitian Times reported in August that they have underpinned the sector for more than 15 years.

Kreuze also described the United States as Haiti’s largest bilateral donor of humanitarian aid. That claim could not be independently confirmed.

International support can buy Haiti time and space, he said. Long-term solutions, however, must be driven and owned by Haitians themselves.

Haiti takes a CARICOM social development chair

On 1 October Haiti took the one-year chair of CARICOM’s Council for Human and Social Development (COHSOD), Juno7 and Le Nouvelliste reported. The council covers education, public health, youth, women, culture, labour and social protection.

Foreign Minister Raina Forbin will coordinate the chair on behalf of the government. Its stated priorities include youth and women’s participation, creative industries and closer cooperation on health and education.

The post is a coordinating role rather than a source of funding. It still gives Haiti a regional voice before the elections. The timetable is covered in Haiti Electoral Council Warns Parties Against Campaigning Before 13 December Vote.

What Is Not Yet Known

The embassy did not say how much new money, if any, comes with renewed US support for Haiti. Nor did it detail what help the armed forces will receive.

It is unclear whether the GSF will reach full strength before March. The two governments also give different dates for the 4,000-officer goal: the end of 2026 and early 2027.

Sources: Le Nouvelliste, US embassy briefing, 2 October 2026; Le Nouvelliste, COHSOD chair, 2 October 2026; Juno7, 2 October 2026; The Haitian Times, 27 September 2026; The Haitian Times, 29 September 2026; The Haitian Times, 17 August 2026.

ENVIRONMENT · GUATEMALA

Key Facts — The country Guatemala lies where three tectonic plates meet, and small quakes are routine. Laguna de Ayarza is a volcanic crater lake in Santa Rosa department, in the south-east.

— What happened Insivumeh, the national seismology institute, said on 2 October 2026 that at least 180 quakes struck near the lagoon in September. The largest, magnitude 4.1, hit on 30 September.

— The numbers Only three were felt: magnitude 3.4 on 19 September, then 4.1 and 3.0 on 30 September. A Rio Times count of Insivumeh’s public map finds 19 quakes on 1 October and 17 on 2 October.

— What it means for you Insivumeh calls the sequence normal for the area. The strongest shaking reached intensity IV, felt as light, though residents of nearby Pinos Altos report cracked walls.

— Still open The swarm’s exact source and duration. Insivumeh plans a field visit to install sensors, and has drawn no link between the quakes and bubbles seen in the lagoon.

The Ayarza seismic swarm in south-eastern Guatemala reached at least 180 quakes in September, the national seismology institute said on Friday. Its report, published on 2 October, puts the largest at magnitude 4.1.

The institute says the sequence fits the area’s history and lies within normal parameters. It also says more quakes cannot be ruled out, and its public map shows they had not stopped by Friday evening.

What the seismology institute reported

Insivumeh, the National Institute of Seismology, Volcanology, Meteorology and Hydrology, places the epicentres about 2 kilometres south of Laguna de Ayarza. They lie in Casillas municipality, close to the border with Jutiapa department.

Activity stayed low for most of September. The rate rose after a magnitude 3.4 quake at 08:15 on 19 September, the institute said.

At 08:24 on 30 September a magnitude 4.1 quake struck, the largest so far, followed by a 3.0 at 08:43. These three are the only quakes residents reported feeling, though others may also have been noticed.

The quakes are shallow and linked to normal faults, where the crust is being pulled apart. La Hora, a Guatemala City daily, reported the same figures on 2 October.

Rio Times count of quakes listed per day on Insivumeh's public seismic map within about 5 km of the Ayarza swarm, 19 September to 2 October 2026 (2 October to 19:14 local time); not an official Insivumeh tally. Source: Rio Times count of Insivumeh public seismic map data, read 3 October 2026.

Still active on 1 and 2 October

Luis Alejandro Argueta Cermeño, Insivumeh’s south-east coordinator, told Prensa Libre of 32 quakes in the 24 hours to 07:00 on 1 October. Two of them were felt, the 4.1 and the 3.0.

A Rio Times count of Insivumeh’s public seismic map, read early on 3 October, finds 19 quakes within about 5 kilometres of the swarm on 1 October. It finds 17 on 2 October, up to the map’s latest entry at 19:14 local time.

None of those exceeded magnitude 2.5, well below the 30 September peak. The daily counts come from the map’s entries and are not an official Insivumeh tally.

Cracks in Pinos Altos, bubbles in the lagoon

In the hamlet of Pinos Altos, near the epicentres, residents told Prensa Libre of underground rumbling, cracked walls and frightened schoolchildren. A teacher showed new cracks in classrooms at the village school, which about 80 children attend.

Many homes there are built of adobe and are damp from the rains. These damage reports come from residents, and no official damage assessment has been published.

Separately, videos of bubbles rising in the lagoon spread on social media in late September. The environment ministry (MARN) said gas can escape through cracks in the floor of the volcanic caldera.

An inspection with Insivumeh and Conred, the national disaster agency, found no sign of boiling water, Prensa Libre reported on 1 October. Insivumeh’s report draws no link between the quakes and the bubbles.

Why the institute is not alarmed

Santa Rosa has a history of swarm-type sequences of shallow quakes, the report notes. The 4.1 quake produced a top intensity of IV on the Modified Mercalli scale, meaning light shaking.

That peak was felt near the point where Santa Rosa, Jutiapa and Jalapa departments meet. The institute urges people to stay calm and to rely only on official channels from Insivumeh and Conred.

It says it will keep issuing synopses and special bulletins as the sequence evolves. The same institute monitors the country’s volcanoes, as in Guatemala’s Volcán De Fuego Eruption Forces Evacuations.

Shallow swarms are not unusual in the region. Colombia saw a comparable episode in late September, covered in Tolima Seismic Swarm: M4.5 Tremor Shakes Central Colombia.

What Is Not Yet Known

Insivumeh has not established the swarm’s precise source, and its analysis is still under way. Geologists and geophysicists are due to visit and install sensors, with no date announced.

Nobody can yet say how long the Ayarza seismic swarm will last or whether stronger quakes will follow. The institute says only that further quakes in the epicentral area cannot be ruled out.

Where is Laguna de Ayarza?

It is a volcanic crater lake in Santa Rosa department, in south-eastern Guatemala. The quakes are centred about 2 kilometres south of it, in Casillas municipality, near the border with Jutiapa.

Is the Ayarza seismic swarm dangerous?

Insivumeh says the sequence is within normal parameters for the area. The strongest shaking so far reached intensity IV, felt as light, although residents of nearby Pinos Altos report cracked walls.

Are the quakes making the lagoon boil?

No. An inspection by Insivumeh, Conred and the environment ministry found no evidence of boiling. Officials say bubbles can come from gas escaping through cracks in the lake floor.

Sources: Insivumeh, synopsis INS-DG-SS-SI-2026-04, seismic activity in Casillas, Santa Rosa, 2 October 2026; Insivumeh, public seismic map, read 3 October 2026; La Hora, “Laguna de Ayarza: Insivumeh registra más de 180 sismos en la zona”, 2 October 2026; Prensa Libre, Pinos Altos report and lagoon inspection report, 1 October 2026.

ECONOMY · COSTA RICA

Key Facts — The country Costa Rica lets its currency, the colón, float. The Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) runs Monex, the wholesale market that sets the daily dollar rate.

— What happened The dollar’s Monex average rose from a record low of 446.80 colones on 17 September to 458.67 on 2 October. That is a 2.7% rise, BCCR data show.

— The numbers The US Federal Reserve raised its rate by a quarter point to 3.75–4.00% on 16 September. The BCCR held its own rate at 3.00% on 24 September.

— What it means for you At Monex averages, US$1,000 fetched 11,870 colones more on 2 October than on 17 September (about US$26). Dollar earners gain; dollar borrowers paid in colones pay slightly more.

— Still open Whether the rise lasts. Analysts expect year-end bonus payments to bring dollars back in, and the BCCR next sets its rate on 26 November.

Costa Rica’s exchange rate has turned after months of record colón strength. The dollar’s average on Monex closed at 458.67 colones on Friday 2 October, up 2.7% from the 17 September low.

The turn began the day after the US Federal Reserve’s first rate rise since 2023, a quarter-point move on 16 September. A currency analyst quoted by Diario Extra on 3 October calls the Fed the main driver, with oil and thin trading also weighing.

From a record low to a four-month high

On 17 September the Monex average fell to 446.80 colones, the lowest since the market opened, BCCR data show. It beat the earlier record of 447.77 set on 11 September.

The dollar then rose in almost every session, reaching 460.45 on 1 October. El Observador noted that was the first close above 460 since early June.

On Friday the average eased 1.78 colones to 458.67, the first fall after five straight rises, La Nación reported. The central bank’s reference rate for Saturday is 455.71 colones to buy and 462.08 to sell.

Monex weighted-average dollar rate in colones, selected sessions 16 September to 2 October 2026; grey bar marks the 17 September record low. Source: Banco Central de Costa Rica (BCCR), 2 October 2026.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Costa Rica markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why analysts point to Washington

Carlos Valerín, a currency market analyst, told Diario Extra the Fed hike was the main factor. He added the BCCR’s decision to hold its rate and talk of further US rises.

The BCCR kept its policy rate at 3.00% by majority vote on 24 September. That leaves the local rate below the new US range of 3.75–4.00%, a gap that favours saving in dollars.

Bank president Róger Madrigal, quoted by Diario Extra, said the wider gap could prompt capital outflows and lift the exchange rate. He said the bank’s stance is to watch the move prudently rather than widen the difference.

Not only the Fed

Economist Daniel Ortiz told Diario Extra that oil near US$100 a barrel raises the dollars needed for fuel imports. Valerín said September and October are thin months, so moves tend to be sharper.

The pressure is regional rather than local. Diario Extra noted the Mexican and Colombian pesos also weakened, and Peru’s sol had its worst month since March.

The colón is still far stronger than a year ago

The rise is small against the colón’s long climb. Friday’s 458.67 is 7.7% below the 497.07 of 2 January and well under 504.02 a year earlier, BCCR data show.

Ortiz said free-zone companies, which export from tax-exempt zones, ran a US$7 billion currency surplus to August. Valerín expects year-end bonuses and transnational payrolls in November and December to push the dollar down again.

For exporters, tourism firms and households paid in dollars, each dollar now buys more colones. Borrowers with dollar loans and colón incomes face slightly higher repayments in local terms.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is unclear whether the move is a turn or a pause. Year-end inflows push the exchange rate down, while oil prices and US rates push it up.

The BCCR has not signalled any change before its final scheduled rate meeting on 26 November. Whether the Fed raises rates again this year is also open.

Sources: Banco Central de Costa Rica (BCCR), Monex trading summary and Monex average exchange rate table, data to 2 October 2026; BCCR monetary policy statement 05-2026, 24 September 2026; Ministry of Finance (Hacienda), BCCR reference rate for 3 October 2026; Diario Extra, 3 October 2026; El Observador, 1 October 2026; La Nación, 2 October 2026; El Financiero, 17 September 2026; Infobae, 22 September 2026. Rate: 457 colones per US$ (2 October 2026 close).

SOCIAL SECURITY · SURINAME

Key Facts — The country Suriname, the former Dutch colony on South America’s north coast. A social security treaty with the Netherlands lets many Dutch benefits, including most disability payments, be paid there.

— What happened On 2 October 2026 GFC Nieuws reported that Surinamers with a Dutch WIA disability benefit may be owed money. The Dutch agency is rechecking 52,000 benefits by hand (UWV, 9 September).

— The numbers The Dutch Court of Audit estimated in December 2025 that at least 16,385 people were underpaid. The average shortfall was €2,745 gross (about US$3,090), up to roughly €25,000 (about US$28,100).

— What it means for you If your WIA started between January 2020 and December 2024, you may be in the review, even living in Suriname. Overpayments do not have to be returned.

— Still open No figure exists for affected people in Suriname. Checks may run into 2027, and requests for a review must be filed before 1 September 2028.

People in Suriname who receive the Dutch WIA benefit for long-term illness may be owed money after years of Dutch miscalculation. The Surinamese news site GFC Nieuws flagged the issue on 2 October 2026, as the Dutch repair operation enters its main phase.

The WIA is the Dutch work-incapacity scheme for employees who cannot work after two years of illness. It is run by UWV, the Dutch employee insurance agency, which has apologised for the errors.

What went wrong at the Dutch agency

The benefit is built on a “daily wage”, worked out from what someone earned in the year before falling ill. UWV says it sometimes got that figure wrong for benefits that started from 2020 to 2024.

The agency lists four problem groups: irregular earnings, holiday pay, year-end bonuses and earlier benefits such as sickness pay. The Netherlands Court of Audit blamed mainly pandemic home working, weaker quality checks and less time to train staff.

In its December 2025 report the court put the number of underpaid people at 16,385 to 20,645. Others were overpaid instead.

On 9 September UWV widened the review to about 73,000 benefits. Some 21,000 were cleared quickly, leaving around 52,000 for a manual check.

WIA benefits started 2020–2024: 73,000 selected for review, 21,000 cleared, 52,000 needing a manual check, including 13,000 re-added. Source: UWV, 9 September 2026.

About 13,000 people had earlier been told no check was needed and will now be included. UWV said it would write to them in October.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Suriname Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why people in Suriname are affected

The Dutch WIA benefit can move abroad only to countries with an agreement. Suriname is one of them.

According to Dutch export figures cited by GFC Nieuws, 87 people in Suriname received the partial WGA strand in 2023. Another 74 received the IVA strand for full, lasting incapacity.

There are no public figures on how many of them fall inside the repair group. The review is no new medical test, and the disability percentage stays as it is.

Family, pension and benefit links between the two countries remain close. For the wider picture, see Suriname Explained 2026: The Oil Hope, the Dutch Legacy, the Economy and What to Watch.

How the compensation works

Where the daily wage was too low, UWV corrects it and the monthly payment rises from then on. Money missed in the past comes as a one-off payment under a scheme in force since 1 September 2026.

The payment covers the period from 1 January 2020 at most, and is free of Dutch wage and income tax. Euro sums here use €0.889 per US dollar (2 October close).

UWV contacts people it has selected, and the past payment follows within six weeks of a decision. Those not contacted can ask for a review themselves, but only before 1 September 2028.

The risk runs the other way too: a corrected benefit can turn out lower. Past overpayments need not be repaid, under a policy confirmed by the Dutch government in July.

What Is Not Yet Known

UWV says the checks could run into 2027. Dutch broadcaster NOS reported that €100 million (about US$112 million) is set aside, but not how much will reach people abroad.

It is also unclear how a higher Dutch benefit interacts with Surinamese tax rules. Readers can check Taxes in Suriname for Expats: Rates, Residency and the Guilder Question and seek advice.

World.title: Masked men rob woman near Blue Marlin Drive; victim injured during struggle
World.content:
Masked men rob woman near Blue Marlin Drive; victim injured during struggle

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize City police are investigating after a woman was reportedly attacked and robbed by two masked men in the Caribbean Shores area on Thursday afternoon.

A 30-year-old woman told police she was walking near the corner of Cottontree/Cotton Wick Street and Blue Marlin Drive at around 1:37 p.m. when two men dressed in black and wearing ski masks approached her from behind near Good Fortune Chinese Shop.

The men allegedly took her black backpack containing approximately $300, a Belize driver’s licence, Social Security card and Atlantic Bank debit card.

Police say a struggle occurred during the robbery, resulting in the woman suffering abrasions to her left wrist and pain to her right shoulder.

The two assailants subsequently fled along Cotton Wick Street. Police investigations continue.

World.title: Rubber Boots Beating: Woman beat by sister-in-law with rubber boots on San Roman banana farm
World.content:
Rubber Boots Beating: Woman beat by sister-in-law with rubber boots on San Roman banana farm

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are seeking a woman following an alleged attack on a banana farm worker in San Roman Village, Stann Creek District, in which the complainant says she was repeatedly struck with a rubber boot.

A 33-year-old woman reported that she returned from work around 7:30 p.m. Thursday and was walking home when her sister-in-law called out to her.

The woman told police that her sister-in-law approached her aggressively, asked, “What is your problem?” and subsequently picked up a black rubber boot and struck her on the forehead.

According to the report, the woman attempted to defend herself but was allegedly struck several more times.

The woman told police she did not know what prompted the confrontation and requested court action.

Police issued her with a medico-legal form and listed the sister-in-law as a wanted person.

World.title: Chad Borland killed, another injured after car plunges 150 feet into bushes off Hummingbird Highway
World.content:
Chad Borland killed, another injured after car plunges 150 feet into bushes off Hummingbird Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a fatal road traffic accident near Belmopan in which a vehicle reportedly left the Hummingbird Highway and travelled approximately 150 feet into thick bushes, leaving one man dead and another injured.

Police received information about the accident around 4:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 1, near La Cabana bar, shortly after Wooden Street.

At the scene, officers encountered Jeffrey Perez with an apparent injury to the back of his head.

Police followed a trail of vehicle debris leading diagonally from the highway into the bushes, where they found a black Mazda extensively damaged and facing away from the highway.

A second man, identified as Chad Borland of University Boulevard, Belmopan, was found motionless approximately one foot away from the vehicle. He was transported to the Western Regional Hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 5:20 p.m.

Preliminary police investigations indicate the Mazda had been travelling from the direction of the roundabout toward Armenia before leaving the roadway.

Police say statements remained to be obtained and surveillance cameras in the vicinity of La Cabana bar were also expected to be reviewed as the investigation continues.

World.title: Toledo man on his way to buy ‘Badman’ at 2 in the morning attacked for $20 with pint bottle
World.content:
Toledo man on his way to buy ‘Badman’ at 2 in the morning attacked for $20 with pint bottle

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are seeking two brothers following an alleged attack in San Felipe Village, Toledo District, in which a 41-year-old man was reportedly wounded with a broken pint bottle after being unable to hand over $20.

Police say they responded to a report of a physical altercation shortly after 2:00 a.m. on Friday and encountered one man suffering injuries to his left ear and the right side of his head.

That man reportedly told police that he had left home between 1:30 and 2:00 a.m. to purchase a “badman” at a village bar when he was confronted by two brothers known to him.

According to the report, the men demanded $20, and when the complainant was unable to produce the money, he was allegedly attacked with a broken pint bottle.

He was taken to the Punta Gorda Community Hospital, where his injuries were certified as wounding. Police say, however, that after being discharged at 5:10 a.m., he declined to provide a formal statement.

The brothers are nevertheless listed by police as wanted in connection with the matter.

World.title: Masked robbers hold up Punta Gorda bar; suspect detained, imitation firearm recovered
World.content:
Masked robbers hold up Punta Gorda bar; suspect detained, imitation firearm recovered

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery at a bar in Punta Gorda Town after two masked men reportedly entered the establishment and made off with cash and other items on Thursday night.

According to police, a bar manager reported that around 10:16 p.m. on October 1, two men entered the establishment on Lucille Melendez Boulevard. One of the men was reportedly armed with what appeared to be a firearm and pointed it at an employee, while his accomplice went into the cashier area and took approximately $400 in cash.

The robbers also allegedly took a pack of cigarettes and an employee’s black and grey bag containing personal documents.

Police say the entire incident lasted approximately three to four minutes before the men escaped through the front door and headed in the direction of a nearby park. Both suspects had their faces and heads covered. No one was injured.

Surveillance footage from inside the establishment reportedly captured the robbery.

Following statements obtained from the manager and two other persons, police conducted a house search and recovered what investigators described as an imitation firearm suspected to have been used in the robbery. A Punta Gorda Town resident was subsequently detained pending investigation.

World.title: Crown seeks life sentence for Krismar Espinosa in execution-style murder of Wilbert Banks Jr.
World.content:
Crown seeks life sentence for Krismar Espinosa in execution-style murder of Wilbert Banks Jr.

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Crown is asking the High Court to impose a life sentence on convicted murderer Krismar Espinosa for the execution-style killing of cyclist and bicycle technician Wilbert “Yellow” Banks Jr., arguing that several aggravating factors make a fixed-term sentence inappropriate.

During mitigation before Justice Nigel Pilgrim, Crown Counsel Maria Nembhard-Santana stressed that Espinosa had previously been convicted of manslaughter in another killing and had only been out of prison for approximately nine months when he was charged with Banks’ murder. The Crown also pointed to the use of a firearm, the seven gunshot wounds suffered by Banks and evidence that the killing had been planned in advance.

Espinosa, meanwhile, declined to personally address the court and called no character witnesses. Through his attorney, he continued to maintain his innocence and relied on a Social Inquiry Report prepared for sentencing.

Justice Pilgrim has reserved sentencing until October 13, 2026. Espinosa remains on remand at the Belize Central Prison.

Banks, 38, was shot seven times on April 5, 2024, in the Lake Garden area near Ladyville. He attempted to drive away after being shot but crashed his vehicle. Police recovered nine 9mm expended shells and a cellphone from the scene.

The prosecution’s key witness was Banks’ former girlfriend, who was Espinosa’s girlfriend at the time. She testified by video link that Espinosa threatened to kill her and her young son unless she lured Banks to the Lake Garden area. She said Banks later drove her there, where Espinosa emerged and opened fire.

Justice Pilgrim found Espinosa guilty of murder on July 31 following a trial without a jury. The court accepted the woman as a credible and reliable witness and rejected Espinosa’s account that he was at home when Banks was killed.

The court also heard emotional victim-impact statements from Banks’ employer Andrew Ordonez, his father Wilbert Banks Sr. and his 14-year-old daughter. His daughter recalled Sunday barbecues, Valentine’s Day gifts and the sense of safety she felt around her father, telling the court that “Father’s Day is no longer the same.”

Banks was well known in Belize’s cycling community and worked at Ordonez Bike Shop. His death was widely mourned after the 2024 killing.

World.title: UNICEF Belize and Special Envoy join forces to promote inclusion of children with disabilities
World.content:
UNICEF Belize and Special Envoy join forces to promote inclusion of children with disabilities

By Zoila Palma: UNICEF Belize and the Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children have joined forces to promote the rights, inclusion, and well-being of children with disabilities across Belize, under the message: “Every Child Seen. Every Child Heard. Every Child Included.”

The partnership aims to challenge stereotypes, raise awareness, and promote a more inclusive Belize where every child is valued, supported, and empowered to reach their full potential.

The initiative will also amplify the voices of children with disabilities and highlight their strengths, achievements, and contributions.

The partners emphasized that children with disabilities should not be defined by their challenges, noting that they are dreamers, leaders, learners, creators, and changemakers whose stories, voices, and rights matter. The initiative encourages families, schools, communities, and organizations to help create environments where every child can thrive.

Through the partnership, UNICEF Belize and the Special Envoy are calling for greater inclusion and support for children with disabilities, with the goal of making inclusion the norm rather than the exception.

World.title: Government and Global Fund strengthen partnership to support vulnerable Belizeans
World.content:
Government and Global Fund strengthen partnership to support vulnerable Belizeans

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize and the Global Fund have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening collaboration and supporting vulnerable populations across the country. The discussions were held between Minister of Economic Transformation Dr. Osmond Martinez and Global Fund Portfolio Manager Marcos Patino Mayer.

Minister Martinez was accompanied by Director Leroy Martinez and Project Manager Ferdy Cabb during the meeting.

Discussions focused on the performance and achievements of Global Fund Cycle 7 being implemented under the Ministry of Economic Transformation, as well as potential funding opportunities and priority areas for Cycle 8.

Minister Martinez expressed appreciation to Patino Mayer and the Global Fund for their continued support to Belize. He highlighted the importance of the organization’s commitment to reaching and supporting some of the country’s most vulnerable populations.

The meeting reaffirmed the commitment of the Government of Belize and the Global Fund to continued partnership and collaboration.

World.title: Triggerman gets life sentence for murder of Paulwell’s daughter and her mother
World.content:
Toshyna Patterson and her daughter Serayah Paulwell were kidnapped and murdered in September 2023.

David Smith, the triggerman in the murder of Member of Parliament Phillip Paulwell’s 10-month-old daughter, Sarayah, and her mother, Toshyna Patterson, has been sentenced to life in prison for the crime.

The Kingston-based painter is to serve a minimum of 45 years behind bars before becoming eligible for parole.

The sentencing was handed down by Chief Justice Bryan Sykes on Friday under a reported plea deal.

Smith was among a number of persons charged in the double murder which rocked the nation.

Patterson and her daughter were reported missing on September 9, 2023. Prosecutors say the mother and daughter were taken to Warieka Hills in St Andrew where they were shot and killed and their bodies burnt.

The alleged mastermind behind the killing, former United States Navy culinary specialist Leoda Bradshaw is charged with two counts of conspiracy to murder, two counts of conspiracy to kidnapping, two counts of kidnapping, and two counts of capital murder.

World.title: Gov’t says its committed to fair resolution in doctors pay dispute
World.content:
In this file photo Minister of Labour and Social Security, Pearnel Charles Jr, speaking during a post-Cabinet press briefing.

Government says its “committed to a fair, lawful and peaceful resolution” to the standoff over overtime pay that has led to junior doctors taking industrial action on Friday.

READ: Brace for delays in health services, JMDA warns amid pay dispute

In a release on Friday, the Minister of Labour and Social Security said it acknowledges the concerns of members of the Jamaica Medical Doctors’ Association (JMDA) as they await the Industrial Disputes Tribunal’s award in the dispute between the association and the Government of Jamaica.

The matter is before the IDT for compulsory arbitration under the Labour Relations and Industrial Disputes Act.

The ministry said the tribunal must be allowed to carry out its functions independently.

Accordingly, the release stated, the minister and the ministry will refrain from commenting on the merits of the dispute or taking any action that could be construed as seeking to influence the tribunal’s decision.

“Our medical doctors provide an invaluable service to Jamaica. Their dedication and sacrifice deserve recognition, and the ministry understands the importance of a timely resolution to these longstanding matters,” it said. “The Government remains committed to a fair, lawful and peaceful resolution and has confidence in the Tribunal’s consideration of the evidence and the issues before it.”

The ministry said it encourages all parties to maintain constructive engagement and industrial harmony while the proceedings are concluded.

“A timely resolution, consistent with due process, remains important to our doctors, the healthcare system and the public we all serve,” the ministry said.

World.title: WATCH: Mandeville Regional in emergency mode amid junior doctors strike
World.content:
MANCHESTER, Jamaica — Senior Medical Officer at the Mandeville Regional Hospital Dr Everton McIntosh is appealing to medical doctors to assist in manning the facility where junior doctors are currently on strike.

“I just want to make an appeal, so if there are any doctors out there who are willing to do some sessions at the hospital, we are inviting persons to come forward… especially for the emergency departments. We would appreciate the assistance,” he told journalists Friday morning.

READ: Brace for delays in health services, JMDA warns amid pay dispute

The doctors on strike are protesting what they say is the slow pace of the review process by the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) to hand down a ruling as it relates to overtime payments.

Dr McIntosh said over 100 junior doctors have stayed off the job with about 24 consultants manning all the wards and departments at the regional facility.

“We should have a total of 133 doctors on duty, but just the consultants are here which is around 24 who are working, so you can see the discrepancy there, out of a total of 133. That has grave implications for the ability for us to cover all of the areas adequately in terms of the wards, the emergency department, the outpatient clinics,” he said while pointing out that there are 315 patients admitted at the hospital as of Friday morning.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: Dad vs son in clash of Butlers
World.content:
Craig Butler (left) and Kyle Butler

KINGSTON, Jamaica — For 90 minutes on Saturday, football will pit father against son when Mona High technical director Craig Butler comes face-to-face with Vauxhall High coach, his son Kyle Butler in an intriguing ISSA Walker Cup quarterfinal.

But while Craig will be desperate to see Mona advance, the veteran football developer admits there would be something special about watching his son lift the Walker Cup with Vauxhall.

Craig, who has spent years nurturing young Jamaican footballers through his Phoenix Academy, said his ultimate wish is for Kyle and his daughter Kaycie to surpass his own achievements.

“I have raised Kyle and Kaycie to surpass my achievements. Only a father who doesn’t love his children would want them not to succeed,” Craig said.

The father-son showdown — set for 2pm at Waterhouse stadium — is an unusual twist to what is already one of the more intriguing Walker Cup quarterfinals, but Craig believes football has provided the family with a unique opportunity to work together, travel and share memorable moments.

“In football, we have an opportunity as a family to work and to spend valuable time and banter,” he said.

Craig has travelled extensively during his football career, taking Jamaican football talent to various parts of the world.

He recently pointed to the progress of Phoenix graduate Daniel Scarlett, who has signed with Australian club Central Coast Mariners, as another example of the opportunities available to young local players.

But on Saturday, the focus will be squarely on Mona and Vauxhall.

Craig has been impressed with the transformation of Vauxhall under Kyle and believes his son has earned the respect of the school community.

“It would be wonderful for Kyle to win the Walker Cup and Manning Cup with Vauxhall. He is well loved there and has done wonders with the school and the players,” he said.

However, Craig knows Kyle faces a major obstacle in Mona, who have developed a football identity over several years.

“Mona is in another mode now. They have ascended with a team built over the last six years,” he said.

“It is a brand of football that is embedded in the school and its players, and it will be hard,” Craig added.

There is also a strong Phoenix connection between the two teams, making Saturday’s contest even more significant for the Butler family.

Craig, however, is not allowing the rivalry to overshadow the bigger picture.

“Both teams are Phoenix and, either way it goes, it will be love again after the game,” he said.

And that sentiment is likely to define the Butler family story long after the final whistle — regardless of whether father Craig or son Kyle is celebrating a place in the Walker Cup semi-finals.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Senior doctors pick up the slack in western region
World.content:
Cornwall Regional Hospital

ST JAMES, Jamaica — Clinical Coordinator for the Western Regional Health Authority (WRHA), Dr Delroy Fray, is seeking to reassure the public that contingency measures are in place to minimise any disruption caused by industrial action taken by doctors.

The doctors are protesting what they say is the slow pace of the review process by the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) to hand down a ruling as it relates to overtime payments.

“We’ve made contingency plans so that our urgent and emergency cases will not be compromised in any way,” Fray told Observer Online on Friday morning.

“We knew what would happen today so yesterday was a planning day for us and the plan was to have our senior doctors cover the gaps,” he said.

The Western Region has four major health care facilities which includes the Cornwall Regional Hospital and Fray said that since 8:00am on Friday, the senior doctors have taken action.

However, he said that they are managing based on the plans put in place.

“I have checked in the morning and we are moving along that line very well. I am going to be monitoring that every four hours to see what the flow is like and how we are coping,” he said.

“Based on the plans I have in place for all the four hospitals, I’m not worried, I think we should be alright and the fact that it is just 24 hours, I think we can manage,” he added.

It was reported that the Noel Holmes hospital in Lucea currently has five doctors on staff which would have normally been nine.

World.title: Brace for delays in health services, JMDA warns amid pay dispute
World.content:
Doctors say if there is no ruling in their wage dispute with the Government by Friday, October 2, 2026, they cannot guarantee normalcy within the health sector across the island (Photo: Adobe Stock)

Jamaicans have been warned to brace for longer wait times and delays in the completion of procedures in the healthcare sector as junior doctors remain restive over the matter of overtime rates which has been before the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) for the past year.

In a press release on Friday, Jamaica Medical Doctors Association (JMDA) President Dr Jubilee Brown said the body “cannot guarantee normalcy from 8 am on Friday, October 2, 2026 to 8 am on Saturday, October 3, 2026.

“Only emergency services will be provided during this period,” the JMDA president said.

She added that the association has activated relevant protocols to minimise adverse outcomes during the period.

According to the JMDA, the Government owes the doctors $31 billion in retroactive overtime, but the Government’s calculation sits at $23 billion.

“We have been working at the same overtime rates since 2021. This is unacceptable. The JMDA calls upon the Industrial Disputes Tribunal to hand down its award without further delay,” Brown said.

World.title: No fallout
World.content:
The scene in Black River in the immediate aftermath of Hurricane Melissa last October. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

DESPITE concerns from some quarters over the slow spending of Hurricane Melissa donations, permanent secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Sheila Sealy Monteith says the Jamaican Diaspora has not raised any complaints about how its contributions are being used.

Sealy Monteith told Parliament’s Internal and External Affairs Committee on Thursday that the ministry had “many opportunities” to receive feedback from the Diaspora but had not received any indication of concern. The assurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the pace at which millions of dollars donated following Hurricane

Melissa have been utilised. Category 5 Melissa left immense damage after slamming into Jamaica’ south-western coast on October 28, 2025 and swept across western and north-western parishes.

During the committee’s deliberations with the ministry, Opposition Member of Parliament Dr Kenneth Russell raised the Auditor General’s finding that only about 1.7 per cent of the donated funds had been used months after the contributions were made.

“Has the ministry, one, received any feedback from the members of the Diaspora and the donors about the slow use of their contributions? And secondly, is the ministry concerned about the reputational risks done to the country and the effect it will have on your ability to raise funds should a similar situation recur?”

Russell queried.

Sealy Monteith responded that the ministry had not seen evidence of a decline in confidence in Jamaica’s ability to handle international support.

“We have used the strength of our diplomacy to ensure that countries who wish to contribute are enabled to contribute, that we are able to record it. We are providing direction for them, and we pass them on to the relevant authorities.

We have not received any indication to date that there has been a loss of confidence in our abilities to use it,” she revealed.

The permanent secretary stressed that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade’s role is primarily to facilitate international assistance, rather than to determine how the funds are ultimately spent.

She said the ministry works with other government entities to ensure that countries and other contributors wishing to assist Jamaica are able to do so and are directed to the relevant authorities.

Sealy Monteith also suggested that the pace at which contributions are absorbed and deployed must be considered in the context of the capacity of the receiving authorities to use the support.

“I think people understand also that when support comes in, it requires the ability to be able to assimilate and to use, and that comes over time as well,” she said. “So, if you’re asking me whether there’s been a fallout of interest and solidarity, I have not seen that. We continue to be a preferred guest on many agendas, and Minister [Kamina Johnson Smith] had a schedule in New York last week that was head-turning because everybody wants Jamaica to be at the table, to sit on our committees, to be there,” she added

World.title: Kevin Smith spoke in  tongues, detective testifies
World.content:
SMITH… late pastor of Pathways International Restoration Kingdom Ministries

A detective constable testified on Thursday that Kevin Smith, the now deceased pastor of Pathways International Restoration Kingdom Ministries in Albion, St James, refused to speak to him on the night of October 17, 2021 when the clergyman was alleged to have killed a male member of his church and ordered another to cut the throat of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner, who was also a member of his flock.

The detective constable is the seventh witness to take the stand in the murder trial of Andre Ruddock,

who is accused of killing Gardner, allegedly on Pastor Smith’s command.

While Smith refused to engage the detective constable in conversation, it was a different story with

Ruddock, who was allegedly eager to speak about the shocking events that unfolded at the church on the night.

According to the investigator, both Smith and Ruddock were wearing nothing but briefs while they were handcuffed and seated on the ground, in the driveway, close to the entrance gate of the premises.

“I spoke to Kevin Smith but he didn’t speak to me. Instead, gate of the premises. “I spoke to Kevin Smith but he didn’t speak to me. Instead, he started talking in a loud voice, in a way I couldn’t understand. It was like when someone was talking in tongues in a church. I informed both Andre Ruddock and Kevin Smith that they would be taken into custody under reasonable suspicion of double murder and wounding with intent. I caused them to be taken to the Montego Bay Police Station lockup,” the detective said.

In relation to Ruddock, the detective explained that he was more cooperative than Smith. The cop testified that he spoke to Ruddock before his futile attempt to talk with Smith. He said that after completing a walkthrough of the church property where the bizarre events unfolded he went to Ruddock, lifted him from off the ground, and took him to an area of the premises where Smith could not hear their conversation.

“After completing the walkthrough and speaking to the detective inspector I came back to where Andre Ruddock was by the big gate. I introduced myself to him and took him up from where he was by the big gate and took him to the area I described as a bathroom right next to the fencing,” the detective constable testified.

“I wanted to speak to him outside of the presence of Kevin Smith. I allowed him to put on some clothes because he was in his underpants. He stated that he had clothes nearby,” he said.

He told the court that Ruddock confessed to killing Gardner by cutting her throat after receiving instructions to do so. When asked who gave the instructions, Ruddock did not say who, but looked in the direction where Pastor Smith was seated on the ground in the driveway of the church.

Prosecutor Latoya Bernard showed the detective numerous photographs of the bizarre scene. He will continue to identify more photographs today when the trial resumes.

World.title: Wie Russland die NATO provoziert. Mit Carlo Masala
World.content:
Eine Drohne mit Sprengstoff an einer ukrainischen Frachtmaschine in Leipzig, Explosionen in Munitionsfabriken und Sabotage auf See. Russland intensiviert seine hybride Kriegsführung mitten in Europa und testet gezielt die roten Linien der NATO. Doch was passiert, wenn ein solcher Anschlag auf deutschem Boden tatsächlich gelingt und den Bündnisfall auslöst? Darüber spricht Gordon Repinski in dieser Folge mit Carlo Masala, Professor für Internationale Politik, Universität der Bundeswehr München.

Das Ziel des Kremls ist es, Panik zu schüren und die westliche Unterstützung für die Ukraine zu brechen. Im Gespräch analysiert Carlo, warum Putin gerade jetzt risikofreudiger wird und weshalb Friedrich Merz in der deutschen Debatte als entscheidender Schutzwall für weitere Hilfen gilt. Ein Wegbrechen dieser Unterstützung hätte fatale finanzielle und militärische Folgen für den gesamten Kontinent.

Gleichzeitig wächst der Druck auf Kiew massiv. Die Episode beleuchtet, wie eine mögliche Rückkehr von Trump ins Weiße Haus die Ukraine zu schmerzhaften Deals zwingen könnte und warum das europäische Superwahljahr 2027 Moskau eine beispiellose Chance bietet, die politische Landschaft endgültig zu seinen Gunsten zu drehen.
