World.title: Latvian PM faces bittersweet victory in election backdropped by Russia
World.content:
His center-right partners, New Unity, are struggling to cross the 5% electoral threshold, which would be a floundering performance for a party that has been home to many Latvian prime ministers, including current European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis.

But for the party’s prime ministerial candidate and ex-Finance Minister Arvils Ašeradens, the low polling numbers are simply the “political pendulum which shifts from one way to the other,” he told POLITICO in Riga last month.

During the last election in 2022, New Unity was the major beneficiary of a rally-round-the-flag moment as Russia had just launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in 2026, voters seem frustrated with Latvia’s high inflation, the ongoing uncertainty surrounding national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.

The prime minister may need to open talks with Ainārs Šlesers, a right-wing veteran of Latvian politics. | Robert Hegedus/EPA

Kulbergs’ other coalition partner, the agrarian Union of Greens and Farmers (known as ZZS), is also polling below the threshold. And if neither party manages to scrape by, it might force Kulbergs to work with the controversial businessman Šlesers, who carefully advocated expanding trade with Russia.

Kulbergs has dismissed this possibility — “as it is given now: no,” he told POLITICO in early September — because he does not trust the people Šlesers has surrounded himself with. Just weeks earlier, however, he had been less definitive, telling POLITICO in July: “I have to see what chess pieces I will get … to make a coalition.”

Šlesers has been a central figure in Latvian politics for decades, most notably as a local “oligarch” who, via family holdings, exerts influence over the Port of Riga. The capital’s harbor has seen its largely Russian and Belarusian hinterland slowly carved off by EU sanctions. And after Kulbergs slapped 300% tariffs on transited Russian grain this month , Šlesers told Latvian national TV such transit should be allowed, though he supports Ukraine’s EU accession.

World.title: ‘Maxi merde’: French presidential campaign rattled by a week of chaos
World.content:
Though that individual, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the current situation, was only referring to the increasingly violent demonstrations outside secondary schools and the government’s slow-footed response to them, it’s a sentiment likely shared by French voters after a week of particularly bleak headlines.

If there are political winners, it’s not immediately clear who they are. Establishment candidates and moderate voices are still struggling to seize the narrative from far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen and her surging far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon — both of whom want to fundamentally reshape France and its relationship with Europe.

A survey by pollster Odoxa this week found that the French disapprove of the government’s handling of the student school protests, but they also disapprove of Mélenchon and his far-left party France Unbowed’s involvement.

Mélenchon’s allies have joined demonstrators outside schools, saying they were there to show support and protect minors from confrontations with police. But the government and France Unbowed’s political opponents accuse them of fanning the flames of violence — allegations they deny.

“There’s a battle over the narrative” between the political extremes, a Socialist Party adviser said.

Whatever the case, the week’s crises are showing just how nasty the campaign can get with two populist candidates unafraid to stoke partisan divisions leading the polls.

World.title: Polanski’s Greens look for their next opening
World.content:
Polanski added: “Through our sustained pressure — and our historic wins — we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check. And started to move them in the right direction.”

The Labour washout in May’s local elections, courtesy of voter defections to right-wing populist Reform UK as well as to the Greens, accelerated Starmer’s exit as prime minister over the summer. Burnham has since promised many of the things that under Starmer were within the Greens’ sole purview — public ownership, care, and housing.

The task for the Green leader now is to decide where to push Labour next.

“It won’t surprise you to hear that I’m not hopeful about Labour’s backbone,” he told the crowd.

Hackney Mayor Zoë Garbett, who won her job in May’s local elections, said there were still “key differences” with the governing party, particularly on Gaza, climate and rent control — but conceded that Burnham had made it more difficult for the Green message.

She said: “People were so fed up in May, they were done with people making promises and not delivering, but we need to put forward what our vision is as well, that’s what this conference and Zack’s speech is about.”

World.title: 17 countries join forces to oppose EU budget cuts
World.content:
"We therefore believe that the overall funding for Cohesion Policy and the CAP must be preserved in the next MFF," the seventeen countries wrote in the letter to Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin seen by POLITICO.

The signatories include Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Romanian President Nicușor Dan coordinated the initiative and will host an informal meeting of those countries in the margins of the next European Council on Oct. 15 and 16.

The Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF, finances everything from farmers’ subsidies to development aid, and is among the toughest negotiations in Brussels. In 2025, the European Commission proposed a budget of nearly €2 trillion for the 2028-2034 period and shifted hundreds of billions from agriculture and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, to new priorities such as defense and competitiveness.

The so-called Friends of Cohesion group warned that further reductions to agricultural and cohesion "would only weaken it [budget] and risk undermining public support for the European project."

Ireland’s negotiating document, or negobox, will set the scene for discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during the summit in Brussels in October.

World.title: G7 agrees to release oil reserves after U.S. push
World.content:
Trump had also threatened to ban exports of diesel altogether — a major worry for European countries because U.S. diesel accounts for more than half of the continent's imports of the fuel.

But that threat is now off the table, G7 leaders said Friday. Under the agreement there would be "no restrictions or bans on exports among G7 countries," the statement read.

French President Emmanuel Macron denied European leaders had been strong-armed into making the concession with the threat of a diesel export, telling press on Friday: "The tone of our discussion was not one of threats; it was constructive."

He added that Trump had been "very clear" that there would be no export ban.

The leaders' statement did not specify that the releases would come from European reserves, but U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post that European countries had agreed to make a major contribution.

"Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The process will begin immediately."

World.title: Šefčovič: Verhandlung mit China noch ohne  Ergebnisse
World.content:
Über die Ergebnisse der Reise sprechen die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs am 15. und 16. Oktober bei ihrem EU-Gipfel in Brüssel. Die EU droht damit, den Zugang chinesischer Unternehmen zum Binnenmarkt einzuschränken, sollten die Gespräche scheitern.

Die EU und China verhandeln seit Juni. Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU haben erklärt, sie wollten die große Menge chinesischer Importe und das hohe Handelsdefizit mit China, nicht länger hinnehmen.

„Ich glaube, unsere chinesischen Partner haben verstanden, dass dies direkte Auswirkungen auf die Zukunft bedeutender europäischer Unternehmen hat – buchstäblich Tausende von Arbeitsplätzen“, berichtete Šefčovič. „Und auch auf das soziale Gefüge und das Sozialmodell, das in Europa über viele, viele Jahrzehnte hinweg entwickelt wurde.“

Im Mittelpunkt der Gespräche steht das wachsende Handelsdefizit der Union mit China von einer Milliarde Euro pro Tag. Um dieses Defizit zu verringern, müssen die Importe aus China reduziert und/oder die EU-Exporte nach China gesteigert werden.

Šefčovič erklärte, er hoffe, aus Peking Ergebnisse zu drei Hauptthemen mitbringen zu können: plötzliche Exportanstiege Chinas in wichtigen Industriezweigen, Maßnahmen zur Steigerung europäischer Warenexporte nach China, Klarheit hinsichtlich chinesischer Exportbeschränkungen für Rohstoffe, insbesondere für Seltene Erden.

In Milwaukee traf sich Šefčovič mit dem chinesischen Vizeminister Li Chenggang. Der slowakische Kommissar erklärte, China habe Verständnis für die Bedenken Europas: „Alle von uns angesprochenen Themen liegen auf dem Tisch. Ich sage nicht, dass wir Zusicherungen haben, dass wir sie lösen werden, aber sie liegen auf dem Tisch.“

World.title: G7 to hold emergency talks over possible diesel release
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney next to French President Emmanuel Macron at a working lunch with leaders of G7, on June 16, 2026 in Evian-les-bains, France. | Pool photo by Evelyn Hockstein via Getty Images

The meeting comes as Trump threatens to ban U.S. diesel exports.

BRUSSELS — The G7 club of rich countries is preparing to convene later today to explore whether to release further diesel reserves to bring down fuel prices.

Four people familiar with the matter confirmed the plan to POLITICO. The meeting will take place after the U.S. pressured European countries to act on their reserves or face an export ban.

The meeting of the Group of Seven, which includes France, Germany, Italy, the U.K., the U.S., Canada and Japan, will come on Friday afternoon amid growing concern over rising diesel costs that have triggered a pressure campaign by Washington.

World.title: Spain faces housing protests in more than 50 cities after parliament rejects tenant protections
World.content:
Demonstrators are set to march in more than 50 Spanish cities on Saturday, a day after parliament voted down two government decrees meant to give tenants stronger protection.

 

The Tenants' Union, which has been coordinating the protests, called the demonstrations. "There is an irreparable disconnect between what the people want and what the parties vote for," it said in a statement.

In Madrid, marchers are due to leave from several points around the city at noon and converge on Plaza de Cibeles in the centre. Activists have already been camped for about a week in Puerta del Sol, one of the capital's main tourist squares.

The anger was triggered by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who was carried out on a stretcher from the Madrid flat where she had lived for around seven decades. Housing campaigners say an investment company had bought the property and sought to raise her rent by 275 percent. After the backlash, the new owners agreed to let her return at a low rent.

Calls for a general election

The government drew up its measures in response to the nationwide protests that followed. The package rejected on Friday would have renewed rental contracts automatically when they expired and restricted evictions of vulnerable tenants. It also took aim at so-called vulture funds, investment firms that buy properties cheaply in pursuit of higher returns.

The decrees needed the votes of the Catalan separatist party Junts, which opposed them on the grounds that they lacked rigour.

The defeat is a further setback for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. It has revived doubts over whether his minority government can last until the next scheduled general election in 2027.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative Popular Party (PP), the main opposition, urged Sánchez after the vote to "call elections as soon as possible". After eight years in power, he said, the prime minister had the backing of "neither the streets nor parliament". Recent opinion polls have generally put the PP ahead of the Socialists.

Housing has been a leading concern for Spaniards for years, with supply falling short of demand and costs soaring, as they have elsewhere in the European Union. Average rents have almost doubled over the past decade and asking prices for homes are up about 90 percent, according to the real estate website Idealista.

World.title: Latvians head to the polls amid concerns over rising cost of living and Russia
World.content:
Polls opened on Saturday in Latvia's parliamentary election shaped by concerns over neighbouring Russia and the cost of living crisis.

 

Some 1.5 million people are eligible to cast ballots in the parliamentary election, Latvia's 11th since gaining independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The poll will see 14 parties run for 100 seats in the Saeima using a proportional system.

Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.

The Baltic state is a key pillar of NATO's eastern defensive flank, and experts say there is widespread support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.

"The stance towards Russia is the main reason for Latvians' Western, NATO and European anchoring," a Western diplomat in Riga said, adding that it would be hard to imagine major political changes.

Polls predict the centre-right United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, will emerge the largest party in parliament in Saturday's vote.

But his centre-right coalition, which also brings together the centrist New Unity, nationalist National Alliance and the Union of Greens and Farmers, is expected to emerge weakened from the election.

The current governing coalition is made up of United List, New Unity, the Union of Greens and Farmers, and the National Alliance. Polls suggest the bloc is unlikely to retain power in its current form after the vote.

Security and economy at the top of voters' minds

Security is at the top of voters' minds in a country bordering Russia which was annexed and ruled by Moscow for much of the 20th century.

According to Roberts Kits, an analyst at the Latvian think tank LaSER, "defence and security will be the priority". Apart from a few dissenting voices, he said, there is broad consensus on maintaining military spending at nearly five percent of GDP and on supporting Ukraine.

But the economy is also a major concern for voters.

Latvia is the least affluent of the three Baltic States in terms of living standards, despite catching up since joining the EU in 2004.

Growth is sluggish, with voters pointing to the cost of living, the state of the healthcare system and the difficulties of public finances. Complicating this are major regional disparities.

The gap between Latvia's capital and the rest of the country is stark. Around Riga, GDP per capita reached 101 percent of the European average in 2024, according to a European Commission report. In other regions, the figure does not exceed 50 percent.

The contrast is sharpest in Latgale, Latvia's easternmost region, where depopulation is accelerating and economic opportunity is scarce. The region is home to a large majority of Russian speakers, and its decline is reflected most visibly in Daugavpils, the country's second-largest city, where 90 percent of the population is Russian-speaking.

"The most important thing is the lack of young people and the lack of good jobs," said Aigars Soikants, a 30-year-old Daugavpils resident. "There isn't enough work. People are leaving."

Despite living in a city with a predominantly Russian-speaking population, Soikants says identity is not what will drive his vote. He plans to back "a centrist or right-wing party which acts in the interest of the country."

Rise of populist parties in Latvia

Similar to other parts of Europe, populist parties have benefited from economic worries in the lead-up to the election. The Sovereign Power (Suverena vara, SV) party, critical of aid to Ukraine and increasing military spending, is polling at nine percent and could reach second place in Parliament.

Considered pro-Russian by its critics, the party, led by Julija Stepanenko, emphasises Latvia's economic difficulties. The party, however, is isolated politically and, barring a huge upset, has no chance of entering a future governing coalition.

Carefully avoiding the word "Ukraine", Vjaceslavs Stepanenko, the head of SV's local list in Latgale and husband of the party’s chairwoman, advocates "stopping all aid to any foreign state".

"We are the ones who need help, not the other way around."

Another populist party, Latvia First (LPV), is also at nine percent, and its businessman leader Ainars Slesers is regularly compared to US President Donald Trump.

The party is winning support with a conservative message and promises of economic revival, and unlike SV, it could become an indispensable partner in coalition talks.

"The big question is whether the United List will cooperate with Slesers' party," said political analyst Sigita Struberga.

Can Russian-speaking voters influence the polls?

Long rallied behind the "Harmony" party, Russian speakers, who make up about 35 percent of Latvia's population, no longer vote as a unified bloc.

Harmony, which won several parliamentary elections without ever entering government, disappeared from parliament in 2022 and has very little chance of returning.

Russian-speaking voters should not be treated as a single bloc with uniform behaviour, according to analyst Kits.

While identity politics remain a factor, a growing share of this electorate is now driven by economic and social concerns.

That shift is visible in Daugavpils, where Valentin Trofimov, a 62-year-old watch repairman, says he will vote for Slesers' party.

His reasons are straightforward — the country, he says, "lacks money for everything", including transport, education and medicine. "Wages are too low," he said.

World.title: Second Kyiv bridge hit in two days as Russia targets Dnipro crossings
World.content:
A Russian strike hit Kyiv's Northern Bridge on Saturday, halting traffic from the left bank to the right and deepening a transport crisis that began when the Southern Bridge was shut a day earlier.

 

Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced the strike on Telegram after a drone alert in the capital. "Northern Bridge has been hit," he wrote. "Emergency services are heading to the scene."

He later reported damage to the road surface and to the overhead wires that power trolleybuses on the bridge. "Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.

The strike is the latest in a series aimed at the crossings over the Dnipro, the river that separates Kyiv's eastern and western districts. Eight bridges connect the two sides, and city officials say the campaign is "tearing Kyiv apart".

The Southern Bridge, a cable-stayed span and one of the city's main crossings, was closed on Friday after waves of fast, jet-powered drones struck. Officials said it had been hit several times since Thursday. Movement on another bridge was also restricted.

The closures brought severe congestion across the city. Cars and buses stood in long queues on major roads as drivers looked for other ways across, and some commuters had to finish their journeys on foot.

Klitschko warned on Friday that the capital should now be on a war footing.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war has largely been fought on the ground in the east, and Kyiv has mostly been spared the destruction seen near the front line.

World.title: The way you speak could reveal early signs of brain ageing
World.content:
The way someone speaks can reveal more about their health and ageing than previously thought, a new study using an automated computer tool called a "speech clock" found. A person's speech age isn't just about vocal style; researchers say it reflects what is happening inside the body, and they hope this could be a low-cost, non-invasive, automated alternative for measuring biological ageing.

 

“Our voice appears to contain much more information about aging than we previously recognised,” said Agustín Ibáñez, senior author of the study at Trinity College Dublin.

An automated computer calculated a person’s speech age and compared it to their actual birth age, revealing whether their speech sounds younger, average, or older than expected, and offering clues about healthy ageing.

“It captures both the passage of chronological time and signals coming from cognition, the brain, systemic biology, and even our accumulated social environment,” he added.

The researchers analysed audio recordings of nearly 3,000 Spanish-speaking adults across Latin America. Participants completed a range of tasks, including narrating a short animated film, retelling a story after a 20-minute gap and naming items within given categories.

Using machine learning, the team examined hundreds of features capturing how people speak and what they say, such as speech rate and pauses, pitch, emotional content, vocabulary, and semantic precision, to estimate chronological age and generate an individual “speech age gap”.

What "older" speech shows

The speech clock distinguished healthy individuals from people with dementia. Healthy participants showed the lowest speech age gaps, while progressively wider gaps were seen in people with Alzheimer’s disease and forms of frontotemporal dementia.

People whose speech appears older than expected for their chronological age showed signs of accelerated ageing across several biological and clinical systems. MRI brain scans indicated greater loss of brain structure and altered brain activity.

Older speech scores were also tied to higher levels of p-Tau217, a key protein in the blood linked to Alzheimer's disease.

Participants with older speech scores performed worse on tests of memory, focus, and problem-solving. This link was present not only for language-related tasks, but also for non-verbal tasks like visual memory.

“The broader finding is nevertheless striking in that a person’s voice may provide a remarkably compact readout of multiple dimensions of aging,” added Ibáñez.

Factors such as chronological age, brain ageing, cognition, and Alzheimer's and dementia phenotypes are traditionally measured with very different and often expensive tools, yet they appear to converge in the way someone speaks, he said.

The authors noted that many current measures of biological ageing require MRI scanners, blood samples or specialised clinical assessments. By contrast, the “speech clock” offers a low-cost, non-invasive, automated alternative that can be carried out remotely on standard devices without specialist medical staff.

The researchers stressed, however, that the speech clock is not yet a diagnostic test for dementia and it cannot establish whether an older-appearing speech profile predicts who will subsequently develop cognitive decline.

World.title: Hungarian restaurants struggle: costs match Europe but revenues lag behind
World.content:
Across the EU, the number of hospitality venues is falling fastest in Hungary. Between 2021 and 2024 the decline was 6 percent, while 22 member states recorded growth. Looking at the past ten years, the situation is even more dramatic: 18.5 percent of hospitality businesses have disappeared.

 

According to a recently published study (source in Hungarian), one reason for the worsening trend is that cheap, poor-quality lángos and goulash bars, geared towards foreign tourists and working with high margins, are pushing quality restaurants out of the market. This segment primarily attracts low-spending visitors, such as stag party tourists, which is problematic for the country’s image as well.

"I dare say that we are the only country in the world where you can get lángos with Greek salad, lángos with beef stew, and I could go on. There is nothing wrong with a simple dish being good. That is not a problem at all. The problem is when we try to serve this simple dish in a way that means it is no longer that dish, and on top of that we try to attach a gastronomic culture to it," said Áron Reményik, author of the study and communications expert at Raconteur Agency.

Hungary becoming expensive

Tourism was at its highest in 2025, but even that failed to really give hospitality a boost. This year, the problems have multiplied: after the election, the strengthening of the forint has made Budapest 12–14 percent more expensive for tourists paying in euros, and nation-branding campaigns have also been halted. In August, 14 percent fewer foreign tourists came to Hungary than a year earlier.

As a result, Hungarian restaurants face huge competitiveness problems, according to the founder of Eventrend Group, a corporate group that operates 35 hospitality venues.

"We have reached European price levels in almost every cost category. We pay almost the same for energy and wages. Today, it is cheaper to employ hospitality workers in southern Italy or southern Spain than in Hungary. In Austria, it may still be a little more expensive, but overall, there is not much difference. Raw material prices are almost at the same level," explained Zoltán Kőrössy to Euronews.

Few Hungarians can afford to eat out regularly

While costs — and therefore often prices — are at a Western European level, revenues are not. In Austria, for example, there is a similar number of hospitality venues, but the sector’s turnover is twice that of Hungary. And this depends not only on tourists but also on domestic guests.

Economist Zoltán Pogátsa recently pointed out (source in Hungarian) that two-thirds of Hungarian society live on less money than the EU’s lower middle class. Yet without a broad, solvent middle class, restaurants that rely on returning guests cannot operate.

It is no surprise that, since measurements began, the number of hospitality venues in the capital fell below 8,000 for the first time in 2024, and by the end of 2025, the Central Statistical Office recorded only 7,778.

According to Reményik, one possible solution would be to extend the certification and inspection system for Hungarikums and authentic Hungarian cuisine to the street-food segment as well.

It would also help if the number of purely tourist-oriented street-food outlets in the busiest tourist zones were limited. That will not, of course, give Hungarians more money to eat out, but the likely fall in rents caused by weaker competition might put struggling quality restaurants in a slightly better position.

World.title: The Disney generation: What unites Baby Boomers, millennials and Gen Z
World.content:
Some stories stay with us long after childhood is over. With time, details of the plot, the order of the songs and even the characters’ names may fade. What remains are the emotions and the ideas these stories gave us about the world.

 

For decades, Disney has been part of childhood for generations of Poles. Research by SWPS University found that 84% of adult Poles regularly watched Disney films and animations as children, while 82% still have a soft spot for them.

But it is not just about nostalgia. Our attachment to these stories is also linked to values that can stay with us well into adulthood.

A scene from 101 Dalmatians Courtesy @Disney/Pixar

The values mentioned most often were friendship and loyalty, cited by 46% of respondents. They were followed by the triumph of good over evil (43%), overcoming difficulties (32%) and family (31%).

Money, fame and prestige did not feature among the most frequently mentioned values, nor did the drive to be the best. For adult Poles, Disney is associated above all with relationships, kindness, personal growth, loyalty and responsibility.

In other words, it seems to be less about what we achieve and more about who we share our lives with and the kind of people we want to be.

With friends like these: A scene from 'The Lion King' Credit: @Disney/Pixar

Friendship before success

In Disney stories, heroes rarely make it on their own. Friends, family and sometimes unexpected allies are there to support them, helping them through their toughest moments.

It is therefore no surprise that friendship and loyalty rank among the values most strongly associated with Disney.

The message remains relevant at any age. Some 89% of Poles say kindness towards others matters, while the same proportion believe in the value of being yourself. Courage is valued by 87%, family by 86%, and 84% agree that love can help us overcome difficulties.

A scene from Cinderella Credit: @Disney/Pixar

The differences between generations are relatively small.

This could help explain why Disney continues to resonate with people who grew up at different times. The characters may change, but the need for connection, friendship and the sense that we are not alone remains the same.

Each generation sees these stories differently

Sharing the same core values does not mean that every generation sees these stories in quite the same way.

For Baby Boomers (born between 1945 and 1965), the idea that the world should have clear rules seems particularly strong. Some 54% say the triumph of good over evil is one of the values reflected in Disney stories. Their responses also highlight honesty, hope, perseverance and a belief in justice.

Still from Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs @Disney/Pixar

Generation X (born between 1965 and 1980) are more likely to associate Disney stories with responsibility, growing up and dealing with adversity. For 74% of respondents in this group, Disney also offered a glimpse of the Western world.

Millennials (born between 1980 and 1995) place more emphasis on authenticity, acceptance and the freedom to live life on their own terms. Characters such as Mulan, Elsa and Vaiana do not simply try to meet other people’s expectations. Their stories are about discovering who they are and finding their place in the world.

A scene from Frozen @Disney/Pixar

“I have the right to be myself”

This shift is most apparent among the youngest participants.

Self-acceptance is mentioned by 12% of the oldest respondents, compared with 29% of Gen Z (born between 1995 and 2010). Independence and diversity show a similar pattern, rising from around 10% among the oldest respondents to 18% among Gen Z.

The difference is even more striking when it comes to pursuing dreams: 14% of Baby Boomers mention this, compared with 38% of Gen Z.

The pattern is reversed when it comes to the belief that good triumphs over evil. This is cited by 54% of the oldest respondents, compared with 24% of the youngest.

This does not mean that younger people have stopped believing in good. Rather, what they expect from a hero appears to have changed.

A scene from Hannah Montana @Disney/Pixar

Simply defeating evil and restoring order is no longer enough. What also matters is whether a hero can choose who they want to be and the path they want to take.

For Gen Z, self-realisation, identity, belonging and acceptance of diversity are particularly important. The key message can be summed up simply: find your own path.

The classics still matter

It might seem that a generation with almost unlimited choice of content would be ready to leave classic Disney behind. Yet Gen Z are not rejecting its core values. Instead, they want to see them combined with a more contemporary approach to storytelling.

Almost half of Gen Z respondents (46%) favour combining Disney classics with modern ideas.

The picture is similar across all respondents. A large majority (87%) want Disney’s classic values to be preserved. Of these, 45% would like them to remain unchanged, while 42% would prefer to see them combined with modern values. Only 4% would like Disney to fully adapt its values to current social trends.

Still from Cars @Disney/Pixar

Contemporary stories are also well received, particularly when they focus on overcoming difficulties (75%), working together (74%) and perseverance (72%).

So the choice is not really between classic Disney and modern storytelling. It is about holding on to values that still resonate while telling stories in a way that reflects the world we live in today.

Lessons from childhood stay with us

This may be why Disney has become a shared experience for so many generations. Not because everyone remembers the same films and characters, but because each generation has found something of its own in these stories.

Still from Cars @Disney/Pixar

Baby Boomers remember justice, honesty and hope. Generation X associate Disney with responsibility, perseverance and the strength to overcome adversity. Millennials value authenticity and the freedom to live life on their own terms. Gen Z place more emphasis on self-realisation, identity and the courage to find their own path.

Yet beneath these differences, the same values come through: friendship, loyalty, family, courage, kindness and perseverance.

Still from The Lion King @Disney/Pixar

They are not new or particularly fashionable. But perhaps that is why they have lasted.

Disney has never been only about castles, crowns and happy endings. Its stories have also taught generations the value of having people they can trust, the strength to get through difficult times and the freedom to choose their own path.

Growing up does not necessarily mean leaving these stories behind. We may forget some of the details, but the lessons can stay with us long after childhood is over.

World.title: ‘It’s given my mental health a massive boost’: Why everyone should hone their bushcraft skills
World.content:
If you’re not a military green-clad survivalist or a forest-bathing wellness enthusiast, you might feel “a little bit lost” in the great outdoors, says bushcraft instructor and conservationist Jim Todd.

 

It’s a problem the brightly coloured Bushcraft Bus – the mobile home of wilderness and nature education – aims to solve.

“We’re trying to fill that gap in the middle, where you don't have to identify with anything. You just need to have a little bit of kit, and just be up for it,” says Jim.

Jim, 39, and Bushcraft Bus co-founder Tom Young, 37, met in Dorset five years ago while qualifying to be bushcraft instructors. Now they host foraging walks, wilderness skills workshops and fire-roasted woodland dinners in the south of England and beyond. In the UK – which ranked 55th out of 61 nations in a global study on “nature connectedness” – some of the people who join them have never even set foot in the woods.

Bushcraft Bus co-founders Jim Todd and Tom Young met five years ago on a bushcraft instructor training course. Bushcraft Bus

It doesn’t take long for them to realise what they’ve been missing.

“The excitement builds through the day,” Tom tells Euronews Earth from their camp in the Cotswolds’ Voltaires Wood. “Some people are quite timid at the start but they’re often the ones who get the most out of it,” adds Jim.

King Alfred’s Cakes or ‘cramp balls’ are a particular crowdpleaser. Resembling round lumps of coal, this fungus is commonly found on fallen ash and beech trees, and can be used as a fire lighter – a discovery that left a recent participant of their woodland cookout “just ecstatic”, recalls Tom.

King Alfred’s Cakes or ‘cramp balls’ can be used as a fire lighter. Bushcraft Bus

What’s the most essential wilderness skill?

Being ‘apocalypse-ready’ isn’t a focus of the Bushcraft Bus – but the skills it teaches feel increasingly important. The UK government recently advised citizens to prepare for threats from the climate crisis and hostile states, including by stocking up on tinned food.

It came after a record-hot summer placed swathes of Europe under heat and water stress – compounded by soaring household bills resulting from tensions in the Middle East, not to mention the looming threat of water- and energy-hungry AI.

Jim says these factors are a motivating force for some participants who join their courses, and many leave less fearful, more confident and better connected.

“When you start thinking through that lens, you realise how little you actually know to defend yourself or survive in that situation,” he says. “We’re so reliant on all of these big systems working. And if any of them collapse, we’re back to basics really quickly… Like, what if there was no heating and it was the middle of winter? Or how do I find water and purify it?”

Jim Todd, co-founder of Bushcraft Bus, demonstrates fire making. Bushcraft Bus

Fire-making is “instrumental” – not only for survival but also for “how much you can enjoy the time that you have in the woods,” says Jim. “Fire ties everything together”, agrees Tom – from “learning about tree identification, so you can burn the right woods, to learning about what to forage and how to cook it”.

For this reason, Tom always carries a ferro rod (a metallic fire starter stick) – a tool that was indispensable on his 66-day solo hike through the European Arctic in 2018.

But bushcraft skills only go so far – and the biggest lifeline often gets overlooked: community. That could mean curating your friendship group: “Making sure you’ve got a friend who’s a nurse and who would know how to treat an injury, and someone else who’s got a mechanical mind who could help turn a dead car into something useful,” says Tom.

Ferro rods are "super light and portable, and they create a really hot spark very reliably," says Tom Young, co-founder of Bushcraft Bus. Bushcraft Bus

‘When you pour energy and curiosity into nature, you get it back’

This collaborative spirit is something off-grid living seems to nurture – not only between fellow humans, but with the land itself.

“A lot of people don’t learn about the woods anymore. So from a very young age, you’re already disconnected,” says Tom.

There are signs that this is slowly starting to change: the UK government recently approved a new Natural History GCSE (an exam subject that can be chosen at 14-years-old) for secondary school students, which it hopes will “grow the next generation of green careers”.

“I think if you can teach people and give people some of that knowledge and awareness, they’ll naturally start caring and appreciating more about those spaces,” says Tom.

Bushcraft Bus teaches woodland skills like tree identification. Bushcraft Bus

This can look like conserving precious resources: “We’ve wheelbarrowed all of our water up a 15-minute steep, bumpy track,” says Jim, sitting in their woodland camp. “So we’re not splashing it around when we’re up here… Instinctively it does reset your brain to be way more conservative with your usage.”

Or being mindful of what you take from the land: “You need to leave some of whatever you’re foraging for the animals,” says Jim – and in the case of mushrooms, for the fungus itself: “The reason they fruit is to spread the spores,” adds Tom.

Connecting with nature is “like a relationship”, muses Jim. “You have to build it – you can’t just expect it to give you everything. You have to pour energy and curiosity into it, and then you get it back. That’s when it starts providing real value to you.”

The co-founders of Bushcraft Bus are NCFE-accredited bushcraft instructors. Bushcraft Bus

‘Exploring the outdoors has given my mental health a massive boost’

Both Jim and Tom admit that in their younger years, they were more interested in going to the pub than on long country walks. These days, it’s more often screens that are keeping teenagers indoors.

Both also think Europe has a lot to learn from other cultures about connecting with nature. During time spent in New Zealand and Canada, they found outdoor skills are embedded more deeply into everyday life. Vast landscapes make the outdoors harder to ignore, while activities such as kayaking, hiking and camping are familiar from a young age.

Bushcraft Bus teaches skills like fire safety and foraging. Bushcraft Bus

“The outdoors is all around you all the time,” says Jim, contrasting that with the UK’s denser landscape, where farmland and privately owned woodland can make natural spaces feel surprisingly inaccessible.

As a result, “we almost see ourselves as separate from the natural world,” reflects Jim. “But I think if you do get out into it, most people very quickly feel this connection to it. And when you add in skills that you can use outside, you are just building that self-reliance and confidence.”

Tom’s experience stands as testament to this: “Exploring the outdoors has given me what feels like a purpose,” he says. “It’s given my mental health that massive boost. In life as well, just talking to people with more confidence, and that’s developed through the years.”

World.title: House prices keep rising across Europe: Which countries saw the biggest increases and why?
World.content:
House prices continue to rise across much of Europe, but the pace varies widely. Portugal, Bulgaria and Spain recorded double-digit annual increases in the second quarter of 2026, while prices fell in Finland, Luxembourg and France.

 

Across the EU, prices rose by 4.7% compared with a year earlier, outpacing inflation of 3.2%.

So where are prices rising fastest, and how much of that growth remains once inflation is taken into account?

Over 15% rise in Portugal and Bulgaria

Among 29 European countries, nine recorded double-digit year-on-year rises in house prices, according to Eurostat. Portugal saw the highest year-on-year increase in the second quarter of 2026, at 16.5%, closely followed by Bulgaria (15.5%).

Mikk Kalmet, areal estate expert at Global Property Guide, noted that strong housing demand continues to outstrip supply in Portugal, particularly in Lisbon, Porto and popular coastal areas. “Limited new construction, foreign investment, tourism-related demand and persistent housing shortages have all contributed to rising prices,” he told Euronews Business.

Kalmet explained that in Bulgaria, rising household incomes, wage growth, relatively affordable mortgage financing and strong demand for property as an investment have supported price increases.

Lithuania (14.3%), Slovakia (13.6%), Croatia (12.7%), Spain (12.1%), Romania (12.1%), Latvia (11.4%) and Hungary (10.2%) also recorded increases of more than 10%.

Denmark (9.4%), Slovenia (9.1%) and Czechia (8.6%) were also close to the 10% level.

House prices also rose by more than the EU average in Cyprus (7.9%), Malta (6.9%), Poland (6.3%), Ireland (6%), Estonia (5.8%), Austria (5.1%) and Sweden (4.8%).

Three countries saw declines

Finland (-2.7%), Luxembourg (-2.2%) and France (-0.8%) were the only countries where house prices declined year on year over this period.

Mikk Kalmet pointed to weak economic growth in Finland, along with subdued consumer confidence and the lingering effects of higher interest rates.

“In France, affordability constraints, relatively weak housing demand and the effects of previously elevated mortgage rates have put downward pressure on prices,” Kalmet said, adding that economic uncertainty has also encouraged some prospective buyers to postpone purchases.

Among the EU’s ‘Big Four’ economies, Spain stands out with a 12.1% rise, while Italy (4%) is below the EU average. Germany recorded only a slight increase of 0.6%, just above France, where house prices fell by 0.8%.

“[In Germany] higher mortgage rates are back. Housing affordability is deteriorating. Demand for mortgage loans is weakening,” Carsten Brzeski and Franziska Biehl from ING wrote in their analysis.

Local fundamentals drive Europe’s housing divide

Kalmet pointed out that the different rates of house price growth largely reflect national housing shortages, income growth, mortgage conditions and demographic trends. “Housing markets are fundamentally local, even though European countries share many of the same economic and monetary conditions,” he said.

Countries experiencing strong demand and limited construction tend to see faster price increases. In contrast, countries with weaker economic growth, subdued household demand or greater sensitivity to borrowing costs have experienced slower growth or declining prices.

Growth is still strong in real terms

When inflation is taken into account, real house price growth is still strong in many countries.

In the EU, with inflation at 3.2%, house prices rose by 1.5% in real terms.

However, growth remained much stronger in several countries. In Portugal, for example, inflation was 3.6% over this period, resulting in real house price growth of 12.1%.

Real growth was also above 7% in Slovakia (9.4%), Bulgaria (9.1%), Lithuania (8.8%), Spain (8.3%), Latvia (7.9%), Denmark (7.7%), Hungary (7.7%) and Croatia (7.5%).

Six countries recorded declines in real terms, led by Luxembourg with a fall of 6.4%. Real house prices also fell by 3.2% in France and 2% in Germany.

Explaining what has driven house prices over this one year, Kalmet said: “Three factors stand out: persistent housing shortages, household income growth and changing mortgage conditions. In many European countries, residential construction has failed to keep pace with housing demand.

What’s next for house prices?

Kalmet expects that persistent housing shortages and continued demand could support further price increases in many European markets. However, growth is likely to remain uneven, and another year of double-digit increases should not be taken for granted.

“The biggest uncertainty is interest rates. The ECB raised rates in September 2026 in response to renewed inflationary pressures. Higher mortgage costs, combined with weaker purchasing power caused by rising energy prices, could slow housing demand,” he said.

Brzeski and Biehl noted that prospective buyers in Germany now face a challenging combination of higher property prices, higher financing costs and the lingering effects of weaker real purchasing power, driven by the adverse economic effects of the war in the Middle East.

World.title: Russia strikes another major bridge in Kyiv, says mayor
World.content:
The attack on Kyiv's Northern Bridge comes after the Southern Bridge on the Dnipro river was hit multiple times by Russia's drones.

A major bridge in Kyiv was targeted in a Russian strike on Saturday, the city's mayor said, as Moscow's intensifies its attacks on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital.

The Northern Bridge across the Dnipro river was struck in the air attack, following a drone alert.

No casualties were reported in the strike.

"Emergency services are heading to the scene," Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a statement posted on Telegram.

Escalating strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure

Klitschko added that the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge were damaged in the attack.

"Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.

The latest attack comes after the last two days saw the city's Southern Bridge being hit several times in a volley of strikes by Russian drones.

The attacks caused traffic chaos in Ukraine's capital, with long lines of stationary cars and buses clogging major roads.

Cars were stuck in traffic jams on Friday after Russian attacks on the Southern Bridge Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.

In the years following its February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks.

Last week, Russia launched what Ukrainians saw as the start of an expected winter bombing campaign focused on facilities that supply power to the capital.

Moscow has previously denied a systematic targeting of civilians during its bombings.

World.title: India news: Cockroach Janta Party announces Delhi march for October 10, calls for election chief's resignation
World.content:
10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 India beat Pakistan by 19 runs to retain Asian Games cricket gold

India set up a total of 211 in 20 overs during the men's cricket final match against Pakistan Image: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP

India successfully defended their Asian Games men's cricket gold medal, beating rivals Pakistan by 19 runs in Saturday's final in Nisshin, Japan.

After posting 211-6 backed by Abhishek Sharma's 61 off 20 balls and a late effort from Tilak Varma and Shivam Dube, India restricted Pakistan to 192-6 despite a big knock of 96 off 51 balls from Hasan Nawaz.

India's Abhishek Sharma propelled his side into a comfortable pace by hitting 61 off just 20 balls Image: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

Nawaz fell four runs short of a century on the final ball of the innings, when he was caught by wicketkeeper Sanju Samson off Dube's bowling. It marked Pakistan's first-ever appearance in a men's Asian Games cricket final.

The event also marked one of the game's fiercest rivalries played out on an unlikely stage: a converted baseball field in suburban Nagoya, where Indians and Pakistanis living in Japan queued for hours to fill the 2,500-capacity venue.

"I think this is never going to happen again, India against Pakistan in Japan," Pakistan supporter Umer Dar, a 26-year-old Nagoya resident, told AFP.

"Even if it's in Japan, the craze of India versus Pakistan is always there," added Tokyo-based India fan Afroz Khan. "Anywhere they play in the world, it's always crazy."

While cricket remains a niche sport in Japan, there has been growing local interest, as shown by India's first-ever T20 international against Japan last week, which India won by just two runs in a rain-shortened match.

World.title: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says
World.content:
The man, who stabbed his fellow pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight, was reportedly barred from flying in his native Oman over security concerns.

The co-pilot accused of stabbing his captain during Flydubai Flight 1073 was wielding a crash ax and attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack," UAE investigators said Saturday, according to Emirati state news agency WAM.

A crash ax is typically stored in the plane's cockpit for use in case of an emergency.

Western and Gulf officials cited by Reuters and AP news agencies named the co-pilot as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami. Emirati authorities have not publicly commented on his identity.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that he had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views.

The attack that took place on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has raised many questions about how the incident unfolded as well as about background checks in aviation hiring.

There were 182 people on board, including four pilots.

After the co-pilot stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash the plane, two other pilots in the cabin took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Flydubai co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman over security concerns

The Wall Street Journal report said the co-pilot was hired by Flydubai despite the ban by Oman, allowing him to fly the jet on a sensitive route connecting the UAE and Israel.

Israel and the UAE, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020.

The newspaper said it could not be determined whether Oman shared concerns about the pilot's radicalization with other countries or airlines.

The nature of his radicalization was also not clear.

US broadcaster CNN cited two sources saying the co-pilot was removed from a job at Oman's national airline last year over concerns about extremist views.

Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya, also citing an informed source, reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday in a video statement that they know the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination" and intended to crash the jet.

Netanyahu also said they were also looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price."

The investigation is ongoing. A Gulf diplomat, in comments to AP, said authorities were attempting to find out whether the Omani co-pilot was a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."

World.title: Morocco's first female head of government: Symbol or real reform?
World.content:
Fatima Zahra Mansouri has been chosen as Morocco's first female prime minister. Is her appointment a kind of symbolism, to show Morocco in a positive light? Or could Mansouri bring genuine changes for Moroccan women?

After the announcement that Morocco would appoint its first female head of government – Marrakech mayor Fatima Zahra Mansouri – citizens interviewed by local television reporters were mostly enthusiastic.

"It would be great if we had a female prime minister for a change. She'd lift our spirits a bit," one woman said.

"Why don't we give women a chance? We've never had one [a female head of government] before," said another. "May God bless her and help her stay on a straight path."

"Regardless of who takes on the role, it should be a change for the better in Morocco," a man added.

Morocco's King Mohammed VI chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri to be the country's first female prime minister following September's parliamentary elections Image: Mosa'ab Elshamy/AP Photo/picture alliance

But there were also naysayers. Some locals questioned how she would take part in official events where tradition and protocol dictate that only men attend.

"People are saying that a nation cannot succeed if a woman is in charge, even if she's only half in charge," one man told a television reporter, referring to the fact that Morocco's King Mohammed VI has the final say in national politics.

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy so elections are held but the king has ultimate executive power. The head of the country's government, or prime minister, leads the cabinet and administration and executes public policy.

The king chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri, minister of planning and mayor of Marrakesh, over Fouzi Lekjaa, head of Morocco's football federation and budget minister. The pair are senior members of the Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, which won the most seats in the country's parliamentary elections in September.

"If you talk to Moroccans, there are some who are really proud of having a woman at the top and they see a chance for her to have impact on women's representation in society," confirms Anja Freudenreich, who heads the Morocco office of Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES) in Rabat. "But others see her appointment as bare symbolism."

Mansouri will lead what is colloquially being called the "World Cup government" as Morocco prepares to invest billions before it hosts the 2030 football World Cup along with Spain and Portugal. Mansouri is seen to have shown leadership after the devastating 2023 Morocco earthquake.

Her appointment makes her the third woman to lead a government in the Arab world.

Morrocan women have become more visible in local politics in recent years. Casablanca and Rabat both have female mayors, and there are a number of female cabinet ministers Image: Abu Adem Muhammed/Anadolu/picture alliance

Will Mansouri improve the lot of Moroccan women?

There is no doubt that Mansouri's appointment has important symbolic value, observers say.

Two Tunisian women, Najla Bouden and current prime minister Sara Zaafarani, became heads of an Arab government before Mansouri's appointment. A 2022 survey by polling organization Arab Barometer found Tunisian attitudes towards women in power had changed as a result.

Researchers from Arab Barometer believed the change — with only 40% agreeing that "in general, men are better at political leadership than women" in 2022 compared to 56% four years earlier — was the result of a "role model effect." Before the appointment of Bouden and Zaafarani, there had been no major changes, they pointed out.

According to a 2025 survey by the organization, attitudes toward women's roles have also been changing in Morocco. Mansouri could accelerate that.

"We've already noticed how impactful this [appointment] is in terms of social and cultural norms," said Stephanie Willman Bordat, co-founder of Rabat-based advocacy organization, Mobilizing for Rights Associates (MRA).

"People in public spaces, in cafes, on trains on their commute and just regular folks are having conversations about women's leadership and the taboo that says women can't be heads of government or women can't be bosses of men. There's good public debate and dialogue on this."

"And on a global level, in terms of women's participation, this is really something to encouraging," Bordat, who has lived in Morocco for two decades, told DW. "Especially when you look at the global climate of backlash and regression in women's rights."

Mansouri's prime ministership "is certainly notable as female leadership in the region is rare," Freudenreich of FES agreed. "It does have a highly symbolic character and I'm sure she does, or she will have, a role model function for women and girls in Morocco as well as in the region."

No major changes from past

However, Mansouri is unlikely to initiate a major change from past politics, Freudenreich suggested.

She's more of a pragmatist than a rebel — a quality that's likely to see her navigate the much-discussed issues of protocol — and her party's electoral manifesto doesn't go into any major detail on women's issues, she pointed out.

Before the September elections, MRA looked at which parties had women's issues in their electoral manifestos. Mansouri's party, PAM, appeared to offer only three such policies.

PAM said it wanted to increase female economic activity, increase vulnerable widows' pensions and ensure better obstetric care. Image: Jalal Morchidi/Anadolu/picture alliance

Other parties were more vocal on women's issues than PAM, with some saying they would push for updates to the Moroccan family code, or "moudawana." This sets rules on all-important aspects of Moroccan women's lives like custody of children, divorce, property rights, marriage, polygamy and domestic violence. It has not been updated since 2004.

Did the king pick a symbol or is he genuine?

In 2023, King Mohammed VI asked the then-prime minister to look into further updates to the family code. Discussions around that are ongoing and reforms are still pending, MRA's Bordat said.

"But what's really interesting is that now we can say, well, women can be heads of government so women can also be heads or co-heads of family," she argued.

The Moroccan king, who took the throne in 1999, has been broadly supportive of women's rights, Ahmed Benchemsi, advocacy and communications director for Human Rights Watch's Middle East and North Africa division, confirmed. Still, his organization would like to see things improve further.

"With regard to women's rights, a symbol won't serve women's rights as much as legal reform," Benchemsi told DW.

Morocco is generally considered comparatively progressive in women's rights and the 2011 Constitution guarantees equality between men and women Image: Moe Zoyari/Sipa USA/picture alliance

"Activism around women's rights remains relatively permitted — an exception to the heightened governmental scrutiny and judicial proceedings against other areas of activism in Morocco," the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace wrote in a July 2025 commentary . "The king's leadership on gender reforms creates space for this activity, as advocates are often working in conjunction with parts of the government rather than against it."

Given popular discontent with the economy and high youth unemployment and protests, "improving women's status is a promise the government can deliver on in a challenging period," the organization noted.

But right now, Bordat argued that Mansouri's appointment shouldn't be seen as "something to be either celebrated or criticized."

The country is still waiting to see how Mansouri will form a governing coalition, she argued. How many female ministers the new government appoints, and what powers they are granted, will also be closely observed.

After that, "the real question is what civil society organizations, NGOs and citizens will do with this opportunity?" Bordat concluded. "That is, how do we hold all of the political parties and all of the newly elected representatives accountable and engaged … so we can continue to advance women's rights in Morocco?"

Edited by: R. Casey.

World.title: Bosnia-Herzegovina shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
World.content:
Bosnia-Herzegovina is governed by a system established after the Bosnian war — more than 30 years ago. Ethnic divisions, a complex administration and European integration all shape the country's political reality.

To call Bosnia-Herzegovina a complicated country is an understatement. The country in the Balkan Peninsula divides its economic, administrative and political responsibilities between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and two semi-autonomous entities that, for the most part, operate independently — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.

Both semi-autonomous entities are further split into several cantons and communities, home to mostly Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in the central-western federation and Bosnian Serbs in Republika Srpska, to the north and east.

This principle of ethnic nationalism is key to the country's central constitutional and political organization. The Bosnian constitution recognizes Bosniaks, who are predominantly Muslim, the largely Orthodox Bosnian Serbs and primarily Catholic Bosnian Croats as "constituent peoples" with equal rights.

Today, the country has a population of around 3.1 million people. Around half are Bosniaks, while 31% are Serb and 15% are Croat. The rest of the inhabitants belong either to one of the 17 officially recognized minorities, like the Roma and Jews, or chose not to identify with any ethnicity at the last official census. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all recognized as official languages.

The central government is led by rotating three-way presidency, made up of one representative from each of the three main constituent groups. The upper house of parliament and key government offices are also divided according to this principle.

This strict balance between the three groups is always maintained, both politically and socially, often leading to ethnic interests and political gridlock dominating the decision-making process.

Dayton Peace Accords brought an end to war

This complex, convoluted and oft dysfunctional structure was set up during the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, and then anchored in the constitution. It was intended to bring an end to the Bosnian war — sparked by the breakup of Yugoslavia in the early 1990s — and legally secure the balance of power between the three feuding ethnic groups.

During the war, from 1992 to 1995, the armed forces of the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats initially fought each other, before all three groups began to clash. Later, the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats joined forces to take on Republika Srpska. Throughout the war, neighboring Serbia and Croatia were actively involved in the fighting.

Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The fighting devastated wide swaths of the country, and resulted in countless war crimes — among them the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide, in which thousands of Bosniaks were killed at the hands of Serb forces.

By the end of the war, some 100,000 people had been killed. A further 2.2 million were displaced by so-called "ethnic cleansing," forced from their homes by expulsions and violence to flee to other communities or abroad.

The fighting only ended after the international community, especially the United States, stepped up its involvement, culminating in the peace deal agreed at a military base near Dayton, Ohio in November 1995.

International oversight — essential, or no longer relevant?

Although Bosnia-Herzegovina has been recognized on the international stage since the signing of the Dayton agreement, and is also represented at the United Nations, the country itself is still, in effect, only partially independent.

The Office of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international institution responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement, has been in place since a UN Security Council resolution in 1995.

The high representative — Christian Schmidt of Germany until this past June, and currently filled by acting head Louis J. Crishock of the US — has sweeping powers. He can dismiss elected officials, pass laws, establish new government agencies and overrule all the country's democratic institutions.

The Dayton Peace Agreement 30 years on To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This authority is often referred to as the Bonn Powers, as they were negotiated during a meeting of the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn, Germany in December 1997. From 2002 to 2011, the high representative also acted as the EU special representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In recent years, there's been much discussion over whether the office is still relevant. Supporters have said the high representative remains a necessary guarantor of the country's unity and functionality. But critics have pointed out the negative impact on Bosnia-Herzegovina's democratic culture, turning the country into a de facto protectorate that, to an extent, frees local politicians of responsibility for their actions.

Separatist ambitions surface once more

The sharpest criticism has come from the Republika Srpska and Milorad Dodik, its most influential leader. Dodik, in office as prime minister and president of the Serb entity until 2025, views the office and the international backing it provides for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as an obstacle to his separatist ambitions.

With strong support from the Serbian capital, Belgrade, Moscow — and, increasingly, the Trump administration — Dodik has flirted with several different scenarios to split his Republika Srpska from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his interpretation, and that of Republika Srpska's political elite, Bosnia-Herzegovina is highly centralized and unitary, which undermines the independence and sovereignty of the Bosnian Serbs.

Milorad Dodik (right, seen here meeting with Vladimir Putin in April 2025), continues to foster a close relationship with Russia Image: press service of kremlin.ru

A similar sentiment prevails among the political representatives of Bosnia's Croats. Although they aren't considering separation, they are trying to squeeze more independence from the central government in Sarajevo — not least with the creation of a third, Croatian, entity. The plan, incidentally, also has the support of the government in neighboring EU member Croatia.

EU support aims to 'foster regional integration'

A potential path out of the current economic and political paralysis is rapprochement with the European Union — the "European perspective," as it's called in Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially supported by all the relevant political actors.

Bosnia-Herzegovina formally submitted its application for EU membership in 2016, and the European Council gave the green light for negotiations to begin in early 2024. But the actual start of membership talks hinges on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, notably in the areas of rule of law, fighting corruption, the prosecution of organized crime and the functionality of state institutions.

EU enlargement: Who's slowing? Who's advancing? Who's next? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU has been financially supporting Bosnia-Herzegovina since 2007 in the framework of pre-accession assistance, and the country is also expected to benefit from the European Commission's Economic and Investment Plan for the Western Balkans. The plan aims to "foster regional integration" — and as a result, infrastructure funding for the Republika Srpska has been partially suspended due to its ongoing separatist rhetoric and policies.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Latvia votes in parliamentary election amid rising costs
World.content:
Around 1.5 million Latvians are eligible to vote in an election which has been dominated by national security concerns and rising living costs. Four Eurofighter jets are on NATO deployment over Latvia during the poll.

Polls opened in Latvia on Saturday with some 1.5 million people eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The election, which sees 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, has been dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Latvia's current prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, has only been in office since May after the previous government collapsed over a dispute about Ukrainian drones.

His center-right, conservative United List alliance was leading in the polls ahead of the vote – but his coalition is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia fears To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.

Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.

Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.

Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.

Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace

Nevertheless, no parties are proposing any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.

Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets have been deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

Once ballots are counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.

Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.

World.title: German reunification: How inequality is shaping a new East German identity
World.content:
German reunification may be 36 years in the past, but when it comes to wealth, the divide between East and West Germany is far from history. East Germans still earn less on average, receive smaller pensions and own less property, according to Elisabeth Kaiser, the Federal Government Commissioner for Eastern Germany.

Kaiser, born in the state of Thuringia in the socialist German Democratic Republic (GDR) in 1987, has put the enduring wealth gap at the center of the debate. A study she presented in Berlin points to decades in which private entrepreneurship and opportunities to invest in one's financial future were restricted in the East. That meant, Kaiser said, that "families have not been able to acquire or pass on as much wealth." The consequences, she argues, have had a profound impact upward mobility.

How important are personal connections and social background?

But it is not only East Germans who see fewer chances of upward mobility these days. Kaiser pointed to the latest "Deutschland-Monitor ," an annual survey she commissioned to make her point. Although this year's survey is still being analyzed, early findings reveal that about two-thirds of respondents across the country believe that financial and social mobility depend crucially on wealth, personal connections and social background.

This perception is reflected in the numbers. Even though the percentage of East German executives in the highest federal agencies has risen from 13.9% in 2022 to 16.3% today, Kaiser says, "The further up the management ladder you go, the lower the percentage of East Germans you find."

How much did the German reunification cost? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

East German leaders remain scarce across the board

Based on these findings, the Commissioner for Eastern Germany calls for greater equality in decision-making. "And that is why I would like to see East Germans sitting at the table wherever decisions are made in the country," she said, "in the ministries, in government agencies, in business, academia, the judiciary, culture and the media."

With just under 20%, East Germans are significantly underrepresented in all sectors relative to their share of the population. To back this up, Kaiser cited the "Elitenmonitor ," another study commissioned by her office. With over 3,000 top positions examined across twelve sectors over a long period of time, the Elitenmonitor study, conducted by the universities of Jena (Thuringia), Leipzig (Saxony), and Zittau/Görlitz (Saxony), can offer more than just a snapshot.

According to the report, the percentage of East Germans in leadership positions in both the public and private sectors only increased from 10.9% to 12.1% from 2018 to 2024. And in the business and cultural sectors, the percentage of East Germans has actually declined.

Most striking of all is that among the 100 largest German companies, all executives are from West Germany — and the same holds true for the military. East Germans are also severely underrepresented in top positions in the judiciary and the media.

Fact check: Fake campaign about alleged division of Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New stereotypes about East Germany

The insufficient representation of East German perspectives in nearly all areas of society also appears to have consequences for how East Germans are viewed. Kaiser says that her generation, born around the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, did not feel East German for a long time. It was only in school and during vocational training that she realized there were differences between East and West that would sometimes put her at a disadvantage.

This has also shaped stereotypes about East Germany, both past and present. "An East German identity is also being created politically to some extent because people are looking for some way to orient themselves, because they're looking for a common bond," Kaiser knows from her many experiences and conversations.

As an example, she cited the symbolic power of the Simson moped, produced in the millions during the GDR era — a symbol of mobility and freedom for many young people at that time.

Leading representatives of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party classified in part as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency, frequently make public appearances riding on Simson mopeds. One of them is Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD candidate who recently won state elections in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Without specifically mentioning the AfD by name, Kaiser lamented the exploitation of cultural symbols for political purposes."It creates a very powerful emotional connection," said Kaiser regarding the use of the Simson brand.

Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As for the AfD and its recent electoral successes in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, Kaiser said that these elections send a dangerous signal. She believes that international investors and skilled workers will ask themselves: Should I go there or not?

Kaiser specifically mentioned sectors that have played an important role as drivers of economic growth and innovation in eastern Germany, such as the semiconductor industry, battery cell research, healthcare, biotechnology and renewable energy. Her concern is that the economic upswing in these sectors could suffer as a result.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured
World.content:
The driver has been identified as an 18-year-old man who is said to have been "revving" when he lost control of his car.

A car drove into a crowd of rugby league supporters in the eastern Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday after its driver appeared to lose control, leaving at least 10 people injured, authorities said.

Several children were reported to be among the wounded.

Two of the injured were in a critical condition, including a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, New South Wales officials said.

What do we know about the car crash in Australia?

The incident occurred in Newcastle's Wallsend ‌suburb, situated some 110 kilometers (68 miles) north of Sydney.

Fans had gathered on the streets to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team who were leaving for the National Rugby League grand final against the Sydney Roosters, slated to be held in ​Sydney on Sunday.

Local reports cited the police as identifying the driver as an 18-year-old man, who was arrested and taken to the hospital for mandatory testing.

Driver 'lost control'

Newcastle Mayor Gavin Morris said in televised remarks that the driver was a rugby fan and that he lost control of his vehicle.

"He was revving the car, he was excited, he was a supporter, he was there for the joy of the moment," Morris told Australian broadcaster ABC.

"Somehow he lost control of the car ... and he's gone into the crowd."

Police said they were probing the incident and initial inquiries indicated it was not terrorism-related.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the incident was "horrible."

"Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans," he said in a statement on X.
